title: Japanese: Hiragana and Katakana
description: Read and write Japanese's two syllabaries from scratch: all 46 hiragana and 46 katakana, their voiced forms, combinations, small っ and long vowels, the sounds used in loanwords, the particles は, へ and を, punctuation and vertical text, and your first words and greetings. Every kana is traced stroke by stroke, heard with your device's Japanese voice and drilled with typed review cards, and every word shows its pitch accent. This course comes before Japanese N5.
author: Erudior
changelog: Pitch accent on every word; pitch marks in the greetings lesson.

lessons.title: How Japanese is written; あいうえお
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japanese looks hard to read at first because a single sentence can mix three different sets of
characters. The good news is that two of them, hiragana and katakana, are small, regular and
completely learnable in a few weeks. This course teaches both, one row at a time, so that by the
end you can read and write anything in kana and you're ready for real vocabulary and grammar in
Japanese N5.

This first lesson explains how the writing system fits together, what a "beat" is, how the five
Japanese vowels sound, and how to write the first five hiragana: あ い う え お. Say every
example out loud. You'll learn the sounds with your mouth and the shapes with your hand, not
only with your eyes.

## Three scripts and romaji

Japanese is written with three scripts, used side by side:

| Script | What it looks like | What it's used for |
|---|---|---|
| **[[hiragana]]** | rounded, flowing: あ か さ | grammar endings, small words, words without a common kanji, and anything written for children or learners |
| **[[katakana]]** | straight and angular: ア カ サ | words borrowed from other languages, foreign names, sound effects, emphasis |
| **[[kanji]]** | complex characters from Chinese: {山|やま} {水|みず} {木|き} | the core of most nouns, verbs and adjectives; each kanji carries a meaning |

Hiragana and katakana are both **[[kana]]**: each character stands for a sound, not a meaning. The
two sets spell exactly the same sounds, a little like capital and small letters in English,
but they are used for different jobs.

There is also **[[romaji]]**, Japanese written in the Latin alphabet: *sushi*, *Tōkyō*, *arigatō*.
Japanese people use romaji for things like station signs for visitors and typing on a computer,
but nobody reads ordinary Japanese in romaji. In this course romaji is a crutch: you'll see it
next to every word for the first seven lessons, and then less and less.

Here is a normal Japanese sentence. The small kana above the kanji are **[[furigana]]**, a reading
aid printed over kanji that a reader might not know:

> {毎朝|まいあさ}コーヒーを{飲|の}みます。 — I drink coffee every morning.

Taken apart:

| Part | Script | Reading | Job in the sentence |
|---|---|---|---|
| {毎朝|まいあさ} | kanji | maiasa | "every morning": a word with a meaning, written with kanji |
| コーヒー | katakana | kōhī | "coffee": a word borrowed from English |
| を | hiragana | o | a small grammar word that marks what you drink |
| {飲|の} | kanji | no- | the meaning part of the verb "drink" |
| みます | hiragana | -mimasu | the verb ending: polite, present tense |

Notice that there are no spaces between words in real Japanese. The change from one script to
another helps the eye find where words begin and end. In this course we write only kana, and
in phrases and sentences we add a space after each word or small grammar word to make reading
easier for beginners (lesson 13 explains this).

## Kana are beats

English speakers think in letters and syllables. Japanese speakers think in beats. Each beat is
called a **[[mora]]** (plural *morae*), and each ordinary kana is one mora. Every mora takes roughly
the same amount of time to say, like notes of equal length in music.

- あさ (asa) — morning: two kana, two beats: あ・さ.
- いいえ (iie) — no: three kana, three beats: い・い・え. The two い are not a single "ee";
  the sound is held for two beats.
- にほん (nihon) — Japan: three beats: に・ほ・ん. The final ん is a beat of its own, even
  though in English we'd call *ni-hon* two syllables.

Keep this idea in mind: getting the number of beats right is one of the most important parts of
sounding Japanese, and lesson 7 comes back to it.

Japanese also has no strong stress like English *PHO-to-graph* or *pho-TO-gra-phy*. Words use a
pattern of higher and lower pitch instead, which you'll pick up by listening. For now, give every
beat the same length and the same weight.

## The five vowels

Japanese has only five vowels, and each one always sounds the same. They are short, clean and
steady: the mouth stays still from the start of the vowel to the end.

| Kana | Romaji | Sounds like | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| あ | a | the *a* in *father*, but short | あさ (asa) — morning |
| い | i | the *ee* in *see*, but short | いえ (ie) — house |
| う | u | the *oo* in *food*, short, with the lips relaxed, not pushed forward | うみ (umi) — sea |
| え | e | the *e* in *bed* | えき (eki) — station |
| お | o | the *o* in *for*, without the *r* | おなか (onaka) — stomach |

The usual order is あ い う え お (a, i, u, e, o), not English a, e, i, o, u. Learn this order
now: the whole kana table, and every Japanese dictionary, follows it.

Three things English speakers need to watch:

- う is unrounded. For English *oo* we push the lips forward into a circle. For う keep the
  lips flat and relaxed, almost as for い, and pull the tongue back. It sounds lighter than
  English *oo*.
- え and お don't glide. English *say* slides from *e* towards *ee* (*say-ee*), and *go*
  slides towards *oo* (*go-oo*). Japanese え and お stay pure all the way through. Say *bed*
  without the *b* and *d*: that's え.
- Short means short. Don't stretch a vowel unless it's written twice. えき is "eh-kee",
  quick, not "ay-keee".

## Words made only of vowels

With just these five kana you can already read some real words:

| Word | Romaji | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| あい | ai | love |
| あお | ao | blue |
| いえ | ie | house |
| うえ | ue | above, on top |
| いいえ | iie | no |
| あう | au | to meet |

Each vowel is said clearly, one after the other: あい is "a-i" in two beats, close to English
*eye* but with both parts given equal time.

```speak
あい
= ai — love
あお
= ao — blue
いえ
= ie — house
うえ
= ue — above, on top
いいえ
= iie — no
```

## Which way Japanese is written

Japanese can be written in two directions:

- horizontally, left to right, top to bottom, like English: this is normal in textbooks,
  on websites, phones and most signs;
- vertically, top to bottom, with the columns going from right to left: this is normal in
  novels, newspapers and some signs and manga.

The kana themselves don't change shape. This course uses horizontal writing; lesson 14 shows how
vertical text works.

## Stroke order and the practice square

Every kana has a fixed **[[stroke order]]**: the strokes are written in a set order and a set
direction. This matters for three reasons. The shape comes out balanced; your handwriting is
easy for Japanese people (and phones that read handwriting) to recognize; and you'll be able to
read other people's quick, joined-up handwriting, which follows the stroke order.

A few general rules hold for most kana:

- top before bottom, left before right;
- horizontal strokes usually go left to right, vertical ones top to bottom;
- a short mark or dot is often written last.

Japanese children practise in a square box divided by a dashed cross. Every kana fills the same
size square, centred in it. English letters vary in height (*h* is tall, *g* hangs down); kana
don't. The tracing pads in this course use the same square.

| Kana | Strokes | How it's written |
|---|---|---|
| あ | 3 | a short horizontal; a vertical that crosses it, bending slightly; then one long stroke that slants down, crosses the vertical, loops back up and sweeps round to the right |
| い | 2 | a longer left stroke with a small hook up at the bottom; a shorter right stroke |
| う | 2 | a short dash at the top; then a stroke that goes right, curves down and swings back to the left |
| え | 2 | a short dash at the top; then a zigzag: across, down to the left, back up a little, and out to the right along the bottom in a small wave |
| お | 3 | a horizontal; a vertical that crosses it, makes a small loop at the bottom left and swings round to the right; then a small dash at the top right |

```trace
あいうえお
```

## Lookalikes: あ and お

あ and お are the first pair learners mix up. Both have a crossed stroke at the top left and a
big curve. The differences:

- お has a small separate dash at the top right; あ has none;
- in あ the long curve is a separate third stroke; in お the vertical itself loops and swings
  round.

A memory hook: the dash at the top right of お is a little flag, and お ("oh!") is waving
it. あ has no flag. Make up your own hooks too, as long as they point at a real difference in
the shape.

## How typing works in this app

You don't need a Japanese keyboard. Wherever this course asks you to type Japanese, type romaji
and the app turns it into kana as you go: *a* becomes あ, *ie* becomes いえ, *iie* becomes
いいえ. You'll see the kana appear in the box. Later lessons show the few combinations that
need special keys (lesson 5 for ん, lesson 7 for small kana), and module 2 shows that capital
letters give katakana. If your device has its own Japanese keyboard, that works too.

Because the app writes the kana for you, a typing question can't test whether you know the
shape of a single kana. That's what the tracing pads and the reading questions are for. Typing
practises spelling words correctly.

## Common mistakes

- Reading Japanese vowels the English way: *e* as "ee", *i* as "eye". In Japanese, e is always
  the *e* of *bed*, and i is always the *ee* of *see*.
- Rounding う and pushing the lips forward. Keep them relaxed.
- Gliding え into "ay-ee" and お into "oh-oo". Hold the vowel still.
- Saying いいえ as two beats ("ee-ay"). It has three: い・い・え.
- Mixing up あ and お. Look for the separate dash at the top right of お.
- Ignoring stroke order because the result "looks right". It won't look right for long, and you
  won't be able to read handwriting.

## Key points

- Japanese uses hiragana, katakana and kanji together; romaji is Japanese in Latin letters, a
  learner's aid.
- Each kana stands for one beat (mora), and beats are all about the same length.
- The five vowels, in order: あ a, い i, う u, え e, お o. Short, pure, no glides; う with
  relaxed lips.
- Japanese is written left to right in rows, or top to bottom in columns from right to left.
- Learn each kana with its stroke order, centred in a square.
- In this app, type romaji and it becomes kana.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The か and さ rows
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 1 you learned the five vowels, あ い う え お. Now you add consonants. The pattern
is simple and it holds for almost the whole table: take a consonant and put each of the five
vowels after it. With k you get か き く け こ (ka ki ku ke ko); with s you get さ し す せ そ
(sa shi su se so). Ten new kana, and with them dozens of real words: かさ (kasa, umbrella), すし
(sushi), ここ (koko, here).

This lesson also introduces the **[[gojūon]]**, the table that orders all the kana. Once you see how
it works, the rest of the course is a matter of filling it in.

## The gojūon table

*Gojūon* means "fifty sounds". It's a grid with the five vowels across and the consonants down.
Each line across is called a row and is named after its first kana: the あ row, the か row, the
さ row. Each line down follows one vowel: the "a" column, the "i" column and so on.

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (vowels) | あ a | い i | う u | え e | お o |
| k | か ka | き ki | く ku | け ke | こ ko |
| s | さ sa | し shi | す su | せ se | そ so |

The order of the rows is fixed: あ, か, さ, た, な, は, ま, や, ら, わ. Dictionaries, phone
contact lists and class registers in Japan are sorted in this order, the way English lists use
a to z. A handy way to remember the row order is to say the first sounds as a chant: "a, ka, sa,
ta, na, ha, ma, ya, ra, wa". The next three lessons add the rows in exactly this order.

Despite the name, the modern table has 46 basic kana, not fifty: some places in the grid are
empty, as you'll see in lesson 5.

## The か row: ka ki ku ke ko

The k is the same as English k, but with less puff of air after it. Hold your hand in front of
your mouth and say English *key*: you feel a puff. Japanese き has a lighter one.

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| か | ka | 3 | かさ (kasa) — umbrella |
| き | ki | 4 | きく (kiku) — to listen, to hear |
| く | ku | 1 | くさ (kusa) — grass |
| け | ke | 3 | けさ (kesa) — this morning |
| こ | ko | 2 | ここ (koko) — here |

How they're written:

- か: first a horizontal that turns down and hooks to the left at the bottom; then a stroke
  that comes down from above, slanting left, across the first; last a short dash on the right.
- き: two horizontals, top to bottom; then a long stroke from the top slanting down to the
  right through both; last a separate curve at the bottom, opening to the right.
- く: a single stroke, like a "less than" sign: down to the left, then down to the right.
- け: a vertical on the left; then a horizontal on the right; then a long vertical through the
  horizontal, curving slightly left at the end.
- こ: a short upper stroke with a small hook at its right end; then a longer lower stroke that
  curves up at the left end and runs right.

More words with these kana and the vowels: あか (aka) — red, あき (aki) — autumn, いけ (ike) —
pond, かお (kao) — face, こえ (koe) — voice, かく (kaku) — to write.

```trace
かきくけこ
```

## The さ row: sa shi su se so

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| さ | sa | 3 | さか (saka) — slope, hill |
| し | shi | 1 | しお (shio) — salt |
| す | su | 2 | すし (sushi) — sushi |
| せ | se | 3 | せかい (sekai) — world |
| そ | so | 1 | そこ (soko) — there (near you) |

The one surprise is し. It isn't "si" but shi, like English *she*, said short. Japanese has
no "si" sound in native words: before い, the s turns into sh. That's why the word is *sushi*,
not "susi". Some romaji systems write し as *si*; in this app you can type either *shi* or
*si*.

How they're written:

- さ: a horizontal; then a stroke from above slanting down to the right through it; last a
  separate curve at the bottom, opening to the right. It looks like き with one horizontal
  fewer.
- し: one stroke straight down, curving round to the right and up at the bottom, like a
  fish-hook.
- す: a long horizontal; then a vertical through its middle that makes a loop below the line
  and ends with a tail down to the left.
- せ: a long horizontal; then a short vertical on the right, crossing the horizontal, with a
  small hook at its foot; then a vertical on the left that crosses the horizontal, goes down and
  turns right along the bottom.
- そ: in its standard school form, one stroke: a small zigzag at the top, then a long line
  across and a wide curve opening to the right at the bottom. Some fonts and handwriting break
  the top into a separate piece; both are correct.

More words: あし (ashi) — leg, foot, いす (isu) — chair, うそ (uso) — a lie, すいか (suika) —
watermelon, おかし (okashi) — sweets, snacks, せき (seki) — seat.

```trace
さしすせそ
```

## Lookalikes

### き and さ

The pair everyone confuses. Both have a slanting stroke and a curve at the bottom.
Count the horizontals: き has two, さ has one.

In many printed fonts the bottom curve of き and さ joins the stroke above it, so the printed き
looks like three strokes and the printed さ like two. When you write by hand, keep the curve
separate: き has 4 strokes and さ has 3.

### こ and い

Both are two short strokes. In こ they lie flat, one above the other; in い they
stand up, one beside the other.

### け and は

け has a vertical on the left with a cross and a long vertical on the right. In
lesson 4 you'll meet は, which starts the same way but has a loop at the bottom right. Look at
the end of the right-hand stroke: straight in け, looped in は.

## Pronunciation

- し is always "shi". Never read it as English "sigh" or "see".
- す often has a very weak, almost whispered う, especially at the end of a word. In the
  polite endings *-desu* and *-masu* (which you'll meet later), most speakers say "dess" and
  "mass". In すし you can hear it too: "s'shi".
- き and し often sound almost whispered when they come between k, s, t or h sounds. Listen in
  あした (ashita) — tomorrow (from lesson 3). You don't need to copy this deliberately yet; just
  don't be surprised when you hear it.
- こ and そ use the pure o of lesson 1: no "oh-oo" glide. ここ is "ko-ko", two short beats.

```speak
かさ
= kasa — umbrella
すし
= sushi — sushi
ここ
= koko — here
あき
= aki — autumn
せかい
= sekai — world
```

## Common mistakes

- Writing or typing "si" and reading し as "see". It's *shi*.
- Mixing up き and さ: count the horizontals (2 for き, 1 for さ).
- Joining the bottom curve of き or さ to the stroke above it because a font does. In
  handwriting, keep it separate.
- Reading こ as English "co" in *cola* with an "oh-oo" glide. Keep it short and pure.
- Saying くさ (kusa, grass) with a rounded English "oo". Remember the flat, relaxed う.
- Reading the gojūon in English vowel order (a, e, i, o, u). It's a, i, u, e, o.

## Key points

- Each row of the gojūon is one consonant plus the five vowels, in the order a, i, u, e, o.
- The row order is あ, か, さ, た, な, は, ま, や, ら, わ.
- か row: か ka, き ki, く ku, け ke, こ ko.
- さ row: さ sa, し shi, す su, せ se, そ so.
- き has two horizontals, さ has one; in handwriting the bottom curve is a separate stroke.
- The u in す is often very weak.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The た and な rows
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now know 15 kana: the vowels and the か and さ rows. This lesson adds the next two rows of
the gojūon, た and な, which brings you to 25, more than half of the basic hiragana. The た row
has two sounds that English speakers need to practise, ち (chi) and つ (tsu); the な row is
completely regular. With these rows you can read everyday words like ねこ (neko, cat), なつ
(natsu, summer) and あなた (anata, you).

## The た row: ta chi tsu te to

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| た | ta | 4 | たこ (tako) — octopus |
| ち | chi | 2 | ちいさい (chiisai) — small |
| つ | tsu | 1 | つくえ (tsukue) — desk |
| て | te | 1 | ていねい (teinei) — polite, careful |
| と | to | 2 | とけい (tokei) — clock, watch |

Just as し broke the pattern of the さ row, two kana break the pattern here:

- ち is chi, like *chee* in *cheese*, said short. Japanese has no native "ti": before い,
  t turns into ch.
- つ is tsu. Before う, t turns into ts. There's no native "tu".

Romaji systems that write them *ti* and *tu* exist, and in this app you can type *ti* or *chi*,
*tu* or *tsu*. When you read, though, always say chi and tsu.

### Practising tsu

English has the ts sound, just never at the start of a word. Say *cats*, then *cats-oo*, then
drop the *ca*: *ts-oo*. Keep the tongue tip touching just behind the top teeth for the t, then
let the air hiss out as s. Don't turn it into "soo" (that's す) or "too" (that's not in the kana
table at all). Try these: つき (tsuki) — moon, くつ (kutsu) — shoes, なつ (natsu) — summer.

The rest of the row is straightforward: t as in English but a little softer, with the tongue
touching the back of the top teeth: た ta, て te, と to.

### How they're written

- た: a horizontal; a stroke from above slanting down to the left through it; then, on the
  right, a short upper stroke and a longer lower stroke, like a small こ.
- ち: a horizontal; then a stroke from above that slants down to the left through it, turns
  and swells out into a big curve to the right, ending open to the left.
- つ: one stroke: across to the right, then curving down and back to the left.
- て: one stroke: across to the right, then back down to the left in a curve, like a
  hook hanging from a rail.
- と: a short slanting stroke at the top; then a curve that starts above, comes down to the
  left and runs out to the right along the bottom.

```trace
たちつてと
```

## The な row: na ni nu ne no

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| な | na | 4 | なつ (natsu) — summer |
| に | ni | 3 | にく (niku) — meat |
| ぬ | nu | 2 | いぬ (inu) — dog |
| ね | ne | 2 | ねこ (neko) — cat |
| の | no | 1 | きのこ (kinoko) — mushroom |

Every kana in this row is just n plus the vowel, as in English *net* or *not*.

### How they're written

- な: a horizontal; a slanting stroke down to the left through it; a short dash at the upper
  right; last a vertical on the right that makes a loop at the bottom and ends going right.
- に: a vertical on the left, with a small hook up at the bottom; then a short upper stroke on
  the right; then a lower stroke on the right. The right side looks like a small こ.
- ぬ: a short stroke slanting down to the right; then one long stroke that starts at the top,
  comes down to the left, swings back up and around to the right, down again and ends in a small
  loop at the bottom right.
- ね: a vertical; then one long stroke that crosses it near the top, zigzags down and round to
  the right, and ends in a small loop at the bottom right.
- の: one stroke: from the middle of the top slanting down to the left, then up and round
  to the right in a big clockwise curve that ends open at the bottom right.

More words: あなた (anata) — you, なに (nani) — what, なか (naka) — inside, にし (nishi) — west,
ぬの (nuno) — cloth, かね (kane) — money (usually said politely as おかね, okane; かね can also mean a bell), この (kono) — this (before a noun).

```trace
なにぬねの
```

## Lookalikes

### ぬ and め

ぬ and め share most of their shape: a short slanting stroke and a long stroke that crosses it
and curves round. The difference is the end: ぬ finishes with a small loop at the bottom right,
め doesn't. You'll learn め in the next lesson; for now, remember that the loop belongs to ぬ.

### ね, れ and わ

These three start the same way, with a vertical crossed by a zigzag, and differ only at the
bottom right:

- ね ends in a small loop (like ぬ, its row-mate);
- れ ends with a tail that kicks out to the right;
- わ ends by curving round and in, without a loop.

You meet れ and わ in lesson 5. Learn ね's loop now and the other two will be easy to tell apart.

### ち and さ

ち looks like さ seen in a mirror. In さ the curve at the bottom is a separate stroke opening to
the right; in ち the long stroke itself bulges out to the right, opening to the left. Say
"ち bulges like a chin" if a hook helps.

### た and な

Both have a horizontal, a slant and something on the right. た has two small horizontals on the
right (a little こ); な has a dot and a looped vertical.

## Pronunciation

- ちいさい (chiisai): four beats, ち・い・さ・い. The い after ち holds the sound for an extra
  beat: "chee-ee-sai".
- ていねい (teinei): four beats. In everyday speech えい sounds like a long e (ええ), so this word
  is close to "teh-neh" with each e held for two beats (tē-nē). Lesson 7 explains why.
- The i of し and ち and the u of つ are often whispered before k, s, t or h sounds: した
  (shita) — under, ちかい (chikai) — near, つくえ (tsukue) — desk.
- Practise ち and つ side by side: くち (kuchi) — mouth, くつ (kutsu) — shoes.

```speak
ねこ
= neko — cat
いぬ
= inu — dog
なつ
= natsu — summer
つくえ
= tsukue — desk
ちいさい
= chiisai — small
```

## Common mistakes

- Reading ち as "ti" or つ as "tu". They are always chi and tsu.
- Saying つ as "soo" or "too". Start with the t of *cats*.
- Mixing up ぬ and め, or ね and れ: look at the bottom right for the loop.
- Writing さ when you mean ち (or the reverse): the curve faces the other way.
- Counting ちいさい as three beats ("chee-sai"). It has four.
- Writing the loop of な or ぬ as a separate stroke. The loop is part of the last stroke.

## Key points

- た row: た ta, ち chi, つ tsu, て te, と to.
- な row: な na, に ni, ぬ nu, ね ne, の no.
- ち is chi and つ is tsu; you can type chi/ti and tsu/tu, but say chi and tsu.
- ぬ and ね end in a loop; め (next lesson) and れ, わ (lesson 5) don't.
- ち and さ are mirror images: ち's curve bulges right and opens left; さ's separate curve opens right.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The は and ま rows
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Two more rows of the gojūon: は (ha hi fu he ho) and ま (ma mi mu me mo). After this lesson you
know 35 of the 46 basic hiragana, and you can read words such as なまえ (namae, name), はな
(hana, flower) and さむい (samui, cold). The は row has one irregular sound, ふ (fu), and two
kana with a second job as grammar words, は and へ. The ま row is completely regular but
includes some of the most easily confused shapes in hiragana.

## The は row: ha hi fu he ho

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| は | ha | 3 | はな (hana) — flower |
| ひ | hi | 1 | ひと (hito) — person |
| ふ | fu | 4 | ふね (fune) — boat, ship |
| へ | he | 1 | へそ (heso) — belly button |
| ほ | ho | 4 | ほし (hoshi) — star |

### The sounds

- は, へ, ほ: an ordinary English h, as in *hat*, *head*, *hot*.
- ひ: an h said with the middle of the tongue raised close to the roof of the mouth, so the air
  hisses a little. English *huge* starts with a similar sound. It's softer than "she" and
  breathier than "he".
- ふ: neither English f nor English h. Bring your lips close together, flat, without letting
  the top teeth touch the lower lip, and blow gently, as if cooling a spoonful of soup. Then
  add a relaxed う. Romaji writes it *fu*, and in this app you can type *fu* or *hu*. When
  you say ふね (fune), ふく (fuku, clothes) or ふたつ (futatsu, two things), the f should
  be light and airy, never the hard English f of *food*.

### How they're written

- は: a vertical on the left, with a small hook up at the bottom; then a short horizontal on
  the right; then a vertical through that horizontal that makes a loop at the bottom and ends
  going right.
- ひ: one stroke: a short rise, then down and round in a wide bowl, up to the right, and a
  small tail kicking down at the end.
- ふ: four separate pieces: a short curved stroke at the top; a curve in the middle that
  sweeps down and hooks back to the left; a dot on the left; a dot on the right.
- へ: one stroke: a short rise up to the right, then a long slope down to the right.
- ほ: a vertical on the left; then on the right a horizontal at the top, a second horizontal
  below it, and a vertical that comes down from the top one, through the second, and loops at
  the bottom.

```trace
はひふへほ
```

### は and へ as grammar words

Two kana in this row have a second reading. When は is used as the grammar word that marks the
topic of a sentence, it's read wa, not ha; when へ marks the direction "to", it's read
e, not he. You'll see the first in the greeting こんにちは (konnichiwa, hello), which ends
with this は. These grammar words are called particles, and lesson 13 teaches them properly.
For now, read は as ha and へ as he inside words: はな (hana), へそ (heso).

## The ま row: ma mi mu me mo

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| ま | ma | 3 | まち (machi) — town |
| み | mi | 2 | みせ (mise) — shop |
| む | mu | 3 | むし (mushi) — insect, bug |
| め | me | 2 | めいし (meishi) — business card |
| も | mo | 3 | もの (mono) — thing |

The m is the same as in English. Remember the flat, relaxed う in む: it's "moo" said short,
without pushing the lips forward.

### How they're written

- ま: two horizontals, top to bottom; then a vertical through both, starting above the top
  one, that loops at the bottom and ends going right.
- み: a stroke that runs across, slants down to the left, makes a loop and runs out to the
  right; then a short stroke that comes down through the right end.
- む: a horizontal; then a vertical through it that makes a loop at the left, runs along the
  bottom and turns up at the right; then a dot at the upper right.
- め: a short stroke slanting down to the right; then a long stroke that starts at the top,
  comes down to the left, swings up and round to the right, and ends at the bottom without a
  loop.
- も: first the vertical, which curves down and round to the right and ends turning up; then
  two horizontals through it, top to bottom. Unlike most kana, the vertical comes before the
  horizontals.

More words: まえ (mae) — front, なまえ (namae) — name, あたま (atama) — head, みみ (mimi) —
ear, むね (mune) — chest, あめ (ame) — rain, もも (momo) — peach, さむい (samui) — cold.

```trace
まみむめも
```

## Lookalikes

### は and ほ (and ま)

All three have a vertical with a loop on the right.

- は: one horizontal on the right, and the looped vertical sticks up above it.
- ほ: two horizontals on the right, and the looped vertical starts at the top one: nothing sticks
  up above it. The top horizontal is like a lid.
- ま: no vertical on the left at all; two horizontals, and the looped vertical sticks up above
  the top one.

A useful way to see it: ほ is a vertical stroke plus something like ま with its top cut off.

### ま and も

Both have two horizontals and a long vertical. In ま the vertical goes straight down and ends in
a loop; in も it curves round and turns up at the bottom like a hook, with no loop, and it's
written first.

### め and ぬ

You saw this pair in lesson 3. Now that you know め: ぬ has a loop at the bottom right, め
doesn't.

### る and ろ (coming in lesson 5)

The ら row has another loop pair: る ends in a small loop at the bottom, ろ doesn't. When you
get there, remember the rule this lesson has taught you twice: look at the end of the last
stroke.

## Pronunciation

- Don't turn ふ into English f. It's softer: lips close, no teeth on the lip.
- ひと (hito): the i is often whispered, so the word can sound like "h'to".
- めいし (meishi): えい is said like a long e (ええ) in normal speech: "mē-shi", three beats.
  Lesson 7 explains this.
- Keep む short and flat: むし (mushi) is "mu-shi", not "moo-shee".

```speak
はな
= hana — flower
ふね
= fune — boat, ship
ほし
= hoshi — star
なまえ
= namae — name
さむい
= samui — cold
```

## Common mistakes

- Saying ふ with the top teeth on the lip, like English *food*.
- Reading は as wa inside a word. はな is hana; は is wa only as a particle.
- Mixing up は, ほ and ま: count the horizontals on the right and check whether the vertical
  sticks up.
- Writing も with the horizontals first. Its curved vertical comes first.
- Giving め a loop. That's ぬ.
- Putting the dot of む on the left. It belongs at the upper right.

## Key points

- は row: は ha, ひ hi, ふ fu, へ he, ほ ho. ふ is a soft "fu" made with the lips, not the teeth.
- ま row: ま ma, み mi, む mu, め me, も mo.
- As particles, は is read wa and へ is read e (lesson 13).
- は has one horizontal on the right, ほ two with a "lid", ま no left vertical.
- も is written vertical first; め has no loop, ぬ does.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The や, ら and わ rows, を and ん
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson finishes the basic hiragana. You add the last three rows of the gojūon, や, ら and
わ, and the one kana that stands outside the grid, ん. That's eleven kana, and at the end you
can read all 46. You'll also meet the Japanese r, which is not the English r, and you'll learn
why two rows have gaps in them.

With every basic kana in hand, you can read your first short conversation, at the end of this
lesson.

## The や row: ya yu yo

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| や | ya | 3 | やま (yama) — mountain |
| ゆ | yu | 2 | ゆき (yuki) — snow |
| よ | yo | 2 | よる (yoru) — night |

The y is the English y of *yes*. Like all Japanese syllables, they're short: よ is "yo", not
"yoh-oo".

### Why the や row has only three kana

The grid has five places in each row, but Japanese has no "yi" or "ye" sound in modern
speech. Those places are empty: the sound "yi" would be heard as い anyway, and "ye" merged with え
long ago. So the や row is just や, ゆ, よ.

### How they're written

- や: a curved stroke that starts on the left, goes right and bends down; a short stroke above
  it, near the middle; then a long stroke from the top down through the first.
- ゆ: a stroke that comes down on the left, turns up and round to the right in a big curve
  back towards the middle; then a long vertical through the middle, curving to the left at the
  bottom.
- よ: a short horizontal on the right; then a vertical that comes down through it, loops at
  the bottom and ends going right.

More words: やさい (yasai) — vegetables, ゆめ (yume) — dream, よむ (yomu) — to read, ふゆ
(fuyu) — winter.

```trace
やゆよ
```

## The ら row: ra ri ru re ro

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| ら | ra | 2 | さくら (sakura) — cherry blossom |
| り | ri | 2 | りす (risu) — squirrel |
| る | ru | 1 | くるま (kuruma) — car |
| れ | re | 2 | れきし (rekishi) — history |
| ろ | ro | 1 | いろ (iro) — colour |

### The Japanese r

Romaji writes this row with r, but the sound is neither English r nor English l. It's a quick
tap: the tip of the tongue flicks once against the ridge just behind the top teeth and comes
straight off again. You already make this sound in American English: the *tt* in *better* or
*water*, said fast, is very close. Say *better*, then *be-ra*, and you have ら.

- Don't round your lips or curl your tongue back as for English r.
- Don't hold the tongue against the ridge as for English l.
- Some speakers make it sound a little like a light d or l. That's fine; a tap is what matters.

Practise: くるま (kuruma) — car, しろ (shiro) — white, くすり (kusuri) — medicine, はる
(haru) — spring, からい (karai) — spicy.

### How they're written

- ら: a short slanting stroke at the top; then a vertical that comes down, rises into a curve
  bulging to the right and ends open at the bottom left.
- り: a shorter left stroke with a small hook up at the bottom; then a longer right stroke that
  comes down and curves to the left. Some fonts join the two, but by hand り has two strokes.
- る: one stroke: across at the top, slanting down to the left, then round in a big curve to
  the right, ending in a small loop at the bottom.
- れ: a vertical; then a stroke that crosses it near the top, zigzags down and finishes with a
  tail that kicks out to the right.
- ろ: one stroke, like る but with no loop: it ends open at the bottom.

```trace
らりるれろ
```

## The わ row: wa and を

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| わ | wa | 2 | わたし (watashi) — I, me |
| を | o (typed wo) | 3 | ほんを よむ (hon o yomu) — to read a book |

The わ row is the most gappy of all. In modern Japanese only わ and を are left (two more old
kana, ゐ and ゑ, dropped out of use in the 20th century; the honors lesson on kana history tells
that story).

- わ is "wa", with the lips only slightly rounded.
- を is read o, exactly like お. It has one job only: it's the particle that marks the
  object of a verb, the thing being eaten, read, bought and so on. In ほんを よむ (hon o
  yomu, to read a book), を tells you that ほん (book) is what is read. You'll never see を
  inside an ordinary word; words with an o sound use お: おかし, おなか. To type を, use *wo*.

How they're written:

- わ: a vertical; then a stroke that crosses it near the top, zigzags down and curves round
  to the right and back in, without a loop.
- を: a short horizontal; a stroke that slants down to the left and swings back up to the
  right; then a curving stroke across the lower right.

## ん: a beat of its own

| Kana | Romaji | Strokes | Word |
|---|---|---|---|
| ん | n | 1 | みかん (mikan) — mandarin orange |

ん is the only kana that's a consonant alone. It never starts a word, but it's a full beat
(mora): ほん (hon, book) has two beats, ほ・ん, and みかん (mikan) has three, み・か・ん. Give ん
the same time as any other kana.

Its sound changes with what comes after it. You don't need to think about this; your mouth does
it naturally as it gets ready for the next sound:

| Before | ん sounds like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| m, b, p | m | さんま (sanma) — Pacific saury, さんぽ (sanpo) — a walk (lesson 6) |
| k, g | ng, as in *sing* | てんき (tenki) — weather |
| t, d, n, r, ch | n, as in *ten* | みんな (minna) — everyone, はんたい (hantai) — opposite |
| a vowel, y, w, s, h, or at the end | a nasal sound in the nose, the tongue not touching | ほん (hon) — book, きんえん (kin'en) — no smoking |

The last line is where English speakers go wrong. In きんえん (kin'en, no smoking), the ん
must not join the next vowel: it's き・ん・え・ん, four beats, and not きねん (kinen,
anniversary), which has three. Romaji uses an apostrophe to show the break: *kin'en*.

How it's written: one stroke, slanting down to the left, then back up and over a small hump,
ending in a tail out to the right.

### Typing ん

- Type *nn*: *honn* → ほん, *mikann* → みかん.
- A single *n* before another consonant also gives ん: *tenki* → てんき, *minna* → みんな.
- A single *n* at the end of the box becomes ん when you press Enter.
- Before a vowel or y, type *n'* and then the vowel: *kin'en* → きんえん. If you type
  *kinen*, the app reads *ne* and you get きねん, a different word.

```trace
わをん
```

## Lookalikes

### ね, れ and わ

Lesson 3 introduced this trio. All three are a vertical crossed by a zigzag; look at the bottom
right:

- ね ends in a loop;
- れ ends with a tail kicking out;
- わ ends curving back in, no loop.

### る and ろ

Again the loop: る has one, ろ doesn't. A hook: る (ru) "rolls up" into a little loop at the
end; ろ is open.

### ゆ and よ

These don't look alike, but their sounds (yu, yo) are easy to mix up when you're reading
fast, and in lesson 7 their small forms ゅ and ょ appear in dozens of combinations. ゆ has a
vertical through the middle of a big curve; よ is a short horizontal and a looped vertical,
like ま with one horizontal.

### ら and ち

Both have a curve bulging to the right. ら has a separate short stroke at the top and no
crossing; ち has a horizontal crossed by the long stroke.

### り and い

い has a short right stroke; in り the right stroke is longer and curves down to the left.

## Dialogue: cherry blossoms

Ken and Yumi are walking past a park in spring. The spaces after some words are for you as a
beginner; real Japanese has no spaces.

```dialogue
# さくら
Ken: ねえ、 あれ なに？
= Nē, are nani? — Hey, what's that?
Yumi: さくら。 きれいね。
= Sakura. Kirei ne. — Cherry blossoms. Pretty, aren't they?
Ken: うん、 きれい。 あした、 はなみ しない？
= Un, kirei. Ashita, hanami shinai? — Yeah, beautiful. Shall we go and look at the blossoms tomorrow?
Yumi: いいね！ みんなと しよう。
= Ii ne! Minna to shiyō. — Sounds good! Let's go with everyone.
Ken: うん。 あしたの あさ、 ここで まってるね。
= Un. Ashita no asa, koko de matteru ne. — OK. I'll wait here tomorrow morning.
```

Notes:

- はなみ (hanami) is "flower viewing": going to look at the cherry blossoms, often with a picnic.
- ね at the end of a sentence asks for agreement, a little like "isn't it?" or "OK?".
- In しよう (shiyō, let's do it) the よ is full size: し・よ・う, three beats. Lesson 7 shows how a
  small ょ changes this.
- と, の and に are particles (small grammar words): "with", "of" and "at". You'll learn them
  properly in later courses.

## Pronunciation

- Tap every r: さくら, くるま, いろ. No English r.
- Give ん a full beat: みかん is three beats, not "mee-kahn" in two.
- を sounds exactly like お. Don't say "wo".
- Keep わ and よ short: no "wah-ah" or "yoh-oo".

```speak
さくら
= sakura — cherry blossom
くるま
= kuruma — car
わたし
= watashi — I, me
みかん
= mikan — mandarin orange
きんえん
= kin'en — no smoking
```

## Common mistakes

- Saying ら row kana with an English r or l. Use a quick tap.
- Reading を as "wo". It's o.
- Writing を inside words (をかし). Words use お; を is only the particle.
- Dropping the beat of ん, or joining it to a following vowel (きんえん is not きねん).
- Typing *kinen* for きんえん. Use *kin'en*.
- Mixing up ね, れ and わ, or る and ろ. Look at the end of the last stroke.

## Key points

- や row: や ya, ゆ yu, よ yo (no yi or ye). ら row: ら ra, り ri, る ru, れ re, ろ ro, with a
  tapped r. わ row: わ wa, を o (typed wo).
- を is used only as the object particle and is read o.
- ん is one full beat; its sound adapts to what follows. Type *nn*, but *n'* before a vowel or y.
- You now know all 46 basic hiragana.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Voiced sounds: ゛ and ゜
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You know all 46 basic hiragana. This lesson gives you 25 more almost for free: you don't learn
new shapes, only two small marks. Two short strokes, ゛, turn か into が (ga) and さ into ざ
(za). A small circle, ゜, turns は into ぱ (pa). With these marks you can write words like
ごはん (gohan, meal), でんわ (denwa, telephone) and さんぽ (sanpo, a walk), and you'll be able to
read most hiragana you see.

## Voiced and voiceless

Put two fingers on the front of your throat and say a long "sss". Nothing happens. Now say a
long "zzz": you feel a buzz. That buzz is your vocal cords vibrating, and a sound made with it
is called **[[voiced]]**. s is voiceless, z is voiced; otherwise they're made the same way. English has
several such pairs: k and g, s and z, t and d, p and b.

Japanese writing uses this directly. The mark ゛, called **[[dakuten]]**, makes a kana's consonant
voiced. Two short strokes at the top right are all it takes:

| Row | Without ゛ | With ゛ | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| か row | か き く け こ | が ぎ ぐ げ ご | k → g |
| さ row | さ し す せ そ | ざ じ ず ぜ ぞ | s → z (し → じ ji) |
| た row | た ち つ て と | だ ぢ づ で ど | t → d (ち → ぢ ji, つ → づ zu) |
| は row | は ひ ふ へ ほ | ば び ぶ べ ぼ | h → b |

The は row also takes a second mark, the small circle ゜, called **[[handakuten]]**. It gives the
p sound:

| Row | With ゜ | Change |
|---|---|---|
| は row | ぱ ぴ ぷ ぺ ぽ | h → p |

Why does h pair with b and p? Because, scholars believe, the consonant of the は row was once
close to p, and later to f; over time it softened to h, but the writing system kept the old
family together. ふ (fu), made with the lips, still shows the old link.

No other rows take these marks: な, ま, や, ら and わ consonants are already voiced.

## The 25 voiced kana

| Kana | Romaji | Word |
|---|---|---|
| が | ga | めがね (megane) — glasses |
| ぎ | gi | かぎ (kagi) — key |
| ぐ | gu | かぐ (kagu) — furniture |
| げ | ge | ひげ (hige) — beard, moustache |
| ご | go | ごはん (gohan) — cooked rice, a meal |
| ざ | za | ひざ (hiza) — knee |
| じ | ji | じかん (jikan) — time |
| ず | zu | みず (mizu) — water |
| ぜ | ze | かぜ (kaze) — wind |
| ぞ | zo | ぞう (zō) — elephant |
| だ | da | だれ (dare) — who |
| ぢ | ji | はなぢ (hanaji) — nosebleed |
| づ | zu | つづく (tsuzuku) — to continue |
| で | de | でんわ (denwa) — telephone |
| ど | do | どこ (doko) — where |
| ば | ba | ことば (kotoba) — word, language |
| び | bi | へび (hebi) — snake |
| ぶ | bu | ぶた (buta) — pig |
| べ | be | べんり (benri) — convenient |
| ぼ | bo | ぼうし (bōshi) — hat, cap |
| ぱ | pa | かんぱい (kanpai) — cheers! (a toast) |
| ぴ | pi | えんぴつ (enpitsu) — pencil |
| ぷ | pu | てんぷら (tenpura) — tempura |
| ぺ | pe | ぺらぺら (perapera) — fluent (in a language) |
| ぽ | po | さんぽ (sanpo) — a walk |

In ぞう and ぼうし the う after an o-sound makes the o long: zō, bōshi. Lesson 7 explains long
vowels. Notice that in most of these words the p comes straight after ん. Apart from loanwords and
sound words such as ぺらぺら and ぴかぴか (pikapika, sparkling), very few Japanese words start
with p.

Most of these sounds are just what the romaji suggests. A few notes:

- じ is "ji", as in *jeep*, said short, not "zi". It's the voiced partner of し (shi).
- ず is "zu"; at the start of a word many speakers say it closer to "dzu".
- In the middle of a word, some speakers, mainly older ones, say が-row kana with a soft
  "ng", like the ng of *singer* (*kagi* close to "ka-ngi", still two beats). Both ways are standard; a plain g is what you'll hear most.

## ぢ and づ: same sounds, rare letters

ぢ sounds exactly like じ (ji), and づ exactly like ず (zu). In nearly every word, you write じ
and ず. ぢ and づ appear in only two kinds of words:

- When two words join and the second one starts with ち or つ, which becomes voiced:
  はな (hana, nose) + ち (chi, blood) → はなぢ (hanaji, nosebleed); て (te, hand) + つくり
  (tsukuri, making) → てづくり (tezukuri, handmade).
- When ち or つ is repeated, the second time voiced: つづく (tsuzuku, to continue), ちぢむ
  (chijimu, to shrink).

So if you hear "ji" or "zu", write じ or ず unless you know the word is one of these. To type
them in this app: *ji* or *zi* gives じ, *zu* gives ず, *di* gives ぢ and *du* gives づ.

## When sounds join: rendaku

The はなぢ example shows something that happens all the time in Japanese: when two words join
into one, the first consonant of the second word often becomes voiced. This is called
**[[rendaku]]**.

| Parts | Joined word |
|---|---|
| ひと (hito) + ひと (hito) | ひとびと (hitobito) — people |
| はな (hana) + ひ (hi, fire) | はなび (hanabi) — fireworks |
| おり (ori, folding) + かみ (kami, paper) | おりがみ (origami) — paper folding |
| やま (yama) + さくら (sakura) | やまざくら (yamazakura) — mountain cherry |

There's no simple rule that predicts every case; you learn each word as it comes. But when you
see a voiced kana in the middle of a word, rendaku is often the reason.

## Writing the marks

Write the whole kana first, then the mark. ゛ is two short strokes at the top right, each going
down slightly to the right, left one first. ゜ is a small circle in the same place. The marks
always come last, and they belong to the kana's own square: don't let them drift into the next
one.

The pads below trace all 25. The base kana are the ones you know; concentrate on placing the
marks.

```trace
がぎぐげござじずぜぞだぢづでどばびぶべぼぱぴぷぺぽ
```

## Lookalikes

### ゛ or ゜

ば (ba) and ぱ (pa) differ only by the mark. Small print makes this harder, so look closely:
two ticks is b, a circle is p. The same goes for び/ぴ, ぶ/ぷ, べ/ぺ and ぼ/ぽ.

### ふ, ぶ and ぷ

ふ already has two dots of its own. ぶ adds the two ticks of ゛ at the top right, and ぷ adds a
circle. Count carefully: ぶ has ふ's own dots plus the two ticks at the top right.

### へ, べ and ぺ

The katakana for these (module 2) look almost the same as the hiragana. Don't worry about that
yet; in hiragana text they're always hiragana.

### Voiced or not?

Many words come in pairs that differ only by ゛, so the marks are never optional:

| Without | With |
|---|---|
| かき (kaki) — persimmon | かぎ (kagi) — key |
| てんき (tenki) — weather | でんき (denki) — electricity, light |
| ふた (futa) — lid | ぶた (buta) — pig |
| さる (saru) — monkey | ざる (zaru) — bamboo strainer |

## Dialogue: where's the key?

Ken is about to go out and can't find something.

```dialogue
# かぎ
Ken: かぎ、 どこ？
= Kagi, doko? — Where's the key?
Yumi: かばんの なか？
= Kaban no naka? — In your bag?
Ken: ない。
= Nai. — It's not there.
Yumi: つくえの うえ？
= Tsukue no ue? — On the desk?
Ken: あ、 ここに ある！ ありがとう。
= A, koko ni aru! Arigatō. — Oh, here it is! Thanks.
Yumi: どういたしまして。
= Dō itashimashite. — You're welcome.
```

Notes:

- かばん (kaban) — bag; ない (nai) — there isn't one, it's not there; ある (aru) — there is.
- In ありがとう (arigatō) and どういたしまして (dō itashimashite), the う after an o-sound
  makes it long, as in ぞう. Lesson 7 explains this.
- In everyday speech the i of し in どういたしまして is often whispered: "itashimash'te".

## Pronunciation

- Make the voiced sounds buzz: ご, ざ, だ, ば should all vibrate at the throat.
- じ is ji (*jeep*), never "zi".
- Keep p light, like k and t: little puff of air.
- Practise the pairs: かき/かぎ, てんき/でんき, ふた/ぶた.

```speak
ごはん
= gohan — cooked rice, a meal
みず
= mizu — water
でんわ
= denwa — telephone
えんぴつ
= enpitsu — pencil
さんぽ
= sanpo — a walk
```

## Common mistakes

- Leaving off ゛ or ゜ when writing. かぎ without its marks is かき, a different word.
- Confusing ゛ and ゜: ば is ba, ぱ is pa.
- Writing ぢ or づ for ordinary ji and zu sounds. Use じ and ず unless the word is one of the
  special cases (はなぢ, つづく…).
- Reading じ as "zi". It's ji.
- Writing the mark before the kana, or in the wrong place. It comes last, at the top right.

## Key points

- ゛ (dakuten) voices the consonant: k → g, s → z, t → d, h → b.
- ゜ (handakuten) on the は row gives p: ぱ ぴ ぷ ぺ ぽ.
- じ and ぢ are both ji; ず and づ are both zu. Write じ and ず except in words like はなぢ and
  つづく.
- When words join, the second often starts with a voiced sound (rendaku): はなび, ひとびと.
- Write the mark last, at the top right of the kana's square.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Combinations, small っ and long vowels
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now read every hiragana and its voiced forms. Three spelling rules remain, and with them
you can write any Japanese word in hiragana:

1. small ゃ, ゅ, ょ after a kana make one-beat combinations such as きゃ (kya) and しょ (sho);
2. a small っ makes a one-beat pause, as in きって (kitte, stamp);
3. long vowels are written with an extra kana, as in おかあさん (okāsan, mother).

All three come down to the idea from lesson 1: Japanese counts beats (morae), and the spelling
shows every beat. Get the beats right and you'll be understood; get them wrong and you may say a
different word.

## Combinations with small ゃ, ゅ, ょ

Take a kana from the "i" column (き, し, ち, に, ひ, み, り and their voiced forms) and write a
small ゃ, ゅ or ょ after it. The two kana together make one beat: the consonant, a y-glide and
the vowel. These are called **[[yōon]]**.

- き (ki) + や (ya), full size: きや (ki-ya), two beats.
- き + small ゃ: きゃ (kya), one beat.

The small kana is about half the normal size and sits in the lower left of its square (in
vertical text, the upper right). Make the size difference obvious when you write.

| | + ゃ | + ゅ | + ょ |
|---|---|---|---|
| き | きゃ kya | きゅ kyu | きょ kyo |
| し | しゃ sha | しゅ shu | しょ sho |
| ち | ちゃ cha | ちゅ chu | ちょ cho |
| に | にゃ nya | にゅ nyu | にょ nyo |
| ひ | ひゃ hya | ひゅ hyu | ひょ hyo |
| み | みゃ mya | みゅ myu | みょ myo |
| り | りゃ rya | りゅ ryu | りょ ryo |
| ぎ | ぎゃ gya | ぎゅ gyu | ぎょ gyo |
| じ | じゃ ja | じゅ ju | じょ jo |
| び | びゃ bya | びゅ byu | びょ byo |
| ぴ | ぴゃ pya | ぴゅ pyu | ぴょ pyo |

That's 33 combinations. Notice that し, ち and じ lose the y in romaji: しゃ is "sha", not
"shya", because sh, ch and j already include the glide. (ぢゃ, ぢゅ, ぢょ also exist but are
extremely rare.)

Each one in a word:

| ゃ | ゅ | ょ |
|---|---|---|
| きゃく (kyaku) — guest, customer | きゅうり (kyūri) — cucumber | きょう (kyō) — today |
| しゃしん (shashin) — photo | しゅくだい (shukudai) — homework | しょくどう (shokudō) — dining hall, canteen |
| おちゃ (ocha) — tea | ちゅうい (chūi) — caution, attention | ちょっと (chotto) — a little |
| こんにゃく (konnyaku) — konjac jelly | ぎゅうにゅう (gyūnyū) — milk | にょろにょろ (nyoronyoro) — wriggling, like a snake |
| ひゃく (hyaku) — hundred | ひゅうひゅう (hyūhyū) — whistling, of wind | ひょうじょう (hyōjō) — facial expression |
| みゃく (myaku) — pulse | ミュージック (myūjikku) — music | みょうじ (myōji) — family name |
| りゃくご (ryakugo) — abbreviation | りゅう (ryū) — dragon | りょこう (ryokō) — trip, travel |
| ぎゃく (gyaku) — the opposite | ぎゅうにく (gyūniku) — beef | ぎょうざ (gyōza) — dumplings |
| じゃんけん (janken) — rock-paper-scissors | じゅぎょう (jugyō) — class, lesson | じょうず (jōzu) — good at, skilful |
| さんびゃく (sanbyaku) — three hundred | びゅうびゅう (byūbyū) — howling, of wind | びょういん (byōin) — hospital |
| はっぴゃく (happyaku) — eight hundred | コンピューター (konpyūtā) — computer | ぴょんぴょん (pyonpyon) — hopping |

Some combinations are rare in native words. みゅ and ぴゅ appear almost only in loanwords, which
are written in katakana (module 2), so the examples above are katakana. にょ, ひゅ and びゅ
mostly turn up in sound words such as にょろにょろ and ひゅうひゅう.

Typing: type the romaji as one syllable: *kya* → きゃ, *sho* → しょ, *cha* → ちゃ, *ja* → じゃ.
The alternative spellings *sya*, *tya* and *zya* (or *jya*) work too. To type a small ゃ, ゅ or
ょ on its own, put x (or l) in front: *xya* → ゃ.

### The size changes the word

| Full-size | Small |
|---|---|
| びよういん (biyōin) — beauty salon, 5 beats | びょういん (byōin) — hospital, 4 beats |
| じゆう (jiyū) — freedom, 3 beats | じゅう (jū) — ten, 2 beats |

## Small っ: a one-beat pause

A small つ, written っ, isn't read "tsu". It's a beat of silence: the mouth gets ready for the
next consonant and holds it for one beat before releasing it. This is called **[[sokuon]]**. In
romaji it's shown by doubling the next consonant.

| Without っ | With っ |
|---|---|
| きて (kite) — come! / wear it | きって (kitte) — postage stamp |
| さか (saka) — slope | さっか (sakka) — writer |
| おと (oto) — sound | おっと (otto) — husband |

Say きって slowly: "ki", then a held silence as your tongue closes for the t, then "te". It's
like the pause in English *bookcase* or *hot tea*, where the k or t is held across two
syllables. Clap the beats: き・っ・て, three claps, the second one silent.

っ usually comes before k, s, sh, t, ch, ts and p sounds: がっこう (gakkō, school), ざっし
(zasshi, magazine), ちょっと (chotto, a little), きっぷ (kippu, ticket), まっちゃ (matcha,
powdered green tea). Before ch, romaji writes *tch* (matcha). At the end of a word, っ is a
sudden stop, as in the cry あっ! (a!, oh!).

Don't confuse っ with doubled n. In みんな (minna, everyone) the first n is ん, a beat with
sound, not a silent っ.

Typing っ: double the next consonant: *kitte* → きって, *gakkou* → がっこう, *maccha* or
*matcha* → まっちゃ. For a small っ alone, type *xtu* or *ltu*.

## Long vowels

A long vowel is held for two beats. In hiragana it's written with a second vowel kana. The
spelling is mostly regular, with two twists: a long e is usually written えい and a long o is
usually written おう.

| Sound | Usually written | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| long a (ā) | ああ | おかあさん (okāsan) — mother, おばあさん (obāsan) — grandmother |
| long i (ī) | いい | おじいさん (ojīsan) — grandfather, ちいさい (chiisai) — small |
| long u (ū) | うう | くうき (kūki) — air, すうがく (sūgaku) — mathematics |
| long e (ē) | えい (sometimes ええ) | せんせい (sensei) — teacher, えいが (eiga) — film; おねえさん (onēsan) — older sister |
| long o (ō) | おう (sometimes おお) | ありがとう (arigatō) — thank you, がっこう (gakkō) — school; おおきい (ōkii) — big |

- えい: in careful speech you may hear "e-i", but in normal speech it's a long e, like ええ: せんせい
  sounds "sen-sē" ("seh" held for two beats, not English "see"). ええ is used in a few words such as ええ (ē, yes) and おねえさん.
- おう: the う is not pronounced as u; it just lengthens the o. ありがとう ends in "tō".
  おお is used in a small set of words, including おおきい (big), おおい (many), とおい (far),
  こおり (ice) and とお (ten). Learn them as you meet them.
- The same rules work across combinations: きょう (kyō, today), じゅう (jū, ten).

Romaji shows long vowels in several ways: with a line over the vowel (*Tōkyō*), by doubling it
(*Tookyoo*), or by following the kana (*Toukyou*); many signs simply leave it out (*Tokyo*).
When you type in this app, follow the kana: *gakkou* → がっこう, *ookii* → おおきい, *sensei*
→ せんせい.

### Why length matters

| Short | Long |
|---|---|
| おばさん (obasan) — aunt | おばあさん (obāsan) — grandmother |
| おじさん (ojisan) — uncle | おじいさん (ojīsan) — grandfather |
| ここ (koko) — here | こうこう (kōkō) — high school |
| ゆき (yuki) — snow | ゆうき (yūki) — courage |
| え (e) — picture | ええ (ē) — yes |

Call your grandmother おばさん and you've made her your aunt. Hold long vowels for a full
second beat.

## Counting beats

Every kana counts as one beat, except that a small ゃ, ゅ or ょ joins the kana before it. っ,
ん and the second half of a long vowel each count as a full beat.

| Word | Beats | Count |
|---|---|---|
| きょう (kyō) — today | 2 | きょ・う |
| きって (kitte) — stamp | 3 | き・っ・て |
| にほん (nihon) — Japan | 3 | に・ほ・ん |
| しゃしん (shashin) — photo | 3 | しゃ・し・ん |
| がっこう (gakkō) — school | 4 | が・っ・こ・う |
| とうきょう (tōkyō) — Tokyo | 4 | と・う・きょ・う |
| びょういん (byōin) — hospital | 4 | びょ・う・い・ん |
| おかあさん (okāsan) — mother | 5 | お・か・あ・さ・ん |

English speakers hear とうきょう as two syllables, "To-kyo". Japanese speakers hear four
beats. Tapping a finger for each beat is the best way to train your ear.

## Writing practice

Small kana can't be traced on the pads, but their shapes are the same as the full-size ones,
just smaller. Practise the kana that combinations start with, then や, ゆ and よ, and when you
write on paper make the small ones half size, low and to the left.

```trace
きしちにひみりぎじびぴやゆよ
```

## Dialogue: plans for today

```dialogue
# きょう
Ken: きょう、 なにを する？
= Kyō, nani o suru? — What are you doing today?
Yumi: えいがを みに いく。
= Eiga o mi ni iku. — I'm going to see a film.
Ken: いいね。 ぼくも いっしょに いって いい？
= Ii ne. Boku mo issho ni itte ii? — Nice. Can I come with you?
Yumi: もちろん。 ろくじに えきで あおう。
= Mochiron. Rokuji ni eki de aō. — Of course. Let's meet at the station at six.
Ken: わかった。 じゃあ、 また あとで。
= Wakatta. Jā, mata ato de. — Got it. See you later, then.
```

Notes:

- Find the three rules in the dialogue: combinations (きょう, いっしょ, じゃあ), small っ
  (いっしょ, いって, わかった) and long vowels (きょう, あおう, じゃあ).
- を in なにを and えいがを is the object particle from lesson 5, read o.
- ぼく (boku) is "I", used mostly by boys and men in casual speech.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the small kana full size: きや (kiya) instead of きゃ (kya), びよういん instead of
  びょういん. Make small kana clearly smaller.
- Reading っ as "tsu". It's a silent beat.
- Leaving out っ or a long vowel: きて for きって, おばさん for おばあさん. They're different
  words.
- Writing a long o as おお where the word uses おう (がっこお instead of がっこう), or a long e
  as ええ where the word uses えい (せんせえ instead of せんせい).
- Pronouncing the う of おう as a separate u: ありがとう is "a-ri-ga-tō", not "a-ri-ga-to-oo".
- Counting きょ as two beats. A combination is one beat.

## Key points

- An "i"-column kana + small ゃ, ゅ, ょ is one beat (yōon): 33 combinations, from きゃ to ぴょ.
- Small っ (sokuon) is a one-beat pause before a consonant, shown in romaji by a doubled letter:
  きって (kitte).
- Long vowels take two beats: ああ, いい, うう, えい (ええ), おう (おお).
- Count beats: っ, ん and the second half of a long vowel are full beats; small ゃゅょ are not.
- Typing: *kya*, *kitte*, *gakkou*; *xya* and *xtu* for small kana alone.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Katakana ア to ソ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now read every hiragana, with its voiced forms, combinations, small っ and long
vowels. Japanese has a second set of kana, **[[katakana]]**, and this module teaches it. The good news
is that you already know all its sounds: katakana spells exactly the same beats as hiragana,
in the same table order, with different shapes. ア is "a" just as あ is; カ is "ka" just as か
is. So the work in this module is mostly learning new shapes and the habits of katakana
spelling, not new sounds.

This lesson covers what katakana is used for and its first three rows: アイウエオ, カキクケコ
and サシスセソ. By the end you'll read real words such as アイス, ココア and スイス, and type
them in this app.

## What katakana is for

Hiragana is the everyday script for native Japanese words and grammar. Katakana has a narrower
set of jobs, and once you know them you can often guess why a word is in katakana before you
read it.

| Use | What it means | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Loanwords | words borrowed from other languages, mostly English | アイス (aisu) — ice cream; カメラ (kamera) — camera |
| Foreign names | people, places and countries outside Japan | スイス (Suisu) — Switzerland; アジア (Ajia) — Asia |
| Sound words | the noises things make, and many words that describe how something moves or feels | ニャー (nyā) — miaow; ドキドキ (dokidoki) — thump-thump (a pounding heart) |
| Emphasis | making a word stand out, like italics or capitals in English | a shop sign may write a native word in katakana to catch the eye |
| Science names | animals and plants in biology, zoos and recipes | イヌ (inu) — dog, in a science text |

Borrowed words are called **[[gairaigo]]**, literally "words that came from outside". There are
thousands of them, from コーヒー (kōhī, coffee) to スマホ (sumaho, smartphone), and they are
the main reason you need katakana: menus, shop signs, station names for foreign visitors and
technology are full of them. Sound words, or **[[onomatopoeia]]**, are just as common in comics
and advertising.

Most of these example words use kana from later lessons; you don't need to read them yet. Just
notice the pattern: when you see katakana, think "borrowed, foreign, a sound, or emphasis".

## Same sounds, new shapes

Katakana and hiragana share the same table. The five vowels come first, then the k-row, s-row
and so on, and the voicing marks ゛ and ゜ work the same way (lesson 11). Every hiragana has
one katakana partner:

| Hiragana | あ | か | さ | た | な |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Katakana | ア | カ | サ | タ | ナ |
| Sound | a | ka | sa | ta | na |

Katakana shapes are angular: mostly straight strokes and sharp corners, where hiragana has
curves and loops. They also tend to have fewer strokes. A few katakana look almost like their
hiragana partner (カ and か, キ and き, ヘ and へ), because both often grew from the same
older character; others look nothing alike (ア and あ). Where a resemblance helps, the tables
below point it out.

Because the sounds are the same, any Japanese word can be written in either script. いぬ and
イヌ both say "inu" (dog). What changes is the feeling: katakana looks foreign, technical or
emphatic.

## The ア row: ア イ ウ エ オ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ア | a | 2 | あ | アイス (aisu) — ice cream |
| イ | i | 2 | い | イギリス (Igirisu) — Britain |
| ウ | u | 3 | う | ウイスキー (uisukī) — whisky |
| エ | e | 3 | え | エアコン (eakon) — air conditioner |
| オ | o | 3 | お | オイル (oiru) — oil |

- ア: a short horizontal stroke that bends down to the left, then a short stroke dropping
  from inside it. It looks like a flag on a short pole.
- イ: a slanting stroke down to the left, then a straight vertical one. Think of a person
  leaning on a post.
- ウ: like う with a roof. A short top stroke, a short left stroke, then a horizontal that
  turns and sweeps down. The top of う becomes the dot on ウ.
- エ: three straight strokes, top, middle (vertical) and bottom, like a capital I.
- オ: a horizontal, a vertical with a small hook at the bottom, then a slant down to the left
  across the middle.

```trace
アイウエオ
```

## The カ row: カ キ ク ケ コ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| カ | ka | 2 | か | カメラ (kamera) — camera |
| キ | ki | 3 | き | キウイ (kiui) — kiwi fruit |
| ク | ku | 2 | く | クイズ (kuizu) — quiz |
| ケ | ke | 3 | け | ケーキ (kēki) — cake |
| コ | ko | 2 | こ | ココア (kokoa) — cocoa, hot chocolate |

- カ is か without its little extra stroke: a bent stroke with a hook, then a slant through it.
- キ is き with its bottom curve removed: two horizontals, then a long stroke down through
  them, leaning slightly.
- ク: a short slant, then a horizontal that turns and sweeps down to the left. A slice of
  pizza seen from the side.
- ケ: a short slant, a horizontal, then a long slant down from the middle of the horizontal.
- コ: two strokes making a box with its left side open. Compare こ, which is just the top and
  bottom lines.

```trace
カキクケコ
```

## The サ row: サ シ ス セ ソ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| サ | sa | 3 | さ | サラダ (sarada) — salad |
| シ | shi | 3 | し | システム (shisutemu) — system |
| ス | su | 2 | す | スキー (sukī) — skiing, skis |
| セ | se | 2 | せ | セーター (sētā) — sweater, jumper |
| ソ | so | 2 | そ | ソース (sōsu) — sauce |

- サ: a horizontal, a short vertical, then a long vertical that curves down to the left.
- シ: two short dots one above the other on the left, then a long stroke that rises from the
  bottom left up to the right. Its sound is "shi", as in hiragana.
- ス: a horizontal that turns and sweeps down to the left, then a short stroke out to the
  right from the middle of the sweep. It looks like someone walking.
- セ is せ with one stroke fewer: a horizontal that turns down with a little hook, then a
  vertical that bends to the right at the bottom.
- ソ: a short dot, then a stroke that falls from the top right down to the left. Two strokes,
  both starting at the top.

```trace
サシスセソ
```

## A first look at ー

Some of the words above contain a dash: ケーキ, スキー, セーター, ソース. In katakana, ー means
"hold the vowel before me for one more beat". ケーキ is "ke-e-ki", three beats, the same as
けえき would be. Lesson 11 covers it properly; for now, read ー as a long vowel. Loanwords use
it all the time, so you'll keep meeting it.

## Words you can read now

Every word below uses only the fifteen katakana from this lesson:

| Word | Romaji | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| アイス | aisu | ice cream (at the start of a word: iced, as in iced coffee) |
| ココア | kokoa | cocoa, hot chocolate |
| キウイ | kiui | kiwi fruit |
| スイス | Suisu | Switzerland |
| カカオ | kakao | cacao (the bean chocolate is made from) |
| オアシス | oashisu | oasis |
| アクセス | akusesu | access (also: how to get to a place) |
| エコ | eko | eco-friendly, ecology |
| ケア | kea | care (skin care, nursing care) |
| カオス | kaosu | chaos |

Notice how English sounds are reshaped. "Ice" has one syllable in English but becomes three
beats, a-i-su, because Japanese adds a vowel after a final consonant. Lesson 12 explains these
patterns; for now just read what is written.

```speak
# Read aloud
アイス
= ice cream
ココア
= cocoa
スイス
= Switzerland
キウイ
= kiwi fruit
ケーキ
= cake
アクセス
= access
```

## Reading: at a café counter

The katakana words in this short exchange are the ones you learned above; the rest is hiragana
you already know.

```dialogue
# At a café counter
Clerk: いらっしゃいませ。
= Welcome!
Ken: ココア、ください。
= A hot chocolate, please.
Clerk: ココアですね。アイスも ありますよ。
= A hot chocolate. We have ice cream too.
Ken: アイス？ じゃあ、アイスも ください。
= Ice cream? Then ice cream too, please.
Clerk: ありがとう ございます。
= Thank you very much.
```

Ken orders ココア and then adds アイス. ください means "please give me"; ですね checks what
someone said ("…, right?"); も means "also". You don't need the grammar yet: the point is to
see katakana words sitting inside a hiragana sentence, which is how you'll meet them in real
Japanese.

## Typing katakana in this app

In this app you type romaji and it turns into kana. Lowercase letters give hiragana; CAPITAL
letters give katakana. Type AISU and you get アイス; type aisu and you get あいす. For ー, press
the - key: KE-KI gives ケーキ. So whenever a question asks for a katakana answer, turn on Caps
Lock (or hold Shift) and type the word in capitals.

| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| KOKOA | ココア |
| SUISU | スイス |
| SHISUTEMU | システム |
| SUKI- | スキー |

## Lookalikes and common mistakes

- シ (shi) and ツ (tsu) are the most famous trap in katakana. Both have two short strokes and
  a long one. In シ the long stroke rises from the bottom left up to the right, and the dots
  sit on the left, one above the other. In ツ (next lesson) the dots sit side by side along the
  top, and the long stroke falls from the top downward. Lesson 9 drills them.
- ソ (so) and ン (n, lesson 10) are the same pair problem: ソ's long stroke falls from the top,
  ン's rises from the bottom. Remember: ソ and ツ fall; シ and ン rise.
- ク, ケ and タ (lesson 9) share a top. ク has two strokes and nothing inside; ケ has a long
  stroke dropping from the horizontal; タ adds a small stroke inside ク.
- コ and ユ (lesson 10): コ is a box open on the left; in ユ the bottom line is longer and
  sticks out past the vertical stroke.
- Don't round the corners. Writing katakana with curves makes ク look like く or ソ look like
  the start of そ.
- Don't write ー as a vowel. ケーキ, not ケエキ: in katakana, loanwords use ー for a long vowel.
- Don't type katakana in lowercase. aisu gives あいす, which looks wrong to a Japanese reader:
  the word for ice cream is written アイス.

## Key points

- Katakana has the same sounds and table order as hiragana, with angular shapes.
- It's used for loanwords (gairaigo), foreign names, sound words (onomatopoeia),
  emphasis, and animal and plant names in science.
- This lesson: アイウエオ カキクケコ サシスセソ. カ, キ, セ and ウ resemble their hiragana
  partners.
- シ rises from the bottom left; ソ falls from the top.
- ー makes the vowel before it one beat longer.
- Type katakana in CAPITALS; - gives ー.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Katakana タ to ホ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Last lesson gave you the first fifteen katakana, アイウエオ カキクケコ サシスセソ, and what
katakana is for. This lesson adds the next fifteen: タチツテト, ナニヌネノ and ハヒフヘホ. That
takes you past the middle of the table. It also settles the most famous katakana trap, シ
against ツ, with one simple rule about which way the long stroke goes.

The sounds are the ones you know from hiragana: チ is "chi", ツ is "tsu" and フ is "fu", just
like ち, つ and ふ.

## The タ row: タ チ ツ テ ト

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| タ | ta | 3 | た | タクシー (takushī) — taxi |
| チ | chi | 3 | ち | チーズ (chīzu) — cheese |
| ツ | tsu | 3 | つ | ツアー (tsuā) — tour, package tour |
| テ | te | 3 | て | テニス (tenisu) — tennis |
| ト | to | 2 | と | トマト (tomato) — tomato |

- タ is ク (lesson 8) with one more stroke: a short slant inside, going down to the right
  until it touches the sweep.
- チ: a short stroke at the top that falls to the left, a long horizontal, then a stroke down
  from the middle that curves to the left.
- ツ: two short strokes side by side along the top, then a long stroke that falls from the top
  right down to the left. More on ツ below.
- テ: a short horizontal, a longer horizontal under it, then a stroke falling to the left from
  the middle of the lower line. Compare チ: チ starts with a slant; テ starts with a flat line.
- ト: a vertical, then a short stroke out to the right from its middle. It looks like と with
  the curve straightened.

```trace
タチツテト
```

## The ナ row: ナ ニ ヌ ネ ノ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ナ | na | 2 | な | ナイフ (naifu) — knife |
| ニ | ni | 2 | に | ニュース (nyūsu) — news |
| ヌ | nu | 2 | ぬ | ヌードル (nūdoru) — noodles (instant-noodle style) |
| ネ | ne | 4 | ね | ネクタイ (nekutai) — necktie |
| ノ | no | 1 | の | ノート (nōto) — notebook |

- ナ: a horizontal, then a long stroke down through it that leans to the left. A cross
  falling over.
- ニ: two horizontals, the lower one longer. It looks like the right-hand part of に.
- ヌ: a stroke like フ (across, then down to the left), then a short slant that crosses it
  from the upper left down to the right.
- ネ: four strokes. A dot at the top, a horizontal that turns down to the left, a vertical
  from the middle, then a short dot to the right of the vertical.
- ノ: a single slanting stroke. The simplest kana there is: の with its loop cut off.

Notice ノート: it means a notebook (the paper kind), not a written note. Loanwords often take
one meaning of the English word, and not always the one you expect.

```trace
ナニヌネノ
```

## The ハ row: ハ ヒ フ ヘ ホ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ハ | ha | 2 | は | ハンカチ (hankachi) — handkerchief |
| ヒ | hi | 2 | ひ | ヒーター (hītā) — heater |
| フ | fu | 1 | ふ | フランス (Furansu) — France |
| ヘ | he | 1 | へ | ヘルメット (herumetto) — helmet |
| ホ | ho | 4 | ほ | ホテル (hoteru) — hotel |

- ハ: two short strokes that spread apart, a slant to the left and then one to the right,
  like a tent with no top.
- ヒ: a short horizontal that rises a little, then a vertical that turns right along the
  bottom.
- フ: one stroke, across and then sweeping down to the left. Its sound is "fu", soft, with the
  lips close together but not touching the teeth, as in hiragana ふ.
- ヘ: the same shape as hiragana へ. In print the katakana one is a little sharper and
  straighter, but you write them the same way.
- ホ: a horizontal, a vertical with a small hook, then a short dot on each side, left first.
  It looks like the right-hand part of ほ without the loop.

ハ is "ha" in words. Only the hiragana particle は is read "wa"; katakana ハ is always "ha".
Similarly katakana ヘ is "he" in words like ヘルメット.

```trace
ハヒフヘホ
```

## シ or ツ? Watch the long stroke

シ (shi, lesson 8) and ツ (tsu) are each two short strokes plus a long one, and in some fonts
they look nearly identical. Two things tell them apart.

| | シ shi | ツ tsu |
|---|---|---|
| Where the short strokes sit | stacked on the left, one above the other | side by side along the top |
| Which way they point | toward the right, almost flat | downward, almost upright |
| The long stroke | rises from the bottom left up to the right | falls from the top right down to the left |

The long stroke is the surest sign, because it shows in handwriting: in シ it is written
upward, so it is thick at the bottom and thin at the top; in ツ it is written downward, so it is
thick at the top. Say it to yourself as "shi rises, tsu falls".

The same rule holds for the pair ソ (so) and ン (n), which you'll meet properly in lesson 10:
ソ falls like ツ, and ン rises like シ. Four kana, one rule.

Try reading these, all real words: シーツ (shītsu, bed sheet), ツナ (tsuna, tuna, as in canned
tuna), スイーツ (suītsu, sweets and desserts), シーソー (shīsō, seesaw).

## Two more lookalike pairs

- ヌ (nu) and ス (su): both start with the same across-and-down stroke. In ス the second stroke
  is short and starts on the sweep, going out to the right. In ヌ it is longer and crosses the
  sweep, from above it to below.
- ナ (na) and メ (me, lesson 10): ナ has a flat horizontal and a long stroke crossing it.
  メ has no horizontal at all: just two slanting strokes, a long one falling to the left and a
  short one crossing it to the right.
- チ (chi) and テ (te): チ begins with a slanted stroke at the top; テ begins with a flat one.

## Words you can read now

These use only katakana from lessons 8 and 9, plus ー:

| Word | Romaji | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| テニス | tenisu | tennis |
| ナイフ | naifu | knife |
| ネクタイ | nekutai | necktie |
| タイ | Tai | Thailand |
| テキスト | tekisuto | textbook (also: text) |
| コスト | kosuto | cost |
| ハイテク | haiteku | high-tech |
| トースト | tōsuto | toast (the bread) |
| コート | kōto | coat (also: a tennis court) |
| スケート | sukēto | skating |

ハイテク is a shortened word: "high technology" cut down to four beats. Japanese often trims
long loanwords like this.

```speak
# Read aloud
テニス
= tennis
ホテル
= hotel
タクシー
= taxi
ノート
= notebook
ナイフ
= knife
フランス
= France
```

## Reading: a taxi to the hotel

```dialogue
# In a taxi
Driver: どちらまで ですか。
= Where to?
Amy: ホテル ナカノ まで、おねがいします。
= To the Hotel Nakano, please.
Driver: ホテル ナカノ ですね。はい。
= The Hotel Nakano. Sure.
Amy: ちかい ですか。
= Is it close?
Driver: はい、すぐ です。あ、あの ホテル です。
= Yes, it's just a moment away. Oh, that's the hotel there.
Amy: ありがとう ございます。
= Thank you very much.
```

Amy names the hotel in katakana, as hotel signs often do. ナカノ (Nakano) is a Japanese place
name, which would normally be written in kanji; a hotel may still spell its name in katakana
to look modern. まで means "as far as"; おねがいします is "please" when you ask for a service.

## Typing these kana

Type in CAPITALS for katakana. Use the same spellings as for hiragana: CHI for チ, TSU for
ツ, FU for フ, and SHI for シ. TI, TU and HU also work.

| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| TENISU | テニス |
| TSUNA | ツナ |
| NAIFU | ナイフ |
| TAKUSHI- | タクシー |

## Common mistakes

- Writing ツ with its long stroke going up, or シ with its stroke going down. It changes the
  letter: シーツ (sheet) written with the strokes swapped reads ツーシ, which is nonsense.
- Reading ハ as "wa". Only the particle は is "wa"; ハ is always "ha".
- Writing ヘ with a curve. It is a sharp, shallow angle, the same as へ.
- Mixing up チ and テ. Check the first stroke: slanted for チ, flat for テ.
- Treating ノート as "a note". It means a notebook; a short written note is メモ (memo).

## Key points

- New katakana: タチツテト ナニヌネノ ハヒフヘホ, with the same sounds as hiragana (チ chi,
  ツ tsu, フ fu).
- ト, ニ, ヘ and ホ look like their hiragana partners (or part of them).
- シ rises, ツ falls: the direction of the long stroke and the position of the short strokes
  tell them apart. ン and ソ follow the same rule.
- ヌ crosses its sweep; ス doesn't. ナ has a horizontal; メ doesn't.
- Loanwords often keep only one meaning of the English word: ノート is a notebook.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Katakana マ to ン
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson finishes the basic katakana: マミムメモ, ヤユヨ, ラリルレロ, ワ, ヲ and ン. After it
you know all 46, the full katakana table, and you can read the names of most countries and a
good part of any café menu. The lesson ends with the lookalikes that cause the most trouble
once the whole set is in play: ソ and ン, ク ケ and タ, ワ ウ and フ, and コ and ユ.

## The マ row: マ ミ ム メ モ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| マ | ma | 2 | ま | マスク (masuku) — face mask |
| ミ | mi | 3 | み | ミルク (miruku) — milk |
| ム | mu | 2 | む | ハム (hamu) — ham |
| メ | me | 2 | め | メロン (meron) — melon |
| モ | mo | 3 | も | モデル (moderu) — model (fashion or product) |

- マ: a horizontal that turns and sweeps down to the left, then a short stroke inside it
  going down to the right. Compare ア, whose second stroke drops to the left.
- ミ: three short strokes, one under the other, each slanting down to the right. Think of
  three lines of rain blown by the wind.
- ム: a stroke that slants down to the left, turns and runs right along the bottom, then a
  short stroke at the right end.
- メ: a long slant down to the left, then a short slant crossing it down to the right. It
  looks like め without the loop.
- モ: a short horizontal, a longer horizontal, then a vertical through both that turns right
  at the bottom. It is も with straight lines.

```trace
マミムメモ
```

## The ヤ row: ヤ ユ ヨ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ヤ | ya | 2 | や | タイヤ (taiya) — tyre, tire |
| ユ | yu | 2 | ゆ | ユニフォーム (yunifōmu) — (sports) uniform |
| ヨ | yo | 3 | よ | ヨーグルト (yōguruto) — yogurt |

- ヤ: a horizontal that turns down with a little hook, then a long stroke down through it. It
  is や without its small stroke.
- ユ: a horizontal that turns down, then a long horizontal along the bottom that sticks out
  past the vertical.
- ヨ: three horizontals joined on the right, like a capital E facing the other way.

As in hiragana, the ヤ row has only three kana. Small ャ ュ ョ make the combinations (キャ,
シュ, チョ…) in lesson 11.

```trace
ヤユヨ
```

## The ラ row: ラ リ ル レ ロ

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ラ | ra | 2 | ら | ラジオ (rajio) — radio |
| リ | ri | 2 | り | リモコン (rimokon) — remote control |
| ル | ru | 2 | る | ルール (rūru) — rule |
| レ | re | 1 | れ | レモン (remon) — lemon |
| ロ | ro | 3 | ろ | ロボット (robotto) — robot |

- ラ: a short horizontal on top, then a stroke like フ under it. Like ら with sharp corners.
- リ: a short vertical, then a longer one that curves down to the left. Almost the same as り.
- ル: a stroke falling to the left, then a vertical that turns up to the right at the bottom.
  Two legs, the right one kicking up.
- レ: one stroke, straight down and then up to the right. It is the right leg of ル on its
  own.
- ロ: a square in three strokes: the left side, then the top and right side in one stroke,
  then the bottom.

The Japanese r is the light tap you learned with hiragana, and it does the work of both
English r and English l. That's why レモン (lemon) and ラジオ (radio) start with the same row.
Lesson 12 comes back to this.

```trace
ラリルレロ
```

## ワ, ヲ and ン

| Katakana | Romaji | Strokes | Hiragana | Word |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ワ | wa | 2 | わ | ワイン (wain) — wine |
| ヲ | o (wo) | 3 | を | rare: the particle を in text written all in katakana |
| ン | n | 2 | ん | サイン (sain) — signature, autograph |

- ワ: a short vertical, then a horizontal that turns and sweeps down to the left.
- ヲ: three strokes; it looks like フ with an extra line across the middle.
- ン: a short stroke at the upper left, then a long stroke that rises from the bottom left up
  to the right.

ヲ is the katakana partner of を, and it is almost never seen. を is a particle, a grammar word,
