and grammar is written in hiragana, so ヲ turns up only when a whole sentence is in katakana:
old telegrams, some machine displays, a robot talking in a comic. You should recognise it, but
you will rarely write it.

ン is the same sound as ん, a beat of its own: サイン is three beats, sa-i-n. Loanwords are full
of it: English n and m before a consonant often become ン (サイン, sign; キャンプ, camp), and
ng usually becomes ング (キング, king).

```trace
ワヲン
```

## The whole table

With this lesson you know every basic katakana. Here they are in table order, read across:

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | ア | イ | ウ | エ | オ |
| k | カ | キ | ク | ケ | コ |
| s | サ | シ | ス | セ | ソ |
| t | タ | チ | ツ | テ | ト |
| n | ナ | ニ | ヌ | ネ | ノ |
| h | ハ | ヒ | フ | ヘ | ホ |
| m | マ | ミ | ム | メ | モ |
| y | ヤ | | ユ | | ヨ |
| r | ラ | リ | ル | レ | ロ |
| w | ワ | | | | ヲ |
| | ン | | | | |

The reference sheet "Katakana chart" has this table with the voiced kana, the combinations and
the loanword sounds.

## Lookalikes

### ソ and ン

Like シ and ツ in lesson 9: ソ's long stroke falls from the top right, ン's
rises from the bottom left. ソ's short stroke points down, almost upright; ン's lies almost
flat, as if it were lying down. Remember: ソ and ツ fall; シ and ン rise.

### ク, ケ and タ

All three begin with a short slant to the left.
- ク: two strokes, nothing inside.
- ケ: the second stroke is a straight horizontal, and the third drops from its middle.
- タ: ク plus a short stroke inside, going down to the right.

### フ, ワ and ウ

Build them up: フ is one stroke; add a short vertical on the left and you
have ワ; add a dot on top of ワ and you have ウ.

### コ, ユ and ヨ

コ is a box open on the left. ユ has a longer bottom line that sticks out
past the vertical. ヨ adds a middle line to コ.

### ロ and a kanji

ロ looks almost exactly like the kanji for "mouth", which you'll
meet when you study kanji. In print the kanji is usually a little larger. The words around it
tell you which one you're reading.

### マ and ア, ル and レ, メ and ナ

マ's inner stroke goes down to the right, ア's down to the
left. レ is one stroke; ル has two. メ has no horizontal; ナ does.

## Countries and everyday words

You can now read the names of many countries. A few follow an older or non-English form of the
name rather than English, so read carefully:

| Word | Romaji | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| アメリカ | Amerika | the United States, America |
| イタリア | Itaria | Italy |
| メキシコ | Mekishiko | Mexico |
| ロシア | Roshia | Russia |
| フランス | Furansu | France |
| イギリス | Igirisu | the United Kingdom, Britain |

And some everyday words that use only basic katakana and ー:

| Word | Romaji | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ラーメン | rāmen | ramen noodles |
| トイレ | toire | toilet, restroom |
| タオル | taoru | towel |
| メール | mēru | email, a text message |
| カレー | karē | curry |
| モノレール | monorēru | monorail |

```speak
# Read aloud
メロン
= melon
レモン
= lemon
ワイン
= wine
ラーメン
= ramen
アメリカ
= the United States
イタリア
= Italy
```

## Reading: at the fruit stand

```dialogue
# At the fruit stand
Clerk: いらっしゃいませ。
= Welcome!
Rina: すみません、メロン ありますか。
= Excuse me, do you have melons?
Clerk: はい、こちらです。おいしい ですよ。
= Yes, over here. They're delicious.
Rina: レモンも ありますか。
= Do you have lemons too?
Clerk: レモンは あちらです。
= The lemons are over there.
Rina: じゃあ、メロンを ひとつと、レモンを みっつ ください。
= Then one melon and three lemons, please.
Clerk: ありがとう ございます。
= Thank you very much.
```

The fruit names are in katakana because they're loanwords: メロン from melon, レモン from
lemon. ひとつ and みっつ are "one" and "three" (things); ありますか asks "is there…?".

## Typing these kana

Capitals give katakana. ン needs care: type NN (or N followed by another consonant). A
single N at the very end also becomes ン when you press Enter. Before a vowel or Y, type N'
(KIN'EN). WO in capitals
gives ヲ.

| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| MERONN | メロン |
| WAINN | ワイン |
| RA-MENN | ラーメン |
| ROSHIA | ロシア |

## Common mistakes

- Writing ン like ソ, or the reverse. サイン with a ソ reads サイソ, which is meaningless.
- Writing ウ without its top dot (that's ワ) or ワ without its left stroke (that's フ).
- Writing ユ like コ. The bottom line of ユ runs past the vertical.
- Reading ル as "l". Japanese has one tap sound for both; ル is "ru".
- Using ヲ in loanwords. A word with an "o" sound uses オ: オイル, not ヲイル.

## Key points

- New katakana: マミムメモ ヤユヨ ラリルレロ ワ ヲ ン. You now know all 46.
- モ, ヤ, ラ, リ and メ look like their hiragana partners.
- ソ falls, ン rises (like ツ and シ).
- フ → ワ → ウ: add a stroke, then a dot. コ, ユ and ヨ differ in their lines.
- ヲ is rare: only the particle を in all-katakana text.
- The ラ row covers both English r and l.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Voiced katakana, ー and small ッ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You know all 46 basic katakana. With hiragana, the next steps were the voicing marks, the
combinations with small ゃゅょ, small っ and long vowels. Katakana has all of these too, and
they work exactly the same way, with one important difference: long vowels are written with a
dash, ー. Put together, these let you read most of the katakana you'll meet on a menu, a sign
or a web page: コーヒー, チケット, ニュース, コンピューター.

## Voiced katakana: ゛ and ゜

Add the two short strokes ゛ to the k-, s-, t- and h-rows, or the small circle ゜ to the
h-row, and the sounds change exactly as in hiragana: k→g, s→z, t→d, h→b, and h→p. The marks
go at the top right and are written last.

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| g | ガ ga | ギ gi | グ gu | ゲ ge | ゴ go |
| z | ザ za | ジ ji | ズ zu | ゼ ze | ゾ zo |
| d | ダ da | ヂ ji | ヅ zu | デ de | ド do |
| b | バ ba | ビ bi | ブ bu | ベ be | ボ bo |
| p | パ pa | ピ pi | プ pu | ペ pe | ポ po |

One word for each:

| Row | Words |
|---|---|
| ガ row | ガム (gamu) — chewing gum; ギター (gitā) — guitar; グラス (gurasu) — (drinking) glass; ゲーム (gēmu) — game; ゴルフ (gorufu) — golf |
| ザ row | ピザ (piza) — pizza; ジーンズ (jīnzu) — jeans; ズボン (zubon) — trousers; ゼロ (zero) — zero; ゾンビ (zonbi) — zombie |
| ダ row | ダンス (dansu) — dance; チヂミ (chijimi) — Korean savoury pancake; ツヅク (tsuzuku) — "to be continued"; デザート (dezāto) — dessert; ドア (doa) — door |
| バ row | バス (basu) — bus; ビール (bīru) — beer; ブーツ (būtsu) — boots; ベッド (beddo) — bed; ボール (bōru) — ball |
| パ row | パン (pan) — bread; ピアノ (piano) — piano; プール (pūru) — swimming pool; ペン (pen) — pen; ポスト (posuto) — postbox, mailbox |

ズボン comes from French and パン from Portuguese: not every loanword is English. パン is one
of the oldest, brought by Portuguese traders in the 1500s.

ヂ and ヅ are even rarer in katakana than ぢ and づ are in hiragana. Loanwords always
write the sounds "ji" and "zu" as ジ and ズ: ジーンズ, never ヂーンヅ. You'll see ヂ in
チヂミ, a dish borrowed from Korean, and ヅ mostly when a native word that uses づ is written in
katakana, like ツヅク at the end of a comic episode.

```trace
ガギグゲゴザジズゼゾダヂヅデドバビブベボパピプペポ
```

## Combinations: キャ to ピョ

Small ャ, ュ and ョ after an i-column kana make one beat, just as in hiragana: キャ is "kya",
シュ is "shu", チョ is "cho". The small kana sits low and is clearly smaller than a full ヤ, ユ
or ヨ.

| | ャ ya | ュ yu | ョ yo |
|---|---|---|---|
| キ | キャ kya | キュ kyu | キョ kyo |
| シ | シャ sha | シュ shu | ショ sho |
| チ | チャ cha | チュ chu | チョ cho |
| ニ | ニャ nya | ニュ nyu | ニョ nyo |
| ヒ | ヒャ hya | ヒュ hyu | ヒョ hyo |
| ミ | ミャ mya | ミュ myu | ミョ myo |
| リ | リャ rya | リュ ryu | リョ ryo |
| ギ | ギャ gya | ギュ gyu | ギョ gyo |
| ジ | ジャ ja | ジュ ju | ジョ jo |
| ビ | ビャ bya | ビュ byu | ビョ byo |
| ピ | ピャ pya | ピュ pyu | ピョ pyo |

Some of these are everywhere in loanwords:

| Word | Romaji | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| キャンプ | kyanpu | camping, a camp |
| シャツ | shatsu | shirt |
| ショッピング | shoppingu | shopping |
| チョコレート | chokorēto | chocolate |
| ニュース | nyūsu | news |
| メニュー | menyū | menu |
| ジュース | jūsu | juice, a soft drink |
| ジャム | jamu | jam |
| リュック | ryukku | backpack (from rucksack) |
| ミュージカル | myūjikaru | musical (the show) |
| ギョーザ | gyōza | gyoza, pan-fried dumplings |

Others, such as ヒャ, ミョ, リャ, ビャ and ピャ, hardly ever appear in loanwords. You'll see
them in sound words (ピョンピョン, hopping), in animal and plant names (ヒョウ, leopard), in
a few foreign place names (ミャンマー, Myanmar) and when native words are written in katakana.
Recognise them; don't worry about finding words for each.

ジュース deserves a note: in Japan it means any sweet soft drink, not only fruit juice.

## The long-vowel mark ー

Hiragana writes a long vowel with an extra vowel kana: おかあさん, おとうさん. Katakana usually
uses a dash instead, the **[[chōonpu]]** (long-vowel mark), ー. It means "hold the vowel before me
for one more beat".

| With ー | Beats | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| コーヒー (kōhī) | ko-o-hi-i, 4 | coffee |
| ケーキ (kēki) | ke-e-ki, 3 | cake |
| スーパー (sūpā) | su-u-pa-a, 4 | supermarket |
| ルール (rūru) | ru-u-ru, 3 | rule |

The length changes the word, so it matters when you read and when you write:

| Short | Long |
|---|---|
| ビル (biru) — a building | ビール (bīru) — beer |
| ハト (hato) — pigeon | ハート (hāto) — heart, a heart shape |

ハト is a native word, written in katakana because it's an animal name.

The direction of ー follows the text. In ordinary horizontal text it is a horizontal line; in
**[[vertical text]]** (top to bottom, as in many books and comics) it turns into a vertical line, │.
Don't confuse it with the kanji for "one", which looks similar but is never used inside a
katakana word; context makes it obvious.

In a few words a long "ei" or "ou" sound is written with a vowel kana instead, and some words
can be spelled either way: メイク and メーク (makeup) both appear. When you're unsure, ー is
the usual choice for loanwords.

Typing: press - for ー. KO-HI- gives コーヒー.

## Small ッ

Small ッ works just like small っ: a one-beat pause before the next consonant, with the mouth
ready to say it.

| Word | Romaji | Beats | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| ベッド | beddo | be-(pause)-do, 3 | bed |
| チケット | chiketto | chi-ke-(pause)-to, 4 | ticket |
| ロボット | robotto | ro-bo-(pause)-to, 4 | robot |
| カップ | kappu | ka-(pause)-pu, 3 | cup |
| キッチン | kitchin | ki-(pause)-chi-n, 4 | kitchen |

ッ follows the Japanese sound, not the English spelling. Tennis has a double n in English but
テニス has no ッ; bed has a single d but ベッド has one. Listen for the short pause and the
snap of the consonant after it.

You'll also see ッ at the end of a word in comics and exclamations: アッ！ (Ah!) shows a sudden
stop.

Typing: double the consonant, as with hiragana. BEDDO gives ベッド, CHIKETTO gives チケット,
KITCHINN gives キッチン (tch gives ッチ).

## Reading real loanwords

With all of this you can read words like these. Say the beats as you go:

| Word | Romaji | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| コンビニ | konbini | convenience store |
| パソコン | pasokon | personal computer |
| コンピューター | konpyūtā | computer |
| エレベーター | erebētā | elevator, lift |
| デパート | depāto | department store |
| スマホ | sumaho | smartphone |
| バーベキュー | bābekyū | barbecue |

コンビニ, パソコン and スマホ are short forms, typical of Japanese: "convenience store" becomes
コンビニ, "personal computer" becomes パソコン.

```speak
# Read aloud
コーヒー
= coffee
チケット
= ticket
ニュース
= news
ジュース
= juice
コンピューター
= computer
ギター
= guitar
```

## Reading: at a coffee shop

```dialogue
# At a coffee shop
Clerk: いらっしゃいませ。ごちゅうもんは？
= Welcome! What would you like?
Leo: コーヒーを ひとつ ください。
= One coffee, please.
Clerk: ホットと アイス、どちらに しますか。
= Hot or iced?
Leo: アイスで おねがいします。あと、チーズケーキも。
= Iced, please. And a cheesecake too.
Clerk: サイズは どう しますか。
= What size would you like?
Leo: レギュラーで。
= Regular.
Clerk: かしこまりました。ぜんぶで ごひゃくごじゅう えん です。
= Certainly. That's 550 yen altogether.
```

Find the katakana features: ー in コーヒー and チーズケーキ, ッ in ホット, the voiced ズ in
サイズ and チーズ, and the combination ギュ in レギュラー. アイス here means "iced", as in iced
coffee.

## Common mistakes

- Writing long vowels with vowel kana in loanwords: コオヒイ instead of コーヒー.
- Leaving out ー or ッ. ビル and ビール are different words, and カプ isn't a word at all:
  cup is カップ.
- Writing the small kana full size: キヤンプ reads ki-ya-n-pu (four beats) instead of
  キャンプ (three).
- Using ヂ or ヅ for the "ji" and "zu" of loanwords. ジーンズ, ズボン, not ヂーンヅ.
- Forgetting the ゛ or swapping it for ゜: バス (bus) and パス (a pass) are different words.
- Writing ー vertically in horizontal text, or horizontally in vertical text.

## Key points

- ゛ and ゜ work as in hiragana: ガ ザ ダ バ パ rows, marks written last at the top right.
- ヂ and ヅ are very rare; loanwords use ジ and ズ.
- Small ャュョ make one-beat combinations; small ッ is a one-beat pause.
- Katakana long vowels use ー, the chōonpu. Each ー is one beat; type it with -.
- ー is horizontal in horizontal text and vertical in vertical text.
- Double letters in English don't decide ッ; the Japanese sound does.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Sounds for foreign words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japanese has fewer sounds than English. There is no "f" before a, i, e or o in the basic table,
no "ti" or "di", no "v", no "w" before i, e or o. Older loanwords simply used the nearest
Japanese beat: ラジオ for radio, チーム for team. Newer ones use a set of extra spellings made
from a katakana plus a small vowel: ファ, ティ, ウェ and so on. These are sometimes called
**[[extended katakana]]**.

This lesson teaches those spellings, then the patterns Japanese uses to fit any English word
into its beats, so you can read new loanwords and write your own name in katakana.

## Small ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ

You already know small ャ ュ ョ. Katakana also has small vowels: ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ. After a kana
they replace its vowel, and the two kana together make one beat. フ (fu) plus small ァ is ファ,
"fa". テ (te) plus small ィ is ティ, "ti".

Size matters. A full-size vowel is a beat of its own: フア would be "fu-a", two beats; ファ is
"fa", one beat.

## The new sounds

| Spelling | Sound | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| ファ | fa | ファン (fan) | fan, supporter |
| フィ | fi | フィルム (firumu) | (camera) film |
| フェ | fe | フェリー (ferī) | ferry |
| フォ | fo | フォーク (fōku) | fork |
| ティ | ti | ティッシュ (tisshu) | tissue, paper tissues |
| ディ | di | ディナー (dinā) | dinner (a restaurant meal) |
| トゥ | tu | タトゥー (tatū) | tattoo |
| ドゥ | du | ヒンドゥー (hindū) | Hindu |
| デュ | dyu | デュエット (dyuetto) | duet |
| ウィ | wi | ウィーン (Wīn) | Vienna |
| ウェ | we | ウェブサイト (webusaito) | website |
| ウォ | wo | ウォーキング (wōkingu) | walking (for exercise) |
| ヴ | vu | ヴァイオリン (vaiorin) | violin (usually バイオリン) |
| シェ | she | シェフ (shefu) | chef |
| ジェ | je | ジェットコースター (jettokōsutā) | roller coaster |
| チェ | che | チェス (chesu) | chess |
| ツァ | tsa | モーツァルト (Mōtsaruto) | Mozart |

A few notes:

- The f-sounds are the Japanese フ sound with a new vowel: lips close, not touching the teeth.
- ティ and ディ let Japanese say "tea" (ティー) and "Disney" (ディズニー) without turning them
  into チー and ジズニー.
- ウィ, ウェ and ウォ are a "w" glide. Older words write them with full-size kana: ウイスキー
  (whisky) is the usual spelling, and ウィスキー also appears.
- ヴ is ウ with ゛: a "v". Many speakers say it just like "b", and most words use the バ row
  instead (バイオリン, ビデオ for video). You'll see ヴ in some names and brand names, and
  combined with small vowels: ヴァ, ヴィ, ヴェ, ヴォ.
- ツァ and its cousins ツィ, ツェ, ツォ are rare, mostly in German and Italian names.

```trace
ヴ
```

ヴ is the only new kana to trace in this lesson; the small vowels can't be traced, and the rest
you already know.

## Old spellings and new spellings

Loanwords that came into Japanese long ago kept their old spellings, even after the new ones
became normal. Both are correct; you can't predict which a word uses, so learn each word as you
meet it.

| Older pattern | Newer pattern |
|---|---|
| チーム (team), ラジオ (radio) | ティー (tea), ディナー (dinner) |
| ツアー (tour), ツー (two) | タトゥー (tattoo) |
| ウイスキー (whisky) | ウェブサイト (website) |
| バイオリン (violin) | ヴァイオリン (violin), a less common spelling |

## Fitting English to Japanese

Every Japanese beat ends in a vowel, except ン and small ッ. English words are full of consonants with no
vowel after them, so Japanese adds one. This added vowel is an **[[epenthetic vowel]]**, and it
follows a pattern:

| Rule | English | Japanese |
|---|---|---|
| Most consonants get u | milk, golf, bus | ミルク, ゴルフ, バス |
| t and d get o | test, bed, card | テスト, ベッド, カード |
| ch and j get i | match, bridge, orange | マッチ, ブリッジ, オレンジ |
| Some older words give k an i | cake, strike | ケーキ, ストライキ (a labour strike) |

The other main patterns:

- l and r: Japanese has one sound for both, the ラ row. So light and right are both ライト,
  and glass and grass are both グラス. Context tells you which.
- "er", "ar", "or" at the end: an unstressed ending becomes a long vowel: computer →
  コンピューター, center → センター, doctor → ドクター, water → ウォーター. Japanese follows the
  British-style pronunciation without the r.
- th: becomes the サ or ザ row: thank you → サンキュー, three → スリー, mother → マザー.
- v: usually the バ row, sometimes ヴ: video → ビデオ.
- ng: becomes ング: king → キング, shopping → ショッピング.
- -tion: becomes ション: station → ステーション, action → アクション.
- A short, stressed vowel before a consonant often brings a small ッ: cup → カップ, hot →
  ホット, bed → ベッド.

Japanese also keeps many English words in a shortened form, and has made new words from
English parts that English speakers wouldn't recognise. These are called **[[wasei-eigo]]**,
"Japan-made English":

| Word | Made from | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| リモコン | remote control | remote control |
| ジェットコースター | jet + coaster | roller coaster |
| サラリーマン | salary + man | office worker (on a salary) |
| マンション | mansion | apartment, condo (not a mansion) |
| ノートパソコン | notebook + personal computer | laptop |

## Your name in katakana

Foreign names are written in katakana by their sound, not their spelling. To write yours:

1. Say your name aloud the way you say it, not the way it's spelled.
2. Split it into Japanese beats, adding vowels where a consonant stands alone.
3. Write each beat in katakana, using ー for long vowels and ッ for a sharp stop.

| Name | Katakana | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| John, Jon | ジョン | both spellings sound the same |
| Emma | エマ | |
| Michael | マイケル | "-chael" is said "kel" |
| Sarah | サラ | |
| Chris | クリス | an extra u after k |
| Kate | ケイト | "ay" written with イ, common in names |
| Peter | ピーター | final "er" → ー |
| David | デイビッド | also デービッド, デイヴィッド |
| Olivia | オリビア | also オリヴィア |

There is often more than one fair spelling. People pick one and keep it; check how others with
your name write it, and choose the one closest to how you say it. A full name keeps its own
order (given name first) and puts a **[[middle dot]]** between the parts: ジョン・スミス (John Smith).

## Reading: at a reception desk

```dialogue
# At a reception desk
Clerk: おなまえは？
= Your name, please?
Jessica: ジェシカ・ブラウン です。
= I'm Jessica Brown.
Clerk: ジェシカさん ですね。おくには どちらですか。
= Jessica. And which country are you from?
Jessica: オーストラリア です。
= Australia.
Clerk: そうですか。シドニー ですか。
= I see. From Sydney?
Jessica: いいえ、メルボルン です。
= No, Melbourne.
```

Every name here follows the rules above. ジェシカ uses the new ジェ; ブラウン has an extra u
after the b; シドニー turns "dney" into ドニー; メルボルン gives each consonant its own beat.

```speak
# Read aloud
パーティー
= party
フォーク
= fork
シェフ
= chef
ウェブサイト
= website
ディナー
= dinner
モーツァルト
= Mozart
```

## Typing these sounds

All of these work with CAPITALS in this app:

| Sound | Type | Sound | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| ファ フィ フェ フォ | FA FI FE FO | ウィ ウェ | WI WE |
| ティ | THI | ウォ | UXO (WO gives ヲ) |
| ディ | DHI | ヴ | VU |
| トゥ | TWU | シェ ジェ チェ | SHE JE CHE |
| ドゥ | DWU | ツァ | TSA |
| デュ | DHU | small ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ | XA XI XU XE XO |

So PA-THI- gives パーティー, FO-KU gives フォーク, and MO-TSARUTO gives モーツァルト.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the small vowel full size: フアン reads fu-a-n, not ファン.
- Using ヲ for "wo": ウォーキング, never ヲーキング.
- "Correcting" old spellings. チーム, ラジオ and ウイスキー are the normal spellings, not
  mistakes.
- Spelling a name from its letters: Michael is マイケル (by sound), not ミチャエル.
- Forgetting that ライト can mean light or right, and グラス glass or grass.
- Assuming a loanword means the same as in English: マンション is an apartment building.

## Key points

- Small ァィゥェォ make one-beat sounds for foreign words: ファ, ティ, ウェ, シェ, ツァ…
- ヴ is "v", but most words use the バ row; ヴ is the one new kana to trace.
- Old loanwords keep old spellings (チーム, ラジオ); newer ones use the new sounds (ティー).
- Japanese adds vowels after consonants: u after most, o after t and d, i after ch and j.
- l and r both become the ラ row; a final "er" becomes ー.
- Write names by sound, with ・ between given name and family name.

The kana from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: は, へ and を as particles
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now read every hiragana and katakana. This module puts them to work. Real Japanese
isn't a list of single words: it's sentences, and sentences are held together by small words
called particles. Three of the most common particles are spelled with a kana that is *not*
read the way you learned it. That one fact trips up nearly every beginner, so this lesson is
about it: は, へ and を, what they do, how they're read and how to type them.

By the end you'll read and write short sentences such as わたしは がくせいです。 (I'm a
student.), がっこうへ いきます。 (I go to school.) and みずを のみます。 (I drink water.)

## What a particle is

A **[[particle]]** is a short word, usually one kana (one beat), that comes right *after* another
word and shows what job that word does in the sentence. English does a similar job with word
order and with little words like "to", "at" and "of", but English puts them *before* the
word: "to school". Japanese puts the particle *after* it:

| Japanese | Word by word | English |
|---|---|---|
| がっこうへ | school + toward | to school |
| みずを | water + (object) | water (as the thing drunk) |
| わたしは | I + (topic) | as for me, I |

The particle belongs to the word in front of it. Say them together, with no pause between:
がっこうへ is one smooth chunk, "gakkō-e". This is why this course writes a space *after* a
particle, never before it.

Japanese has a dozen or so common particles, and almost all of them are written exactly as
they sound: か is "ka", も is "mo", の is "no". Only three are spelled with an older kana:

| Particle | Read | Job | Typed as |
|---|---|---|---|
| は | wa | marks the topic | ha |
| へ | e | marks the direction | he |
| を | o | marks the object | wo |

The spelling is a leftover from how Japanese was written before the spelling reforms of the
1940s. Words were respelled to match speech, but these three particles were so familiar in
their old form that they kept it. A handy side effect: を always comes right after a word, and a
は read "wa" does too, so they help you see where words end (but は also starts words such as
はな, so read the whole phrase).

## は, the topic marker, read "wa"

は after a word marks the **[[topic]]**: what the sentence is about. That's why it's called a
**[[topic marker]]**. A rough English version is "as for …": わたしは がくせいです。 is "As for me,
(I) am a student", or simply "I'm a student."

わたしは がくせいです。 — I'm a student.
せんせいは にほんへ いきます。 — The teacher is going to Japan.
ほんは ここです。 — The book is here. (ここ = here)

です at the end means "is", "am" or "are", in a polite way. It never changes for I, you, he or
they. Its final す is usually said very lightly, almost "des".

Read は as "wa" only when it's the particle. Inside a word it is always "ha", as you learned
in Lesson 4:

| Word | Read | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| はな | hana | flower; also nose |
| はし | hashi | chopsticks; also bridge |
| はなは きれいです。 | hana wa kirei desu | The flowers are pretty. |

The last line is the best test: the first は starts the word はな, so it's "ha"; the second is
the particle after はな, so it's "wa". How do you tell? A particle always follows a complete
word, and it's where this course puts the space.

Two everyday greetings end in a は that is read "wa": こんにちは (hello) and こんばんは (good
evening). They began as the first half of longer sentences ("as for today …", "as for this
evening …"), so the は is really the particle, frozen in place. You'll use them in Lesson 15.

## へ, the direction marker, read "e"

へ after a place marks where someone or something is heading: "to" or "toward". It goes with
verbs of movement such as いく (to go) and かえる (to go home, to return).

がっこうへ いきます。 — I go to school. / I'm going to school.
にほんへ いきます。 — I'm going to Japan.
うちへ かえります。 — I'm going home.

Inside a word, へ is "he", as always: へや (heya) — room, へた (heta) — bad at something.

You'll also see に used in the same place: がっこうに いきます means the same and is at least as
common in speech. へ puts a little more weight on the direction, and it's the one this
lesson practises because of its spelling. At the top of a note or a letter, へ after a name
means "To …": ゆきさんへ — To Yuki. You'll see that in Lesson 14.

## を, the object marker, read "o"

を marks the **[[object]]**: the thing the action is done to. In "I drink water", water is the
object, so it takes を.

みずを のみます。 — I drink water.
ほんを よみます。 — I read a book. / I'm reading a book.
ごはんを たべます。 — I eat a meal. / I eat rice.

In standard Tokyo speech を sounds exactly like お. Some people say "wo" when singing or
speaking very carefully, and you'll be understood either way, but "o" is the everyday
pronunciation. Unlike は and へ, を is used for nothing else in modern Japanese: it's the
particle and only the particle. So any word that starts with an "o" sound is spelled with
お: おちゃ (tea), おかね (money), おとこ (man).

## Sentences: the verb comes last

Put the three particles together and you can see the basic shape of a Japanese sentence:

| Topic | Place or object | Verb |
|---|---|---|
| わたしは | がっこうへ | いきます。 |
| わたしは | みずを | のみます。 |
| せんせいは | ほんを | よみます。 |
| がくせいは | うちへ | かえります。 |

The verb (or です) always comes at the end. The particles do the work English does with word
order, so the order before the verb can move a little, but topic first is the normal choice.

Notice too what Japanese leaves out. There's no "a" or "the", and nouns don't change for one
or many: ほん is "a book", "the book" or "books". And when it's clear who is acting, the topic
is dropped: if you're talking about yourself, がっこうへ いきます。 is a complete sentence,
"(I) go to school." Saying わたしは in every sentence sounds stiff.

### Verbs in this lesson

Dictionaries, and your word list, give verbs in their plain form. In sentences this lesson
uses the polite form ending in ます, which you'll use with people you don't know well (more
on politeness in Lesson 15):

| Plain form | Polite form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| いく | いきます | to go |
| かえる | かえります | to go home, to return |
| のむ | のみます | to drink |
| たべる | たべます | to eat |
| よむ | よみます | to read |

The ます form covers both "I drink" and "I will drink", and often "I'm drinking" too.

## Questions with か

To make a question, put か (read "ka", as spelled) at the end. Your voice can rise, but the
か is what makes it a question, and in careful writing it ends with 。, not a question mark:

がくせいですか。 — Are you a student?
にほんへ いきますか。 — Are you going to Japan?
どこへ いきますか。 — Where are you going? (どこ = where)

The answer to a yes-or-no question can start with はい (yes): はい、がくせいです。 The 、 is a
comma; Lesson 14 covers it.

## Typing the particles

The converter in this app types what you spell, not what you hear. So spell the particles by
their kana:

| You want | Type | If you type the sound instead |
|---|---|---|
| は (wa) | ha | wa gives わ |
| へ (e) | he | e gives え |
| を (o) | wo | o gives お |

So "I'm a student" is typed *watashi ha gakusei desu*. Phone and computer keyboards in Japan
work the same way, which is why Japanese people type "ha" for the particle too.

## Spaces

Normal Japanese is written without spaces: わたしはがくせいです。 Readers find the word
breaks from the particles and from the switch between hiragana, katakana and kanji. A text
written all in hiragana, with no kanji to break it up, is hard to read without help, so
picture books for small children and some beginners' books leave a space after each chunk
(a word plus its particles). That practice is called **[[wakachigaki]]**.

This course does the same: a space after each particle, and after a word when the next word
starts a new chunk. When you type an answer, spaces don't matter, and the app ignores them.
Out in the world, expect none.

## Reading: a morning

```dialogue
# A morning
ゆき: けんさん、どこへ いきますか。
= Ken, where are you going?
けん: がっこうへ いきます。ゆきさんは？
= I'm going to school. And you, Yuki?
ゆき: わたしも がっこうへ いきます。
= I'm going to school too.
けん: ゆきさんは がくせいですか。
= Are you a student?
ゆき: いいえ、せんせいです。
= No, I'm a teacher.
けん: そうですか。
= Oh, I see.
```

も after わたし means "too" or "also", and it replaces は: わたしも, not わたしはも. さん after a
name is a polite title, like Mr or Ms (Lesson 15); いいえ is "no", and そうですか is "I see" or
"Is that so?" Notice that ゆき answers with せんせいです and leaves out わたしは: the topic is
already clear.

Now a short text. Read it aloud, giving each particle its spoken sound:

> わたしは けんです。がくせいです。
>
> あさ、ごはんを たべます。みずを のみます。がっこうへ いきます。
>
> がっこうで ほんを よみます。それから、うちへ かえります。

I'm Ken. I'm a student. In the morning I have a meal and drink water. I go to school. At
school I read books. Then I go home. (あさ = morning, それから = after that, then; で after a
place means "at", and it's read "de", as spelled.)

## Say it

```speak
わたしは がくせいです。
= I'm a student.
がっこうへ いきます。
= I go to school.
みずを のみます。
= I drink water.
ほんを よみます。
= I read a book.
うちへ かえります。
= I'm going home.
にほんへ いきますか。
= Are you going to Japan?
```

## Trace the three particles

You learned these shapes in Module 1. Trace them once more now that you know their second
job: は, へ and を.

```trace
はへを
```

## Common mistakes

- Writing the particle as it sounds: わたしわ, がっこうえ, みずお. These are spelling
  mistakes every Japanese child is corrected on at school. The particle is は, へ, を.
- The opposite: reading は as "wa" inside a word. はな is "hana", never "wana"; へや is
  "heya".
- Writing を in an ordinary word: をちゃ for おちゃ. を is only ever the particle.
- Putting the particle before the word, English-style: へがっこう. It always comes after.
- Typing *wa* for the topic particle and getting わ. Type *ha*.
- Saying わたしは in every sentence. Once the topic is clear, drop it.

## Key points

- A particle is a short word right after another word that shows its job in the sentence.
- は (topic) is read "wa", へ (direction) is read "e", を (object) is read "o"; inside
  ordinary words は and へ keep their sounds "ha" and "he", and を appears only as a particle.
- Type them *ha*, *he*, *wo*.
- Shape of a sentence: topic は … place へ / object を … verb last. Leave out the topic when
  it's clear.
- か at the end makes a question; です and ます endings are polite.
- Real Japanese has no spaces; this course adds one after each particle to help you.

lessons.title: Punctuation and vertical text
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Lesson 13 you wrote sentences ending in 。 and met a comma 、 after はい. Japanese has its
own set of punctuation marks. A few look like English ones, a few don't exist in English at
all, and every one of them sits in a square of its own, just like a kana. This lesson covers
the marks you'll see every day, where they go, and what changes when Japanese is written in
columns from top to bottom, as it is in most novels, newspapers and manga.

## Every mark takes a full square

Picture the square practice box you traced kana in. In Japanese typesetting every character,
whether a kana, a kanji or a punctuation mark, takes up one such square. Marks made to fit
that square are called **[[full-width]]**. That's why Japanese punctuation looks roomier than
English: 。 has empty space around it, and there's no extra space typed after it, because the
square already provides it.

Your device has both kinds. When you type Japanese, the app gives you the full-width marks:
the full stop key becomes 。 and the comma key becomes 、.

## 。 and 、: the full stop and the comma

| Mark | Name | Everyday name | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| 。 | **[[kuten]]** | まる (circle) | ends a sentence |
| 、 | **[[tōten]]** | てん (dot) | a pause inside a sentence |

。 is a small hollow circle. In horizontal text it sits low in its square, toward the left,
where an English full stop would be. It ends every sentence, including questions that end in
か:

きょうは あめです。 — It's raining today. (きょう = today, あめ = rain)
がくせいですか。 — Are you a student?

、 is a short slanted tick. It marks a pause:
after a word that opens the sentence, after a long topic, between two halves of a sentence,
and sometimes between items in a list. Japanese writers use it more freely than English
writers use commas; read it as "breathe here".

はい、がくせいです。 — Yes, I'm a student.
あした、いっしょに いきましょう。 — Let's go together tomorrow. (あした = tomorrow,
いっしょに = together, いきましょう = let's go)

You may also meet a comma and a full stop shaped like English ones but full-width (，．). Some
scientific and official papers written left to right use them. Everyday texts use 、 and 。.

## 「」 and 『』: quotation marks

| Mark | Name | Job |
|---|---|---|
| 「 」 | **[[kagikakko]]** | quotes speech or thought; marks a name or a term |
| 『 』 | **[[nijūkagikakko]]** | a quote inside a quote; titles of books and films |

The brackets 「」 are the Japanese quotation marks. Their name means "hook brackets", and
that's the shape: the opening one is a hook at the top left, the closing one a hook at the
bottom right. After a quote, the particle と (read "to", as spelled) marks what was said:

せんせいは 「おはようございます」と いいました。 — The teacher said, "Good morning."
ともだちは 「いっしょに いきましょう」と いいました。 — My friend said, "Let's go together."

いいました is "said" (from いう, to say). Notice there's no comma before the quote, and the
sentence's 。 comes after と いいました.

What about the full stop at the end of the quoted sentence itself? Most books and newspapers
leave it out: 「おはようございます」, not 「おはようございます。」. You'll see the second
form in some school writing, and neither is wrong, but the first is what you'll meet most.

『』 are the same hooks drawn double. They go around a quote inside a quote, and around the
title of a book, film or album:

ゆきさんは 「『こころ』を よみました」と いいました。 — Yuki said, "I read *Kokoro*."
(よみました = read, in the past; こころ is a famous Japanese novel.)

## ・, 〜 and ー

| Mark | Name | Job |
|---|---|---|
| ・ | **[[nakaguro]]** | separates the parts of a foreign name; separates short items in a list |
| 〜 | **[[wave dash]]** | "from … to" in ranges; a stretched sound in casual writing |
| ー | (long-vowel mark, Lesson 11) | lengthens the vowel before it |

・ is a dot in the middle of its square. Katakana runs every word together, so a foreign full
name needs it to show where the first name ends: ジョン・スミス (John Smith), マリア・ロペス
(Maria Lopez). It also lists short things: コーヒー・こうちゃ・ジュース (coffee, black tea,
juice).

〜 means "from … to" between two numbers. Shop signs show opening hours like this:
10:00〜20:00, "10 a.m. to 8 p.m." In friendly messages it also drags a sound out: ありがと〜
is a cheerful, stretched "thaaanks".

ー is not punctuation but you'll see it beside these marks. Don't mix it up with 〜 or with
a hyphen; it belongs to the word: コーヒー.

## ？ and ！

Question marks and exclamation marks are borrowed from European writing, and Japanese uses
them in their full-width form: ？ and ！.

In careful writing, such as a letter, a school essay or a newspaper, a question ends with
か。 and needs no ？. In everyday writing, messages, manga and ads, ？ is common, and it's
the only way to show a question that has no か, one asked just by raising your voice:
ゆきさんは？ (And you, Yuki?) ！ shows excitement: いいですね！ (That sounds good!)

When a sentence continues after ？ or ！ inside a line, Japanese leaves one full-width
space after the mark. After 。 and 、, never.

## A note, a sign and a message

A note left on a desk. へ after a name means "To …", and より (yori) after the writer's name
means "From …":

> ゆきさんへ
>
> きょうは あめですね。いっしょに コーヒーを のみませんか。
>
> けんより

To Yuki — It's raining today, isn't it? Would you like to have a coffee together? — From Ken.
(ね at the end asks for agreement, like "isn't it?"; のみませんか is a polite invitation,
"won't you drink …?")

A café sign:

> カフェ・ハナ
>
> 10:00〜20:00
>
> コーヒー・こうちゃ・ジュース

Café Hana. Open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Coffee, tea, juice.

A form you fill in, where ： (a full-width colon) follows each label:

> なまえ：ジョン・スミス

Name: John Smith. (なまえ = name)

And a chat between friends, where ？ and ！ are at home:

```dialogue
# Messages
ゆき: けんさん、あした いっしょに コーヒーを のみませんか？
= Ken, would you like to have a coffee together tomorrow?
けん: いいですね！　なんじ？
= Sounds good! What time?
ゆき: 10じは どうですか。
= How about ten o'clock?
けん: はい、だいじょうぶです。カフェ・ハナで！
= Yes, that works. See you at Café Hana!
ゆき: じゃあ、あした！　ありがと〜
= OK, tomorrow, then! Thaaanks!
```

なんじ is "what time"; 10じ (じゅうじ) is ten o'clock; だいじょうぶ is "fine, all right"; で
after a place is "at". In a printed book, ゆき's first message would end か。, but in a chat
か？ is normal.

## Horizontal and vertical writing

Japanese can be written two ways, and both are completely normal:

| | **[[yokogaki]]** (horizontal) | **[[tategaki]]** (vertical) |
|---|---|---|
| Lines | left to right, like English | top to bottom |
| Next line | below | to the left |
| Where | websites, phones, science and maths books, most textbooks, forms | novels, newspapers, manga, many magazines, greeting cards, calligraphy |
| Books open | on the left, like English books | on the right: the "back" of an English book is the front |

To read vertical text, start at the top right. Read down the first column, then go to the top
of the next column to its left, and so on. Here is a shorter version of the note from above,
in columns. Start in the right-hand column and read each column top to bottom:

| 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| け | の | コ | あ | き | ゆ |
| ん | み | ー | め | ょ | き |
| よ | ま | ヒ | で | う | さ |
| り | せ | ー | す | は | ん |
| | ん | を | ね | | へ |
| | か | | 。 | | |
| | 。 | | | | |

A table can't turn the marks, so here's what a real vertical page does differently:

- ー turns to run downward, a vertical line in the middle of the column. コーヒー in column 4
  would show two short vertical bars.
- 。 and 、 move to the top right of their square, close to the character above them.
- Small kana (ょ in きょう, ゃ, ゅ, っ) sit in the top right of their square, not the bottom
  left as in horizontal text.
- 「」 turn too, becoming corner shapes ﹁ (opening, at the top) and ﹂ (closing, at the
  bottom).
- 〜 becomes a vertical wave.

Everything else, kana and kanji alike, stays upright: you never turn your head to read
Japanese, whichever way it runs.

## Say it

Punctuation is silent, but it tells you where to pause. Read these aloud, with a short breath
at each 、 and a full stop at each 。:

```speak
はい、がくせいです。
= Yes, I'm a student.
きょうは あめですね。
= It's raining today, isn't it?
あした、いっしょに いきましょう。
= Let's go together tomorrow.
せんせいは 「おはようございます」と いいました。
= The teacher said, "Good morning."
なまえは ジョン・スミスです。
= My name is John Smith.
```

## The repetition mark ゝ

You may sometimes meet ゝ, a mark that repeats the kana before it, and ゞ, which repeats it
voiced. It's an **[[iteration mark]]**, mostly seen in older writing and in a few names: the
carmaker Isuzu writes its name いすゞ (the same as いすず). Katakana has its own pair, ヽ and
ヾ. You don't need to write them; just recognise them as "say the last kana again".

## Common mistakes

- Using an English full stop or comma in Japanese text (がくせいです.). Use 。 and 、.
- Adding a space after 。 or 、. The square already holds the space.
- Using English quotation marks ("…") around Japanese speech. Use 「」, and 『』 inside them.
- Writing ？ after か in a formal letter. か。 is enough.
- Reading a vertical page left to right. Start in the top right corner.
- Confusing ー (part of a word) with 〜 (a range or a stretched sound) or a hyphen.

## Key points

- Every mark takes a full square: 。 (kuten) ends a sentence, 、 (tōten) is a pause.
- 「」 quote speech, followed by と いいました; 『』 go inside them and around titles. The 。
  before a closing 」 is usually left out.
- ・ separates parts of foreign names and short list items; 〜 means "from … to" (and stretches
  sounds in casual messages).
- Formal questions end か。; ？ and ！ are for everyday writing.
- Yokogaki runs left to right; tategaki runs top to bottom in columns from right to left. In
  vertical text ー, 「」 and 〜 turn, and 。、 and small kana move to the top right.
- ゝ repeats the kana before it; you only need to recognise it.

lessons.title: First words and greetings
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last core lesson of the course, and the one where kana turns into conversation.
You'll learn about thirty-five greetings and everyday phrases, all written in kana, and,
just as important, *when* to use each one. Japanese greetings change with the time of day,
with the situation (leaving home, starting a meal) and with who you're talking to. Pick the
wrong level and you'll still be understood, but you'll sound either stiff or rude; pick the
right one and people will notice.

## Polite and casual

Lesson 13 introduced です and ます, the polite sentence endings. Many greetings have a
polite form and a short, casual one:

| Polite | Casual | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| おはようございます | おはよう | good morning |
| ありがとうございます | ありがとう | thank you / thanks |
| おやすみなさい | おやすみ | good night |
| おかえりなさい | おかえり | welcome home |

The rule of thumb:

- Use the polite form with anyone you don't know well, anyone older or senior to you (a
  teacher, a boss, a customer), and staff in shops and offices. As a learner, polite is
  always the safe choice.
- Use the casual form with family, close friends, and people younger than you whom you know
  well.

ございます is a very polite word for "there is" or "is"; tacked onto a greeting it simply
makes it formal. It's said "go-zai-mas", with the final す very light.

## Through the day

| Phrase | When |
|---|---|
| おはようございます (ohayō gozaimasu) | in the morning, until about 10 or 11 |
| こんにちは (konnichiwa) | from late morning to early evening |
| こんばんは (konbanwa) | in the evening, after dark |
| おやすみなさい (oyasuminasai) | going to bed, or parting late at night |

こんにちは and こんばんは are the two greetings spelled with the particle は from Lesson 13,
so they end in "wa" but are written は. こんにちわ is a very common mistake, even among
Japanese people in casual messages, but は is the correct spelling.

They are also greetings for people *outside* your circle: a neighbour, a shopkeeper, someone
you meet in the afternoon. You don't say こんにちは to your own family, and co-workers who see
each other every day don't keep repeating it. The morning greeting is different: it's said
to everyone, as おはよう to family and friends and おはようございます to colleagues and
teachers.

## Saying goodbye

さようなら (sayōnara) is the goodbye every learner knows, and it's real, but Japanese people
use it less than you'd expect. It sounds rather final, a parting for a long time. Children
say it to their teacher at the end of the school day, and it's fine at the end of a formal
event, but between friends it would sound oddly heavy. Spoken quickly it's often さよなら.

What people actually say:

| Phrase | Use |
|---|---|
| じゃあね | "bye, then": friends and family |
| またね | "see you": friends and family |
| また あした | "see you tomorrow": classmates, friends, colleagues |
| しつれいします | "excuse me": leaving a teacher's room or an office, and entering one |

しつれいします literally means "I'm going to be rude", that is, "excuse me for disturbing
you". You say it as you go in or out of someone's room and at the end of a phone call.

## Thank you and sorry

| Phrase | Use |
|---|---|
| ありがとうございます | thank you (polite) |
| ありがとう | thanks (casual) |
| どうも ありがとう ございます | thank you very much |
| どういたしまして | you're welcome |
| すみません | excuse me; sorry; thank you for the trouble |
| ごめんなさい | I'm sorry |

For something that's already finished, such as a meal you were served or help that's over,
people often switch to the past form ありがとうございました. Shop staff say it as you leave.

どういたしまして really is "you're welcome", but it can sound a little formal or textbook-like.
Many people just wave thanks away with いいえ (no, not at all) or a quick いえいえ.

すみません is the most useful word in this lesson. It does three jobs:

1. Getting attention: calling a waiter, or before asking a stranger the way. すみません、…
2. A light apology: bumping into someone, being a little late.
3. Thanks, when someone has gone to trouble for you: it acknowledges the bother you've caused
   ("sorry to put you out"), so it's often said where English says "thank you".

In fast speech it often sounds like すいません; write すみません.

ごめんなさい is a real, personal apology, mostly to family, friends and people you're close
to. With a teacher or at work, use すみません (and later you'll learn even more formal ways to
apologise). ごめん is the very casual short form.

## Yes and no

はい (hai) is "yes", but it's also "I'm listening", "here!" when your name is called, and
"here you are" when handing something over.

いいえ (iie) is "no", but Japanese avoids a flat "no" more than English does. To decline
something, people often soften it, for example with a polite thanks, instead of a bare いいえ.
You'll hear いいえ most often in its other use: brushing off thanks or an apology, "not at all".

## Meeting someone

When you meet someone for the first time:

1. はじめまして — "how do you do", literally "for the first time". Only at a first meeting.
2. Your name + です: スミスです (I'm Smith).
3. よろしく おねがいします — "please treat me well". It has no English equivalent; it asks for
   a good relationship from now on. You'll also hear it when someone takes on a job for you,
   or at the start of working together.

The other person answers こちらこそ (kochira koso, "likewise") and よろしく おねがいします.
Among young people or friends of friends, the short よろしく is enough.

さん after a person's name is a polite title: たなかさん is Mr or Ms Tanaka, and it works with
first names too (ゆきさん). Use it for everyone else, but never for yourself: say スミスです,
not スミスさんです.

## Asking and answering

| Phrase | Use |
|---|---|
| おねがいします | please (asking for something): コーヒー、おねがいします |
| どうぞ | please, go ahead; here you are (offering something) |
| わかりました | I understand; OK, will do |
| わかりません | I don't understand; I don't know |
| もう いちど おねがいします | once more, please |

English has one "please"; Japanese has two. おねがいします is for asking: "a coffee, please".
どうぞ is for offering: holding a door, handing over a seat or a cup, "please, go ahead".

## At home and at meals

These come in pairs, and they're said every day in every Japanese home:

| You say | The other person says |
|---|---|
| いってきます (leaving home: "I'm off") | いってらっしゃい ("see you, take care") |
| ただいま (coming home: "I'm home") | おかえりなさい ("welcome home") |

いってきます literally means "I'll go and come back"; いってらっしゃい is "go and come back".
Both have a small っ, so hold the beat: "it-te-ki-mas".

Before eating, put your hands together and say いただきます; after eating, ごちそうさまでした
(more casually, ごちそうさま). Neither has an English equivalent: いただきます is a humble
"I gratefully receive", a thank-you for the food and everyone who made it; ごちそうさまでした
thanks whoever provided the meal. It's also said to the staff as you leave a restaurant.

## A few more

- おげんきですか — "how are you?", literally "are you well?" (げんき = healthy, well). It's for
  someone you haven't seen for a while, not a daily "how are you": you don't ask it of
  someone you saw yesterday. A typical answer: はい、げんきです。
- おめでとうございます — "congratulations", for a birthday, a new job, a wedding. Casual:
  おめでとう.
- いらっしゃいませ — "welcome (come in)", said by staff when you enter a shop or restaurant.
  Customers don't say it back; a nod is enough.

## Pronunciation

- Long vowels matter: おはよう is "o-ha-yō" (よう is a long o), ありがとう "a-ri-ga-tō",
  どうぞ "dō-zo". Give each beat its time.
- こんにちは has five beats: こ・ん・に・ち・は, with ん a full beat of its own.
- The す of ございます, します, です is very light, and often you hear only "s".
- In ごちそうさまでした the し is whispered: "go-chi-sō-sa-ma-desh'ta".
- Each word also has its own pitch: some beats are said higher, some lower (lesson 1). The line
  over a word shows the high beats, and a short tick shows where the pitch drops: [ありがとう:2]
  drops after あり, [すみません:4] after すみませ, and [はい:1] after は, while [こんにちは:0] has no drop
  and stays level to the end. Your word list shows this for every word. You don't need to learn
  it yet; listen and copy the tune.

## Dialogue: meeting a neighbour

```dialogue
# A new neighbour
たなか: こんにちは。
= Hello.
スミス: こんにちは。はじめまして。スミスです。
= Hello. How do you do? I'm Smith.
たなか: はじめまして、たなかです。
= How do you do? I'm Tanaka.
スミス: よろしく おねがいします。
= I'm glad to know you.
たなか: こちらこそ、よろしく おねがいします。スミスさんは がくせいですか。
= Likewise, it's a pleasure. Are you a student, Mr Smith?
スミス: すみません、もう いちど おねがいします。
= Sorry, could you say that once more?
たなか: スミスさんは、がくせいですか。
= Are you a student?
スミス: ああ、はい、がくせいです。
= Oh, yes, I'm a student.
たなか: そうですか。じゃあ、また。
= I see. Well, see you.
スミス: しつれいします。
= Goodbye.
```

じゃあ、また is a friendly short goodbye between neighbours. ああ is "oh", the sound you make
when you suddenly understand.

## Dialogue: at home

```dialogue
# A school day
こども: いってきます！
= I'm off!
おかあさん: いってらっしゃい。
= See you later, take care.
こども: ただいま。
= I'm home.
おかあさん: おかえり。ごはんですよ。
= Welcome back. Dinner's ready.
こども: いただきます。
= (before eating) Thanks for the food.
こども: ごちそうさまでした。おやすみなさい。
= (after eating) That was delicious. Good night.
おかあさん: おやすみ。
= Good night.
```

こども is "child" and おかあさん "mother"; よ at the end of ごはんですよ adds "you know", telling the listener something. The mother uses casual forms with her child
(おかえり, おやすみ); the child uses the full おやすみなさい, which children are taught to say
to their parents.

## Say it

```speak
おはようございます。
= Good morning.
こんにちは。
= Hello.
こんばんは。
= Good evening.
ありがとうございます。
= Thank you.
すみません。
= Excuse me.
はじめまして。よろしく おねがいします。
= How do you do? Glad to know you.
いただきます。
= (before a meal) Thanks for the food.
ごちそうさまでした。
= (after a meal) Thank you, that was delicious.
いってきます。
= I'm off.
ただいま。
= I'm home.
```

## Common mistakes

- Writing こんにちわ or こんばんわ. The last kana is the particle は.
- Saying さようなら to friends every day. Use じゃあね or またね; さようなら is for longer or
  more formal partings.
- Casual forms with a teacher or a stranger (ありがとう, おはよう). Use the polite form.
- Asking おげんきですか every time you see someone. Save it for after time apart.
- Using どうぞ to ask for something. To ask, say おねがいします; どうぞ offers.
- Calling yourself さん (スミスさんです).
- Saying ごめんなさい to your boss. すみません fits there.
- Answering すみません with どういたしまして. When someone thanks you with すみません, a
  simple いいえ works better.

## Key points

- Many greetings have a polite form (おはようございます, ありがとうございます, おやすみなさい)
  and a casual one (おはよう, ありがとう, おやすみ); polite is the safe default.
- こんにちは and こんばんは end in the particle は, read "wa".
- さようなら is a fairly formal or final goodbye; friends say じゃあね or またね, and
  しつれいします is for leaving (and entering) a room.
- すみません is "excuse me", "sorry" and "thanks for the trouble"; ごめんなさい is a personal
  apology.
- おねがいします asks; どうぞ offers.
- Daily pairs: いってきます / いってらっしゃい, ただいま / おかえりなさい, and いただきます
  before a meal, ごちそうさまでした after.
- はじめまして starts a self-introduction at a first meeting, よろしく おねがいします ends it; さん goes after other
  people's names, never your own.

lessons.title: Where kana came from
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now read and write all of hiragana and katakana. This honors lesson asks where they
came from: both grew out of Chinese characters used for their sound, simplified in two
different ways. You'll also meet a poem that uses every kana once, two kana dropped from
spelling in 1946, and the "variant" kana still seen on old shop signs. Along the way you'll
find out why the particle は is read "wa" and why カ and か look related.

Nothing here is needed for the next course. Kanji appear with their readings above them; you
don't need to learn them, only to see the shapes the kana came from.

## Before kana: borrowing Chinese characters

Japanese had no writing system of its own. Chinese characters reached Japan from the Asian
mainland, many of them by way of Korea, and for a long time educated people in Japan wrote in
Chinese. But Japanese is a very different language, with particles and changing verb endings
(たべる, たべます, たべた) that Chinese characters have no natural way to show. Names and poems
were a special problem: a poem is made of sounds, and they had to be written down exactly.

The solution was to borrow characters for their sound only and ignore their meaning. If a
character was read roughly "ya" and another roughly "ma", writing them one after the other
could spell the Japanese word やま (mountain), whatever the two characters meant on their own.
For example, {也|や} and {麻|ま} together spell {也麻|やま}. Characters used this way are called
**[[man'yōgana]]**, after the {万葉集|まんようしゅう} (Man'yōshū), a huge collection of Japanese
poems put together in the 700s that is full of them.

Man'yōgana worked, but it was slow and confusing:

- Each character was a full kanji, often with many strokes, just to write one short sound.
- The same sound could be written with many different characters.
- In a text mixing both uses, readers had to work out whether a character stood for its
  meaning or only for its sound.

Over the next two centuries, two shortcuts grew out of man'yōgana: one by making whole
characters flowing and simple, the other by keeping only a piece of each character. These
became hiragana and katakana.

The word "kana" itself reflects this history. It's usually written {仮名|かな}, "borrowed (or
temporary) names", in contrast to {真名|まな} (mana), "true names", an old word for the
Chinese characters themselves.

## Hiragana: kanji written fast

Write any character quickly with a brush, again and again, and its strokes start to run
together. Chinese and Japanese calligraphy has a very fluid style, **[[cursive script]]**, in which
whole characters become a few sweeping curves. Hiragana came from writing man'yōgana in this
cursive way and then simplifying the shapes even further, until each one was a small, rounded
sign for a single sound.

Here are some well-established pairs. Look at the shape of the kanji, then at the kana, and you
can often see the kana as a quick, rounded version of the whole character.

| Hiragana | Came from | Hiragana | Came from |
|---|---|---|---|
| あ | {安|あん} | な | {奈|な} |
| い | {以|い} | ぬ | {奴|ぬ} |
| う | {宇|う} | ま | {末|まつ} |
| え | {衣|え} | め | {女|め} |
| お | {於|お} | ゆ | {由|ゆ} |
| か | {加|か} | よ | {与|よ} |
| さ | {左|さ} | り | {利|り} |
| た | {太|た} | わ | {和|わ} |

The reading above each kanji is today's, which isn't always the sound it stood for:
{安|あん} and {末|まつ} were used for just "a" and "ma".

The name {平仮名|ひらがな} (hiragana) means something like "plain" or "ordinary" kana, and its
curves show its origin: it was born from a moving brush.

## Katakana: pieces of kanji

In Buddhist temples, monks studying Chinese sutras needed to show how to read them in
Japanese: which ending to add, which particle to supply, how to pronounce a name. They wrote
small notes in the narrow space between the lines. There was no room for full characters, so they wrote just one part of each
man'yōgana: a left side, a top, a corner. These clipped shapes became katakana.

The name says it: {片仮名|かたかな} (katakana) means "fragment kana" or "partial kana".

| Katakana | Came from | Which part |
|---|---|---|
| ア | {阿|あ} | the left side |
| イ | {伊|い} | the left side (the "person" part) |
| ウ | {宇|う} | the top |
| エ | {江|え} | the right side |
| オ | {於|お} | the left side |
| カ | {加|か} | the left side |
| タ | {多|た} | the top half |
| ヌ | {奴|ぬ} | the right side |
| ロ | {呂|ろ} | the top box |
| ル | {流|る} | the bottom |

A few katakana are whole characters that were simple to begin with:

| Katakana | Came from |
|---|---|
| ニ | {二|に} (two) |
| ハ | {八|はち} (eight) |
| ミ | {三|さん} (three), its lines tilted |
| チ | {千|せん} (thousand) |

Some sounds share a source: か and カ both come from {加|か}, う and ウ from {宇|う}, お and
オ from {於|お}, ぬ and ヌ from {奴|ぬ}. Hiragana made the whole character flow; katakana cut
off a piece. That's why some pairs look like cousins (か/カ, へ/ヘ,
り/リ) and others look nothing alike (ぬ/ヌ, あ/ア).

Katakana grew up among scholars, in the margins of serious texts, and kept an angular,
careful look. From the late 1800s many laws and official documents mixed kanji with katakana,
and telegrams were sent in katakana. In the 1900s hiragana took over those jobs, and katakana
settled into the role you learned in module 2: loanwords, foreign names, sound words and
emphasis.

## Women's writing in the Heian period

The **[[Heian period]]** (794–1185) is named after its capital, {平安京|へいあんきょう}
(Heian-kyō), today's Kyoto. In this age of court culture, hiragana became a real writing
system with its own literature.

At court, men were expected to write official documents in Chinese. Hiragana became linked
with women and was called **[[onnade]]**, "women's hand", while writing in Chinese characters was
"men's hand". Women at court used hiragana for letters, diaries, poetry and stories, and
produced some of the greatest works of Japanese literature. Around the year 1000, Murasaki Shikibu wrote {源氏物語|げんじものがたり}
(The Tale of Genji), a long novel of court life, and Sei Shōnagon wrote
{枕草子|まくらのそうし} (The Pillow Book), a collection of sharp observations and lists.

Men used hiragana too, especially for Japanese poetry. Around 935 the poet Ki no Tsurayuki
wrote a travel diary, the {土佐日記|とさにっき} (Tosa Diary), in hiragana, and opened it by
pretending to be a woman, since a kana diary was thought of as women's writing.

Over time the line between "men's" and "women's" writing faded, leading to the mix used today:
kanji for the main parts of words, kana for endings, particles and the rest.

```timeline
title: Kana through the centuries
era: 710–794 | Nara period
era: 794–1185 | Heian period
event: 712 | The Kojiki, an early history, uses man'yōgana for songs and names
event: 8th century | The Man'yōshū poetry collection is compiled, full of man'yōgana
event: 9th century | Hiragana develops from cursive man'yōgana; monks clip man'yōgana into katakana
event: c. 935 | Ki no Tsurayuki writes the Tosa Diary in hiragana
event: c. 1000 | The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book are written in kana
event: 11th century | The iroha poem is known and in use
event: 1900 | One hiragana shape per sound is set for schools; the others become hentaigana
event: 1946 | Modern kana spelling replaces historical spelling; ゐ and ゑ drop out
event: 2017 | Unicode adds hentaigana
caption: Dates for the early centuries are approximate: the scripts changed gradually.
```

## The iroha: every kana once

A **[[pangram]]** is a sentence that uses every letter of an alphabet, like the English "The quick
brown fox jumps over the lazy dog". Japanese has a much more elegant one, the **[[iroha]]**, a poem
that uses every one of the 47 kana of its time exactly once, with no repeats. (ん wasn't
part of it.) It was already known in the 1000s.

Here it is in hiragana, in its traditional form:

> いろはにほへと　ちりぬるを
>
> わかよたれそ　つねならむ
>
> うゐのおくやま　けふこえて
>
> あさきゆめみし　ゑひもせす

A few things to notice:

- Every kana appears once, including ゐ, ゑ and を.
- There are no ゛ marks. Old texts often left out the voicing marks, so わかよ is read
  "waga yo" (my world) and せす at the end is "sezu". The poem only needed each basic shape once.
- It's in old spelling: けふ is the pre-1946 spelling of "today".
- It has a rhythm. The phrases mostly alternate seven and five beats (いろはにほへと is
  seven, ちりぬるを is five; わかよたれそ is the one six), close to the rhythm of much
  Japanese poetry.

In plain English, the poem says roughly this: flowers are bright with color, but they scatter;
nothing in our world lasts forever. Today we cross the deep mountains of change, and we'll no
longer see shallow dreams or be lost in a daze. Its theme is the Buddhist idea that everything
passes, which also explains the serious, quiet tone.

### Iroha as an order

Because it contains every kana once and was easy to memorize, the iroha served for centuries
the way "A, B, C" does in English: as an order. Dictionaries and lists were arranged and numbered
い, ろ, は, に… In modern times the gojūon order from lesson 2 (あいうえお, かきくけこ…), a tidier
arrangement by sound, took over. But the iroha hasn't vanished:

- In Japanese, いろは means "the ABCs" or basics of something, as in "the iroha of cooking".
- Japanese laws and some formal documents still label small sub-items イ, ロ, ハ, the way
  English documents use (a), (b), (c).
- Japanese names for musical notes use iroha order: ハ, ニ, ホ, ヘ, ト, イ, ロ are C, D, E, F,
  G, A, B. C major is {ハ長調|はちょうちょう}.

## ゐ, ゑ and the 1946 spelling reform

The iroha contains two kana you haven't learned: ゐ (katakana ヰ) and ゑ (katakana ヱ). Long
ago they stood for the sounds "wi" and "we", which is why they sit in the わ row in old charts.
Over the centuries Japanese speakers stopped making the w sound in these syllables, and ゐ came
to sound just like い, and ゑ just like え.

Spelling didn't follow the sounds. People kept writing words as classical texts had, a system
now called **[[historical kana usage]]**, and the gap between spelling and speech grew wide:

| Old spelling | Modern spelling | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| けふ | きょう | today |
| てふてふ | ちょうちょう | butterfly |
| かは | かわ | river |
| おもふ | おもう | to think |
| こゑ | こえ | voice |
| ゐる | いる | to be (for people and animals) |

In 1946, the government issued **[[modern kana usage]]**, a new standard that spells words
largely as they're pronounced in modern standard Japanese. ゐ and ゑ were replaced by い and え, and
spellings like けふ became きょう. (The rules were revised in 1986, with only small changes.)

The reform kept a few traditional spellings on purpose, and you already know them: the
particles は, へ and を, read "wa", "e" and "o". That answers the puzzle from lesson 13: in old
spelling, many "wa" sounds were written with は, and the reform kept that spelling for the
particle. It also kept ぢ and づ in words like はなぢ
(nosebleed) and つづく (to continue), where a ち or つ has become voiced.

ゐ and ゑ still appear here and there, mostly to give a name an old-fashioned, classic feel. Two
well-known drink brands spell themselves with them: ニッカウヰスキー (Nikka Whisky) and
ヱビスビール (Yebisu beer). You read ヰ as "i" and ヱ as "e" (the brand names are pronounced
"uisukii" and "ebisu").

## Hentaigana: the kana that were set aside

Early kana writers had no single fixed shape for each sound. Since many kanji had been used
for the same sound, there were several hiragana for "ka": besides the か from {加|か}, there
was one from {可|か}, among others. Writers chose among them for variety or beauty.

In 1900, as schools were standardized across the country, the Ministry of Education's rules
for elementary schools set one hiragana shape for each sound, the ones you've learned. The
others became **[[hentaigana]]**, "variant kana". They weren't banned, but they dropped out of
everyday writing and printing.

You can still see hentaigana:

- on the signs and curtains of traditional shops, especially soba noodle restaurants, which
  often spell そば with variant kana for an old-fashioned look;
- in calligraphy, and in old books, letters and records, which anyone reading historical
  documents has to learn to read.

So that historians and libraries could type them, hentaigana were added to Unicode, the world
standard for computer text, in 2017. Few devices have a font for them yet, so this lesson
describes them rather than showing them.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking katakana came from hiragana, or the other way round. Both came separately from
  man'yōgana: hiragana from whole cursive characters, katakana from pieces.
- Thinking a kana "means" what its source kanji meant. あ doesn't mean "peace" (a meaning of
  {安|あん}); man'yōgana were chosen for sound, and the meaning was set aside.
- Reading ゐ and ゑ as "wi" and "we" in modern words. In anything written today they're read
  "i" and "e".
- Thinking hentaigana are mistakes or "wrong" kana. They're old alternatives that were set
  aside in 1900, still correct in calligraphy and historical writing.

## Key points

- Japanese borrowed Chinese characters; **[[man'yōgana]]** used them for their sound alone, as in
  the 8th-century Man'yōshū.
- Hiragana came from man'yōgana written in cursive and simplified (あ←{安|あん}, い←{以|い},
  か←{加|か}); katakana came from one piece of a man'yōgana (ア←{阿|あ}, イ←{伊|い}, カ←{加|か}),
  first as monks' reading notes.
- In the Heian period (794–1185) hiragana was linked with women's writing (**[[onnade]]**), and
  women at court wrote classics such as The Tale of Genji in it.
- The **[[iroha]]** is a poem using each of 47 kana once; it was the standard order for centuries
  and still labels items (イ, ロ, ハ) and musical notes.
- ゐ and ゑ once sounded "wi" and "we"; the 1946 **[[modern kana usage]]** replaced them with い and
  え and spelled words by sound, but kept は, へ, を for particles.
- **[[Hentaigana]]** are the variant kana set aside in 1900; they live on in calligraphy, shop
  signs and, since 2017, in Unicode.

lessons.title: Typing Japanese on phones and computers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In this app you type romaji and it becomes kana: neko gives ねこ, and capitals give katakana.
That's a small version of what Japanese people use every day. This lesson shows how real
Japanese typing works on a computer and on a phone, so you can set up your own devices, type
messages and search the web in Japanese. It also collects the tricky cases (ん, っ, small
kana, ー, ぢ and づ, を) in one place.

Nothing new about kana is taught here, and you can read the lesson without changing any
settings. If you'd like to try along, add a Japanese keyboard on your device first (see
"Setting it up" below).

## Two steps: kana, then kanji

Japanese typing on a computer happens in two steps.

1. You type kana. You type romaji on an ordinary keyboard, and the input software turns
   it into hiragana as you go, usually shown underlined to mean "not finished yet".
2. You convert. Press the space bar, and the software offers kanji (or katakana) for what
   you typed. Press Enter to accept it.

The software that does this sits between the keyboard and every app on your device. Windows,
macOS, Android and iOS each come with one; on Linux you may need to install one.

Try it in your head with にほんご (the Japanese language). You type nihongo; the screen shows
にほんご, underlined; you press Space and it becomes {日本語|にほんご}; you press Enter, and
it's done. If you press Enter without converting, you keep the hiragana にほんご. That's often
what you want: words that are usually written in kana, particles and verb endings are simply
confirmed as they are.

## Kanji conversion and homophones

The second step is called **[[kanji conversion]]**, in Japanese {変換|へんかん} (henkan). It's
needed because Japanese has many words that sound the same but are written with different
kanji. The software has to guess which one you mean.

| You type | Some choices | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| はし (hashi) | {橋|はし} | bridge |
| | {箸|はし} | chopsticks |
| | {端|はし} | edge |
| きしゃ (kisha) | {記者|きしゃ} | reporter |
| | {汽車|きしゃ} | steam train |
| | {貴社|きしゃ} | your company (formal) |

If the first guess is wrong, press Space again: a list of **[[candidates]]** opens, and each press
moves to the next one. Pick the right one with the arrow keys or its number, and press Enter.
The software learns from your choices and puts the words you use most at the top.

Conversion works best on whole phrases, not single words. Type a short phrase, like
"hashi wo watatta" (crossed the bridge), and the software uses the context: with を わたった
after it, はし is far more likely to be {橋|はし} than {箸|はし}. Long sentences are split
into parts, and if the software splits them in the wrong place you can move between the parts
and fix each one.

For a learner, conversion has a useful side effect: you can only type kanji by typing their
reading. You'll never need to look up how to "spell" a kanji on a keyboard; if you can say it,
you can type it.

### Useful keys on a computer

These work in the Japanese input software built into Windows, and many also work on other
systems:

| Key | While typing, turns your kana into |
|---|---|
| F6 | hiragana |
| F7 | katakana |
| F8 | half-width katakana |
| F9 | full-width romaji |
| F10 | half-width romaji |

F7 is handy for loanwords: type ko-hi-, press F7, and you get コーヒー without searching the
candidate list.

**[[Full-width]]** and **[[half-width]]** are two sizes of character. Japanese text sits on a grid of
squares, and full-width characters take a whole square: all kana and kanji, and the wide
letters and digits (ＡＢＣ１２３) sometimes used in Japanese text. Half-width characters take
half a square: ordinary English letters and digits, and an old narrow katakana (ｶﾀｶﾅ) that
appears on receipts and in old systems. In everyday writing, use full-width kana and
half-width English letters and numbers.

### Keys on a Japanese keyboard

A keyboard sold in Japan has the same letters as yours plus a few extra keys. You'll see
{変換|へんかん} (henkan, convert) and {無変換|むへんかん} (muhenkan, no conversion) on either
side of a short space bar, a key labeled {半角|はんかく}/{全角|ぜんかく} (half-width /
full-width) at the top left that switches Japanese input on and off, and a key labeled
カタカナ/ひらがな. Every
letter key is also printed with a kana, for the kana input method below.

## Romaji input and kana input

Typing romaji is called **[[romaji input]]**, and it's by far the most common method. It takes two
keystrokes for most kana (k + a for か), but you only need to know the Latin keyboard.

The other method is **[[kana input]]**: each key of a Japanese keyboard is labeled with a kana,
and one press types one kana (the key for か types か). It's faster once learned, but you must
learn a second keyboard layout, and fewer people use it. If you're learning on a keyboard
without kana printed on the keys, stick with romaji input.

## The tricky cases

Most kana are typed just as you learned them in this course: ka, shi, tsu, fu, kya, ja. A few
need care. The app's converter handles the common cases (doubled consonants, x for small
kana, the hyphen) the same way your computer and phone do; try the rarer spellings in the
table on your own device.

| To get | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ん | nn | Safe at the end of a word and before a consonant. A single n also works before most consonants: kanji gives かんじ. |
| ん before a vowel or y | n' | kin'en gives きんえん (no smoking); kinen gives きねん (anniversary). kon'ya gives こんや (tonight). Input software differs on nn here: in this app nn before a vowel or y gives ん plus an n-kana (kinnen gives きんねん, konnya gives こんにゃ), so n' is the safe choice everywhere. |
| っ | double the next consonant | kitte gives きって, kippu gives きっぷ, zasshi gives ざっし. Before ch, double the c: kocchi gives こっち. |
| small kana alone | x or l before it | xtu or ltu gives っ; xa gives ぁ; xya gives ゃ. |
| ー | the hyphen key | ko-hi- in katakana gives コーヒー; ra-men gives ラーメン. Doubling the vowel instead (koohii) gives コオヒイ. |
| ぢ, づ | di, du | ji and zu give じ and ず. So はなぢ is hanadi, つづく is tsuduku. |
| を | wo | o gives お. |
| は, へ as particles | ha, he | The keyboard follows the spelling, not the sound: watashi ha gives わたしは. |
| loanword sounds | fa, vu, thi, dhi | ファ, ヴ, ティ, ディ; or build any of them with x: te + xi gives てぃ. |

Two habits help. First, type the way the word is spelled, not the way it sounds: the
particle は is "ha", おおきい is ookii and とおり is toori, and えいご is eigo even though
it sounds like "ēgo". Second, when the software shows something odd, look at the underlined
kana before converting. Most typing mistakes are a missing n or a missing doubled consonant,
and they're easy to spot in kana.

Punctuation comes out Japanese too: the period key gives 。 and the comma key gives 、 while
Japanese input is on. On a US keyboard the square brackets [ ] usually give the Japanese
quotation marks 「」.

## Typing on a phone: the 12-key layout and flick input

On phones, most Japanese people don't use a full keyboard at all. They use the **12-key
layout**, a grid descended from the number pad of older mobile phones. Each key carries a
whole row of the gojūon table:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| あ | か | さ |
| た | な | は |
| ま | や | ら |
| ゛゜ small | わ | 、。？！ |

On most phones, the bottom-left key changes the kana you just typed: press it after か for が,
after は for ば and again for ぱ, and after つ for small っ or づ (press again to move between
them). The bottom-right key gives punctuation.

There are two ways to choose a kana from a key.

- **[[Toggle input]]**: tap the key repeatedly. One tap of あ gives あ, two taps い, three う, and
  so on, as on old phone keypads.
- **[[Flick input]]**: touch the key and slide your finger. A tap gives the a-sound, and the four
  directions give the other vowels: left for i, up for u, right for e, down for o. So for す,
  touch the さ key and flick up; for ね, touch な and flick right.

The direction is the same on every key, so once you know "left i, up u, right e, down o", you
know the whole keyboard. The keys for the rows with gaps are a little different: on the わ key,
a tap gives わ, left gives を, up gives ん and right gives ー; the や key gives や, ゆ and よ on
tap, up and down.

Flick input is fast in practice, because each kana is one touch. Above the keyboard, a bar of **[[predictive conversion]]**
suggestions shows likely words and kanji as you type, so you often tap a whole word after a
kana or two.

Most phones also offer a full QWERTY keyboard with romaji input, which you may find easier at
first. It's worth trying flick input anyway: it trains you to think of kana by their rows, the
gojūon table you learned in this course.

## Setting it up

You add Japanese as an extra keyboard or input source in your device's settings, under
language or keyboard settings, then switch to it when you need it. On a computer, choose the
Japanese input method and set it to romaji input (it usually is by default). On a phone, add
the Japanese keyboard and choose the 12-key ("kana") layout, the QWERTY ("romaji") layout, or
both. Menus change between versions, so look for "Japanese" in your keyboard settings.

## Common mistakes

- Typing a single n before a vowel: kinen gives きねん, not きんえん. Use n'.
- Expecting "wa" to give the particle は. It gives わ; type ha.
- Expecting "o" to give the particle を. It gives お; type wo.
- Typing zu or ji for ぢ and づ in words like はなぢ and つづく. Use di and du.
- Pressing Space on everything. Particles, endings and kana words are confirmed with Enter as
  they are; converting them can turn them into unwanted kanji.
- Typing long vowels the way they sound: えいご is eigo, not eego, and ありがとう is
  arigatou, not arigatoo.
- Sending half-width katakana (ｶﾀｶﾅ) by accident. If your katakana look narrow, convert with F7
  instead of F8.

## Key points

- Computer typing has two steps: type romaji to get kana, then press Space for **kanji
  conversion** and Enter to accept. Kana-only words are just confirmed with Enter.
- Many words sound alike ({橋|はし}, {箸|はし}, {端|はし}), so the software offers
  **[[candidates]]** and uses the context of the phrase.
- **[[Romaji input]]** is the usual method; **[[kana input]]** uses kana printed on the keys.
- Tricky cases: nn for ん (n' before a vowel or y), a doubled consonant for っ, x or l for small kana, the hyphen
  for ー, di and du for ぢ and づ, wo for を, ha and he for the particles.
- On phones, the **[[12-key layout]]** has one key per gojūon row. With **[[flick input]]**, a tap is
  the a-sound and left, up, right, down give i, u, e, o.

lessons.title: Kana in print and handwriting
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've traced every kana in this course, stroke by stroke. Then you look at a Japanese book,
a sign or a website, and some kana look a little different from what you learned to write.
That isn't a mistake on either side: printed type and handwriting follow different rules. This
lesson explains the differences, introduces the two main families of Japanese type, and gives
practical advice for neat handwriting, ending with the one thing every learner wants to write
well: their own name.

## Fonts are designed, handwriting is written

When you write by hand, each kana is a series of strokes made in a fixed order, and the shape
comes from the movement: where the pen starts, where it lifts off, which way it turns. A
font is a drawing of the finished shape, made by a designer to look good on paper or a screen
at many sizes. Designers often join strokes that are separate in handwriting, separate strokes
that join, or simplify small details. As a reader, you learn to see both forms as the same
kana. As a writer, follow the handwritten form, which is the one this app traces.

The best-known differences:

| Kana | What you may see in print | How to write it |
|---|---|---|
| き | the curved bottom part joined to the slanting line | four strokes: two short horizontals, the slanting line, then the bottom curve as a separate stroke |
| さ | the bottom curve joined to the slanting line | three strokes: the horizontal, the slanting line, then the bottom curve separately |
| り | the two parts joined into one line | two strokes: a short left stroke, then the long right one; a small gap between them |
| ふ | the first strokes linked into one | four separate strokes |
| そ | either a single zigzag stroke, or a separate short mark on top | the single-stroke form taught in school; both are correct |
| ゆ | the inner curl and the middle line looking like one shape | two strokes: the curled stroke first, then the long line through the middle |

The き and さ difference surprises most learners. In many fonts these kana look as if the
bottom curve grows straight out of the slanting stroke. Write them that way and your
handwriting will look like an imitation of print. Lift the pen and make the curve its own
stroke.

Practice the kana from the table in their handwritten form:

```trace
きさりふそゆ
```

There's also a typeface designed to bridge the gap, **[[kyōkashotai]]**, "textbook style". It
imitates careful handwriting with a brush or pen, stroke for stroke, and Japanese school
textbooks use it so that children learn to write the shapes they read. If your device has a
textbook-style font, it's a good model for your own writing.

## Mincho and gothic

Almost all Japanese text you'll read is set in one of two families of type.

**[[Mincho]]** ({明朝|みんちょう}) type has thin horizontal strokes, thicker vertical strokes, and
small triangular tips on the right end of horizontals, as if made with a brush or pen held at
an angle. The name refers to the Ming dynasty of China, whose printed books inspired the
style. Mincho is the standard type for books, novels, newspapers and long passages of text.
In spirit it's like a serif typeface (such as Times) in English.

**[[Gothic]]** type has strokes of even thickness all the way along, with plain, square ends. It's
clear at small sizes and from a distance, so it's used for signs, headings, labels and most
screen text, including the text in this app. It's like a sans-serif typeface (such as Arial).
The name has nothing to do with medieval Gothic lettering; it comes from an old English name
for sans-serif type.

A third style you'll see often is **[[rounded gothic]]**, gothic with rounded ends, which looks
soft and friendly; it's popular for children's materials, packaging and casual signs.

| Style | Look | Typical uses |
|---|---|---|
| mincho | thin horizontals, thick verticals, small tips at stroke ends | books, newspapers, formal documents |
| gothic | even strokes, square ends | signs, headings, screens, labels |
