| rounded gothic | even strokes, round ends | children's books, packaging, friendly signs |
| textbook style | like careful handwriting | school textbooks |

You don't need to choose a font to learn Japanese, but knowing the families helps you read:
the same kana can look sharp and elegant in mincho and blocky in gothic. Fonts you may meet on
your devices include Yu Mincho and Yu Gothic on Windows, Hiragino Mincho and Hiragino Sans on
Apple devices, and Noto Serif CJK and Noto Sans CJK (the mincho and gothic styles) on many
others.

## Writing neatly in the square

The tracing pads in this course are squares with a dashed cross, like Japanese practice
paper. That square is the key to neat Japanese. Japanese schoolchildren write essays on
**[[genkō yōshi]]**, manuscript paper printed with a grid of squares, one square for every
character.

- One kana, one square. Every kana gets its own square, and so do small kana (っ, ゃ),
  ー and the punctuation marks 。 and 、.
- Center and fill. Place each kana in the middle of its square, filling most of it. A row
  of kana that are all about the same size looks neat even if each one isn't perfect.
- Small kana are small. っ, ゃ, ゅ, ょ are about half size. In horizontal writing they sit
  in the lower left of their square; in vertical writing, in the upper right.
- Marks at the top right. ゛ and ゜ go at the top right of the kana, inside the same square,
  and are written last.
- ー follows the text. It's horizontal in horizontal writing and vertical in vertical
  writing.
- Kana are a little smaller than kanji. When you mix them, many people write kana slightly
  smaller than the kanji around them, which makes the kanji stand out as the main words.

### How strokes end

Japanese teachers talk about three ways a stroke can end, and getting them right makes your
writing look natural:

- **[[tome]]**, a stop: the pen stops firmly and lifts straight off, giving a blunt end. Most
  horizontal strokes end this way.
- **[[hane]]**, a flick: at the end the pen turns sharply and flicks off, often pointing toward the
  next stroke. The first stroke of い ends with a small hane toward the second.
- **[[harai]]**, a sweep: the pen keeps moving as it lifts, so the stroke thins out to a point, as
  at the end of ノ or of the long upward stroke of シ.

You don't need to master these to be readable, but if your writing looks stiff, look at where
your strokes end. Hane and harai are what give handwriting its flow.

## Common handwriting mistakes

Many of these you met as lookalikes in the core lessons. In handwriting they matter even more,
because a reader can't rely on a font's clear shapes.

- シ and ツ, ソ and ン. The direction of the long stroke decides. シ and ン: the long stroke
  sweeps up from the bottom left. ツ and ソ: it comes down from the top. The short strokes of
  シ are placed one above the other at the left; those of ツ sit side by side along the top.
- ぬ and め, ね and れ. ぬ and ね end with a small loop; め and れ don't. Close the loop
  clearly, and don't add one where there isn't one.
- る and ろ. る ends with a loop at the bottom; ろ ends open.
- は and ほ. ほ has a horizontal line across the top of the right part; は doesn't.
- ち and ら, さ and ち. ら has a short separate stroke on top where ち has a crossing
  horizontal. さ and ち are near mirror images: さ's bottom curve bulges to the left and is a
  separate stroke; ち's bulges to the right and continues from its vertical stroke.
- ク, ケ and タ. ケ's second stroke is a horizontal, and its third sweeps down from the middle
  of it;
  タ has a short extra stroke inside ク.
- ー and the kanji {一|いち}. In handwriting they can look alike. ー follows a kana and is
  a little shorter and lighter; in vertical text it turns vertical, while {一|いち} always
  stays horizontal.
- Strokes in the wrong order. It may look fine on its own, but the shape and balance come
  from the order, and wrong habits are hard to unlearn. If a kana keeps looking odd, trace it
  again with the arrows.
- Writing print forms. Joining き's or さ's bottom curve to the slanting line, or drawing り
  as one line, because that's how a font shows it.

## Writing your name in katakana

Foreign names are written in katakana, and writing your own is a satisfying first real use of
it. Module 2 showed how English sounds are fitted to Japanese; here are a few practical rules.

1. Write the sound, not the spelling. "Smith" is スミス (su-mi-su): the extra vowels come
   from Japanese syllables, not from the English letters. "Kate" is ケイト, "Chris" is クリス.
2. Long vowels take ー. "Laura" is ローラ; "James" is ジェームズ; "Emily" is エミリー,
   with the long final "ee" sound shown by ー.
3. Choose the common spelling. Many names have one usual katakana form, and a quick search
   for your name plus "katakana" will show it. Some have more than one in use:
   "David" is often デイビッド or デービッド.
4. Separate given and family names with ・ (a small dot in the middle of the line):
   ジョン・スミス, エミリー・ブラウン.
5. Write it in the square. One kana, ー or ・ per square. Each kana, including ッ and the
   small ャ ュ ョ, follows the rules above.

| Name | Katakana | Beats |
|---|---|---|
| Sarah | サラ | sa-ra |
| John | ジョン | jo-n |
| Michael | マイケル | ma-i-ke-ru |
| Emily | エミリー | e-mi-ri-ー |
| Daniel | ダニエル | da-ni-e-ru |
| Brown | ブラウン | bu-ra-u-n |

Write your own name five times in the squares of a notebook (or on graph paper), checking the
direction of every stroke of シ, ツ, ソ and ン if your name has them. Then write it once
vertically, top to bottom, with any ー turned vertical.

## Key points

- Fonts are designed shapes; handwriting follows strokes. Write き and さ with a separate bottom
  curve, り with a gap, ふ in four strokes, ゆ in two.
- **[[Mincho]]** (thin and thick strokes) is the type of books and newspapers; **[[gothic]]** (even
  strokes) is for signs, headings and screens; **[[rounded gothic]]** is the friendly variant.
- **[[Kyōkashotai]]**, textbook style, imitates careful handwriting and is a good model.
- On **[[genkō yōshi]]** and in practice squares: one character per square, centered, small kana
  half size, ゛゜ top right, ー following the direction of the text.
- Stroke endings: **[[tome]]** (stop), **[[hane]]** (flick), **[[harai]]** (sweep).
- Write your name in katakana by its sound, with ー for long vowels and ・ between names.

questions.stem: What are man'yōgana?
choices: Chinese characters used for their sound, not their meaning
An early form of katakana used only by monks
Kanji that were simplified by the 1946 reform
Hiragana written by women at the Heian court
questions.explanation: Man'yōgana are whole Chinese characters borrowed for their sound alone, so {也|や} plus {麻|ま} could spell やま whatever the characters meant. Katakana and hiragana both grew out of them later; they weren't themselves a kind of katakana or hiragana.

questions.stem: Where did hiragana come from?
choices: From pieces cut off kanji, written beside Chinese texts
From man'yōgana written in flowing cursive and simplified
From katakana, rounded off to look softer
From a new set of signs invented in 1900
questions.explanation: Hiragana are whole man'yōgana written quickly in cursive brush style until they became small rounded signs. Cutting off a piece of a kanji is how katakana began; hiragana didn't come from katakana, and 1900 is when one shape per sound was fixed, not when hiragana began.

questions.stem: Which katakana came from the left side of the kanji {阿|あ}?
questions.explanation: ア is the left part of {阿|あ}. ウ is the top of {宇|う}, オ is part of {於|お}, and イ is the left side of {伊|い}.

questions.stem: Match each hiragana to the kanji it developed from.
questions.explanation: あ←{安|あん}, い←{以|い}, か←{加|か}, め←{女|め}, わ←{和|わ}: each is the whole kanji written in cursive. {阿|あ} and {江|え} are sources of katakana (ア and エ), which took only a piece of the character.

questions.stem: The name katakana ({片仮名|かたかな}) means roughly "fragment kana". Why does the name fit?
choices: Katakana were used only for parts of words
Katakana are made of one part of a kanji
Katakana were written on fragments of paper
Katakana have fewer kana than hiragana
questions.explanation: Each katakana keeps just one piece of a man'yōgana: ア is the left side of {阿|あ}, ウ the top of {宇|う}. The name isn't about parts of words or scraps of paper, and both scripts have the same set of sounds.

questions.stem: In the Heian period, hiragana was known as onnade. What does onnade mean?
questions.explanation: Onnade means "women's hand". At the Heian court men were expected to write official texts in Chinese, and hiragana was linked with women, who wrote classics such as The Tale of Genji in it. Temple writing fits katakana's origin among monks better.

questions.stem: What makes the iroha poem special?
choices: It lists the kana in gojūon order
It was the first text ever written in katakana
It uses each kana of its time exactly once
It is written only with the five vowels
questions.explanation: The iroha uses each of the 47 kana of its time once and only once, which is why it served as an alphabet order. Its order comes from the words of the poem, not from the gojūon table (あいうえお…), which is a different, later order.

questions.stem: In iroha order, which kana comes after い and ろ?
questions.explanation: The poem begins いろはにほへと, so the order is い, ろ, は, に, ほ… That's why sub-items in Japanese laws are labeled イ, ロ, ハ, the way English uses (a), (b), (c). に and ほ come after は.

questions.stem: Which two kana were dropped from everyday spelling by the 1946 reform?
questions.explanation: ゐ and ゑ had long sounded like い and え, and modern kana usage replaced them. を, は and へ were kept for particles, ぢ and づ were kept in words like はなぢ and つづく, and ん was never in question.

questions.stem: Before 1946, "today" was spelled けふ. Type the modern spelling in hiragana (kyou): ___
questions.explanation: The modern spelling is きょう, written as it sounds. けふ is the historical kana spelling, read "kyō" even before the reform.

questions.stem: The old spelling こゑ (voice) is written in modern kana as the word you hear. Listen. Which is it?
questions.explanation: You heard こえ, the modern spelling: ゑ became え in 1946. こゑ is the old spelling, not the modern one; こい ends in "i", and ごえ starts with a voiced "go".

questions.stem: What are hentaigana?
choices: Variant hiragana set aside when one shape per sound was fixed in 1900
Kanji simplified after the Second World War
questions.explanation: Hentaigana are the other hiragana shapes, from other source kanji, that dropped out of everyday use when the 1900 school rules chose one shape per sound. They still appear in calligraphy and on traditional shop signs, and Unicode added them in 2017.

questions.stem: Why is the particle は read "wa"?
choices: The 1946 reform kept the particle's traditional spelling, though it is pronounced "wa"
は is pronounced "wa" in every word
It is a printing mistake that was never corrected
は is the katakana form of わ
questions.explanation: Modern kana usage spells most words by sound but deliberately kept は, へ and を for the particles. In ordinary words, は is read "ha" (はな, はし). It isn't a mistake, and the katakana for "wa" is ワ.

questions.stem: You type "nihongo" and the screen shows にほんご, underlined. What does pressing Space do?
choices: Confirms the hiragana as it is
Converts it, offering {日本語|にほんご}
Adds a space after にほんご
questions.explanation: While Japanese input is on, Space starts kanji conversion: にほんご becomes {日本語|にほんご}, and Enter accepts it. Pressing Enter without converting is what keeps the hiragana as it is.

questions.stem: Why does kanji conversion often offer a list of candidates?
choices: Many words sound the same but are written with different kanji
Every kanji has exactly one reading
The software can't tell hiragana from katakana
Kanji can only be typed with kana input
questions.explanation: Homophones are common: はし can be {橋|はし} (bridge), {箸|はし} (chopsticks) or {端|はし} (edge). The software guesses from context and lets you choose. Kanji are typed by their reading with romaji input too, not only with kana input.

questions.stem: Type "kin'en" (no smoking) in hiragana. Remember: ん before a vowel needs n': ___
questions.explanation: Type "kin'en" to get きんえん. With a single n, "kinen" gives きねん (anniversary), a different word; and in this app "kinnen" gives きんねん, because nn before a vowel is read as ん plus ね.

questions.stem: Which keystrokes give きねん (anniversary)?
questions.explanation: きねん is ki-ne-n, so "kinen" is right: the final n becomes ん. "kin'en" makes ん before the e, giving きんえん (no smoking); "kinnen" gives きんねん in this app; "kien" gives きえん.

questions.stem: How do you type the particle を on a computer?
questions.explanation: を is typed "wo". Typing "o" gives お, which sounds the same but is the wrong spelling for the particle; "wa" gives わ.

questions.stem: Type "kitte" (stamp) in hiragana. Double the t for small っ: ___
questions.explanation: Doubling the consonant that follows っ gives small っ: "kitte" becomes きって. "kite" would give きて, a different word with one beat fewer.

questions.stem: Which keystrokes type はなぢ (nosebleed) with the correct spelling?
questions.explanation: ぢ is typed "di". "hanaji" and "hanazi" both give はなじ, which sounds the same but is spelled wrong; "hanachi" gives はなち.

questions.stem: With flick input, you touch the た key and flick up. Which kana do you get?
questions.explanation: Up is the u-sound on every key, so the た key gives つ. Left gives ち (i), right gives て (e) and down gives と (o).

questions.stem: On the 12-key layout with toggle input, you tap the か key three times. Which kana do you get?
questions.explanation: Toggle input steps through the row: one tap か, two き, three く. け would take four taps and こ five.

questions.stem: On the わ key of a phone keyboard, which way do you flick for ん?
questions.explanation: On the わ key, a tap is わ, left is を, up is ん and right is ー. The わ row has gaps, so its key holds these instead of the usual five sounds.

questions.stem: Listen, then type the word in katakana (use CAPITALS, and the hyphen key for ー): ___
questions.explanation: You heard コーヒー (coffee): type KO-HI- (or ko-hi-, then F7 on a computer). Each long vowel is ー, typed with the hyphen key; KOHI would give コヒ, which is too short.

questions.stem: Your katakana come out narrow, like ｶﾀｶﾅ. What happened?
choices: They were turned into kana input
They were converted to half-width katakana
questions.explanation: Narrow katakana are half-width, an old form found on receipts and in old systems (F8 in Windows Japanese input). Convert with F7 for normal full-width katakana. Mincho is a type style, not a width.

questions.stem: In this app, capitals give katakana. Which keystrokes type ラーメン (ramen)?
questions.explanation: The long vowel is ー, typed with the hyphen key: RA-MEN. RAAMEN gives ラアメン (in katakana, long vowels use ー, not a second ア), and RAMEN is a beat short.

questions.stem: In many fonts the bottom curve of き looks joined to the slanting stroke. How many strokes do you use to write き by hand?
questions.explanation: き has four strokes: two short horizontals, the slanting line, and the bottom curve as a separate stroke. Copying the joined print form gives three, which looks like an imitation of a font.

questions.stem: Which type style has thin horizontal strokes, thicker vertical strokes and small triangular tips?
questions.explanation: That's mincho, the type of books and newspapers. Gothic and rounded gothic have strokes of even thickness, and textbook style imitates handwriting.

questions.stem: Which type style is most typical of signs, headings and screens?
questions.explanation: Gothic, with even strokes and plain ends, stays clear at small sizes and from a distance. Mincho is mainly for long text in books and newspapers, and hentaigana are old variant kana, not a type style.

questions.stem: Why do Japanese school textbooks use kyōkashotai (textbook style)?
choices: It shows every kana in katakana
It imitates careful handwriting, so children read the shapes they write
questions.explanation: Textbook style follows handwritten strokes, so a child reading it sees き and さ with their separate bottom curves, as they should be written. It has nothing to do with size, hentaigana or katakana.

questions.stem: In vertical writing on genkō yōshi, where does a small っ go?
choices: In the upper right of its own square
In the lower left of its own square
Squeezed into the square of the kana before it
In the middle of its square, full size
questions.explanation: Small kana get their own square and sit in the upper right in vertical writing. The lower left is their place in horizontal writing; they never share a square or grow to full size, which would turn っ into つ.

questions.stem: Which katakana has two short strokes stacked on the left and a long stroke sweeping up from the bottom left?
questions.explanation: That's シ. ツ has its short strokes side by side along the top and a long stroke coming down from the top; ソ also has its long stroke coming down; ン has only one short stroke.

questions.stem: A stroke that ends with a sharp flick, like the end of the first stroke of い, is called…
questions.explanation: A flick is hane. Tome is a firm stop, harai is a sweep that thins to a point, and onnade is an old name for hiragana writing.

questions.stem: Type the name Emily in katakana (use CAPITALS: EMIRI-): ___
questions.explanation: Emily is エミリー: e-mi-ri with ー for the long final "ee". Without the hyphen you get エミリ, a beat short.

questions.stem: Type the family name Smith in katakana (use CAPITALS: SUMISU): ___
questions.explanation: Smith is スミス: Japanese has no "sm" cluster or final "th", so vowels are added and "th" becomes ス. Write the sound, not the English spelling.

questions.stem: Which is the usual katakana spelling of the name Laura?
questions.explanation: Laura is ローラ: the "au" is said as a long "o", shown with ー. ラウラ follows the English letters instead of the sound; ロウラ and ラーラ aren't the spellings used for this name.

questions.stem: How do you separate a given name and a family name written in katakana?
choices: With ・, as in ジョン・スミス
questions.explanation: A small middle dot ・ separates the parts of a foreign name: ジョン・スミス. 、 and 。 are the comma and period, and ー marks a long vowel.

questions.stem: Which hiragana has a horizontal line across the top of its right part?
questions.explanation: ほ closes its right part with a line across the top; は doesn't, which is the easiest way to tell them apart. い has no horizontal lines at all, and ま isn't split into a left and right part.

questions.stem: Listen. Which name did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard マイケル (Michael): ma-i-ke-ru. マイクル has ku in place of ke, メイケル starts with me, and マケル is missing the i.

questions.stem: Which script is mainly used for words borrowed from other languages, such as "coffee"?
questions.explanation: Katakana writes loanwords, foreign names and sound effects: コーヒー (kōhī, coffee). Hiragana writes grammar endings and native words, kanji carry meanings, and romaji is only Japanese in Latin letters.

questions.stem: In the sentence {毎朝|まいあさ}コーヒーを{飲|の}みます。 (I drink coffee every morning), which part is written in hiragana?
questions.explanation: を is a hiragana grammar word (read o) that marks what is drunk. コーヒー is katakana, a loanword; {毎朝|まいあさ} and {飲|の} are kanji, shown here with furigana above them.

questions.stem: What is romaji?
choices: Japanese written in the Latin alphabet
questions.explanation: Romaji is Japanese in Latin letters, like "sushi" or "arigatō". The rounded script is hiragana, characters from Chinese are kanji, and small kana over kanji are furigana.

questions.stem: What are the small kana printed above a kanji, as in {山|やま}, called?
questions.explanation: Furigana show how a kanji is read. They are written in kana, but the name for them is furigana, not katakana; the gojūon is the kana table.

questions.stem: How many beats (morae) does いいえ (iie, no) have?
questions.explanation: Each kana is one beat: い・い・え is three. The double い is held for two beats, so it is not "ee-ay" in two beats, as an English speaker might say it.

questions.stem: How many beats does にほん (nihon, Japan) have?
questions.explanation: に・ほ・ん: three beats, because ん counts as a beat of its own. In English we would call "ni-hon" two syllables, but Japanese counts the final n.

questions.stem: Which kana is "e"?
questions.explanation: え is e, as in "bed". あ is a, お is o, and う is u; え and う both begin with a short dash at the top, but え continues in a zigzag.

questions.stem: Which kana is "o"?
questions.explanation: お is o. It is easy to confuse with あ (a): look for the separate little dash at the top right, which お has and あ doesn't.

questions.stem: What is the usual order of the Japanese vowels?
questions.explanation: あ い う え お: a, i, u, e, o. The English order a, e, i, o, u is the usual wrong guess. The whole kana table and Japanese dictionaries follow a, i, u, e, o.

questions.stem: How is Japanese う different from the "oo" in English "food"?
choices: It is said with the lips tightly rounded
It is said with relaxed lips, not pushed forward
questions.explanation: う is short and unrounded: keep the lips relaxed and flat. English "oo" pushes the lips forward into a circle, which is exactly what to avoid. う is not long unless it's written twice, and it is not silent (though it can be whispered, as in す).

questions.stem: Which description of え is right?
questions.explanation: え is the e of "bed", held steady. English "say" glides from e to ee; Japanese え doesn't. "ee" is い and the "a" of "father" is あ.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The five vowels in order: あ a, い i, う u, え e, お o. Watch あ and お: お has the extra dash at the top right.

questions.stem: Type "ie" (house) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: いえ (ie) — house: type "ie" and the app writes い and え. Two beats, "i-e".

questions.stem: Type "ao" (blue) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: あお (ao) — blue: あ then お, two clear beats.

questions.stem: Type "iie" (no) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: いいえ (iie) — no: two い and an え, three beats. Typing only one i gives いえ (ie), which means "house".

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard いえ (ie), house: two beats. いいえ (iie, no) has three, うえ (ue, above) starts with the flat う, and あい (ai, love) starts with あ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard うえ (ue), above, on top. It is easy to mix up with いえ (ie, house): listen for the relaxed u at the start instead of the bright i.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: あおい (aoi) means "blue" (the adjective form of あお). Three beats: あ・お・い; type "aoi".

questions.stem: Which statement about stroke order is true?
choices: Any order is fine as long as the result looks right
Only kanji have a stroke order
Each kana has a fixed order and direction of strokes
Strokes are usually written from bottom to top
questions.explanation: Every kana (and kanji) has a fixed stroke order and direction. Following it keeps the shape balanced and makes handwriting readable; strokes generally go top to bottom and left to right, not bottom to top.

questions.stem: In vertical Japanese text, in which order are the columns read?
choices: either way, as the writer likes
questions.explanation: Vertical text is read top to bottom, starting with the rightmost column and moving left. Horizontal text goes left to right, like English.

questions.stem: How is し read?
questions.explanation: し is "shi", like English "she", said short. Japanese has no native "si": before i, s becomes sh. You may type "si" in the app, but read it shi. "chi" is ち and "su" is す.

questions.stem: Which kana is "ki"?
questions.explanation: き is ki. It looks like さ (sa), but き has two horizontal strokes and さ only one.

questions.stem: Which kana is "sa"?
questions.explanation: さ is sa: one horizontal, a slanting stroke, and a separate curve at the bottom. き (ki) has two horizontals; ち (chi, next lesson) is like a mirror image of さ.

questions.stem: Which kana is "ke"?
questions.explanation: け is ke: a vertical on the left and a crossed long vertical on the right. か is ka, せ is se and こ is ko.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The か row is k plus each vowel in order: か ka, き ki, く ku, け ke, こ ko.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The さ row is regular except し, which is shi, not si: さ sa, し shi, す su, せ se, そ so.

questions.stem: What does "gojūon" mean?
questions.explanation: Gojūon means "fifty sounds": the grid of kana with vowels across and rows down. The modern table actually has 46 basic kana, because some places are empty.

questions.stem: Which row comes right after the か row in the gojūon?
questions.explanation: The order is あ, か, さ, た, な, は, ま, や, ら, わ, so さ follows か. あ comes before か; た and な come after さ.

questions.stem: Which set is the "o" column so far, kana that all end in the vowel o?
questions.explanation: お (o), こ (ko) and そ (so) all end in o, so they stand in the same column. The other sets are the a column, the u column and the e column.

questions.stem: Type "kasa" (umbrella) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: かさ (kasa) — umbrella: か then さ.

questions.stem: Type "sushi" in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: すし (sushi): す and し. You can type "sushi" or "susi"; either way the second kana is し, read shi.

questions.stem: Type "koko" (here) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: ここ (koko) — here: two こ, two short beats with a pure o.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard あき (aki), autumn. あさ (asa) is morning and あか (aka) is red: listen to the second beat, ki. いけ (ike) is pond.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard しお (shio), salt: "shi" then a pure "o". すし (sushi) also has shi, but it starts with su.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: かお (kao) — face: か then お. Two beats, "ka-o", not one English-style "cow".

questions.stem: Which word means "salt"?
questions.explanation: しお (shio) is salt. すし is sushi, せかい (sekai) is world and そこ (soko) is there.

questions.stem: What does くさ (kusa) mean?
questions.explanation: くさ (kusa) is grass. Umbrella is かさ (kasa), this morning is けさ (kesa) and slope is さか (saka): all built from the same few kana, so read each one carefully.

questions.stem: How do you tell き from さ when they are handwritten?
choices: さ has two horizontal strokes, き has one
き has two horizontal strokes, さ has one
き has no curve at the bottom
They are the same kana in different styles
questions.explanation: Count the horizontals: き (ki) has two, さ (sa) has one. Both have a separate curve at the bottom when written by hand.

questions.stem: How many strokes does き have when written by hand?
questions.explanation: き has four strokes: two horizontals, the long slanting stroke and the separate curve at the bottom. Many printed fonts join the last two, which makes it look like three.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "ashi" (leg, foot)?
questions.explanation: "shi" is し, so ashi is あし. あさ (asa) is morning, and あす and あせ are other words (tomorrow, sweat), not "ashi".

questions.stem: Which kana is "tsu"?
questions.explanation: つ is tsu: one stroke across and curving down. そ is so, し is shi and う is the vowel u.

questions.stem: How is ち read?
questions.explanation: ち is chi, as in "cheese". Before i, t becomes ch, so there is no native "ti". You may type "ti", but read it chi. tsu is つ and shi is し.

questions.stem: Which kana is "nu"?
questions.explanation: ぬ is nu. め (me) has the same shape without the small loop at the bottom right; ね (ne) has a vertical stroke on the left; の (no) is a single stroke.

questions.stem: Which kana is "ne"?
questions.explanation: ね is ne: a vertical crossed by a zigzag that ends in a loop. れ (re) ends with a tail kicking out, わ (wa) curves back in, and ぬ (nu) has no vertical.

questions.stem: Which kana is "chi"?
questions.explanation: ち is chi. さ (sa) looks like its mirror image: in さ the bottom curve is a separate stroke opening to the right, while ち bulges to the right. ら (ra) has no horizontal; た is ta.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: た ta, ち chi, つ tsu, て te, と to. "ti" and "tu" are only typing spellings; the sounds are chi and tsu.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The な row is completely regular: な na, に ni, ぬ nu, ね ne, の no.

questions.stem: Type "neko" (cat) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: ねこ (neko) — cat: ね then こ.

questions.stem: Type "natsu" (summer) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: なつ (natsu) — summer: な then つ. Type "tsu" (or "tu") for つ.

questions.stem: Type "tsukue" (desk) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: つくえ (tsukue) — desk: つ, く, え. Three beats.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard くつ (kutsu), shoes, ending in tsu. くち (kuchi) is mouth, ending in chi: the contrast this lesson practises. くさ is grass and くし is comb.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard なか (naka), inside. なつ (natsu) is summer, なに (nani) is what and にく (niku) is meat.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: いぬ (inu) — dog: い then ぬ.

questions.stem: What does あなた (anata) mean?
questions.explanation: あなた (anata) means "you". What is なに (nani), inside is なか (naka) and summer is なつ (natsu).

questions.stem: Which word means "clock, watch"?
questions.explanation: とけい (tokei) is a clock or watch. たこ (tako) is octopus, つき (tsuki) is moon and そと (soto) is outside.

questions.stem: How many beats does ちいさい (chiisai, small) have?
questions.explanation: ち・い・さ・い: four beats. The い after ち holds the sound for a second beat, so it's not "chee-sai" in three.

questions.stem: How many strokes does た have?
questions.explanation: た has four strokes: a horizontal, a slanting stroke, and the two short strokes on the right that look like a small こ.

questions.stem: What is the difference between ぬ and め?
choices: め ends in a small loop; ぬ does not
ぬ ends in a small loop; め does not
ぬ has an extra dot at the top
め is written in one stroke
questions.explanation: ぬ (nu) finishes with a small loop at the bottom right; め (me) doesn't. Both have two strokes and no dot.

questions.stem: How do you say つくえ (desk)?
questions.explanation: つ is tsu, so つくえ is tsukue, starting with the ts of "cats". "tu" is only a typing spelling, "su" would be す and "chi" would be ち.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "nani" (what)?
questions.explanation: na + ni: なに. なね would be "nane"; にな reverses the kana; り is "ri", not "ni".

questions.stem: Which romaji is usually written for ふ?
questions.explanation: ふ is written "fu" (you may also type "hu"). The sound is a soft f made with the lips alone, not the teeth. ha is は, he is へ and mu is む.

questions.stem: Which kana is "ho"?
questions.explanation: ほ is ho: a vertical on the left and, on the right, two horizontals with the looped vertical starting at the top one. は (ha) has only one horizontal; ま (ma) has no left vertical; け (ke) has no loop.

questions.stem: Which kana is "ma"?
questions.explanation: ま is ma: two horizontals and a vertical that ends in a loop. も (mo) ends in a hook that turns up, with no loop; ほ and は have a vertical on the left.

questions.stem: Which kana is "me"?
questions.explanation: め is me. ぬ (nu) is the same shape with a small loop at the end; ね (ne) has a vertical on the left; の (no) is one stroke.

questions.stem: Which kana is "mo"?
questions.explanation: も is mo: a curved vertical that turns up at the bottom, crossed by two horizontals. ま (ma) has a loop instead of the hook; む is mu.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: は ha, ひ hi, ふ fu, へ he, ほ ho. Inside ordinary words, は and へ keep these readings.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The ま row is regular: ま ma, み mi, む mu, め me, も mo. "nu" is ぬ, the lookalike of め.

questions.stem: Type "hana" (flower) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: はな (hana) — flower: は then な. Inside a word, は is read ha.

questions.stem: Type "namae" (name) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: なまえ (namae) — name: な, ま, え. Three beats.

questions.stem: Type "fune" (boat) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: ふね (fune) — boat, ship: ふ then ね. "fu" and "hu" both type ふ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard ほし (hoshi), star. はし (hashi) starts with ha; ほね (hone) is bone; むし (mushi) is insect.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard あめ (ame), rain. The other words differ only in the second beat: ma, mi, ne.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: さむい (samui) — cold (of weather): さ, む, い. Keep む short and flat.

questions.stem: When は is the topic particle, as at the end of こんにちは (hello), how is it read?
questions.explanation: As a particle, は is read wa: こんにちは is "konnichiwa". Inside ordinary words it stays ha, as in はな (hana). Lesson 13 teaches the particles.

questions.stem: How is へ read when it is the particle meaning "to" (a direction)?
questions.explanation: The direction particle へ is read e. Inside words it's he, as in へそ (heso). べ (be) is its voiced form, which comes in lesson 6.

questions.stem: What does みみ (mimi) mean?
questions.explanation: みみ (mimi) is ear. Shop is みせ (mise), peach is もも (momo) and insect is むし (mushi).

questions.stem: Which stroke of も is written first?
questions.explanation: も starts with its curved vertical, then the two horizontals from top to bottom. That's unusual: in ま the horizontals come first. も has no dot.

questions.stem: How is ふ pronounced?
choices: Like English f, with the top teeth on the lower lip
With the lips close together, blowing gently, no teeth on the lip
questions.explanation: ふ is made with the lips alone, as if cooling soup: a soft sound between f and h. English f uses the teeth, which makes it too hard; a plain h loses the lip sound.

questions.stem: How many strokes does ふ have?
questions.explanation: ふ has four separate pieces: the short top stroke, the middle curve, and a dot on each side.

questions.stem: Which word means "person"?
questions.explanation: ひと (hito) is person. ふね (fune) is boat, ほし (hoshi) is star and もの (mono) is thing.

questions.stem: How is を read?
questions.explanation: を is read o, the same sound as お. It's typed "wo" in the app, but that's only a typing spelling. wa is わ and n is ん.

questions.stem: Where is を used?
choices: Only as the particle that marks the object of a verb
In any word with an o sound
questions.explanation: を has one job: marking the object, as in ほんを よむ (hon o yomu, to read a book). Words with an o sound are spelled with お: おかし, not をかし.

questions.stem: Which kana is "re"?
questions.explanation: れ is re: the zigzag ends with a tail kicking out to the right. ね (ne) ends in a loop, わ (wa) curves back in, and ぬ (nu) has no vertical.

questions.stem: Which kana is "wa"?
questions.explanation: わ is wa: a vertical and a zigzag that curves round and back in, with no loop. れ (re) has a tail, ね (ne) a loop; る (ru) has no vertical.

questions.stem: Which kana is "ru"?
questions.explanation: る is ru: it ends in a small loop at the bottom. ろ (ro) is the same shape without the loop. ら is ra, そ is so.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: や ya, ゆ yu, よ yo; り ri, ろ ro. There are no "yi" or "ye" kana in modern Japanese, which is why the や row has only three.

questions.stem: These kana look alike. Match each one to its sound.
questions.explanation: Look at the bottom right. ね and ぬ end in a loop; れ ends in an outward tail; わ and め curve without a loop. ね, れ and わ have a vertical on the left; ぬ and め don't.

questions.stem: How is the Japanese r in ら, り, る, れ, ろ made?
choices: Like English r, with the lips rounded and the tongue curled back
Like English l, with the tongue held against the ridge
With one quick tap of the tongue tip behind the top teeth
questions.explanation: The Japanese r is a single quick tap, close to the tt in American "better". English r curls the tongue and rounds the lips; English l holds the tongue in place. Neither is right.

questions.stem: How many beats does みかん (mikan, mandarin orange) have?
questions.explanation: み・か・ん: three beats. ん is a full beat, even though English would hear "mi-kan" as two syllables.

questions.stem: How many beats does きんえん (kin'en, no smoking) have?
questions.explanation: き・ん・え・ん: four beats. The first ん must not join the え; if it does, you say きねん (kinen, anniversary), which has three.

questions.stem: Type "yama" (mountain) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: やま (yama) — mountain: や then ま.

questions.stem: Type "hon" (book) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: ほん (hon) — book. Type "honn", or "hon": a single n at the end becomes ん when you press Enter.

questions.stem: Type "kin'en" (no smoking) in hiragana. Remember the apostrophe after the n: ___
questions.explanation: きんえん: type "kin'en". Without the apostrophe, "kinen" gives きねん (kinen, anniversary), because the app reads "ne" as ね.

questions.stem: Type "hon o yomu" (to read a book) in hiragana. Type the particle as "wo": ___
questions.explanation: ほんを よむ: the object particle is を, typed "wo" and read o. Spaces don't matter in the answer.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard くるま (kuruma), car, with a tapped r. くるみ (kurumi) is walnut, くすり (kusuri) is medicine and くもり (kumori) is cloudy weather.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard よる (yoru), night. はる (haru) is spring, よむ (yomu) is to read and いる (iru) is to be (for people and animals).

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: さくら (sakura) — cherry blossom: さ, く, ら. Type "ra" for the tapped ら.

questions.stem: Ken says: あした、 はなみ しない？ What is he suggesting?
choices: Going to look at the cherry blossoms tomorrow
questions.explanation: あした (ashita) is tomorrow and はなみ (hanami) is flower viewing; しない？ (shinai?) is "won't we do it?", a friendly suggestion.

questions.stem: Read: ゆき、 きれいね。 What does it mean?
choices: The snow is pretty, isn't it?
It's a pretty night, isn't it?
questions.explanation: ゆき (yuki) is snow, きれい (kirei) is pretty, and ね asks for agreement: "isn't it?". Night would be よる (yoru).

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "okashi" (sweets)?
questions.explanation: Ordinary words with an o sound use お, so it's おかし. を is only the object particle; ち would make "chi", not "shi".

questions.stem: Which kana is "ga"?
questions.explanation: が is ga: か with the dakuten ゛. Plain か is ka, ざ is za and ぱ is pa.

questions.stem: Which kana writes "ji" in ordinary words such as じかん (time)?
questions.explanation: じ, from し with ゛. ぢ sounds the same but is used only in special cases such as はなぢ; し without the mark is shi, and ず is zu.

questions.stem: Which kana is "pa"?
questions.explanation: ぱ is pa: は with the small circle ゜. ば (ba) has the two ticks ゛ instead; は is ha and ほ is ho.

questions.stem: In the kana system, which row do the b sounds (ば び ぶ べ ぼ) come from?
questions.explanation: ば, び, ぶ, べ, ぼ are は-row kana with ゛, and ぱ-row kana are は with ゜. The は row's consonant was once close to p, which is why h, b and p belong together.

questions.stem: Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: ゛ voices the consonant: か → が ga, さ → ざ za, た → だ da, は → ば ba; ゜ gives ぱ pa.

questions.stem: These differ only by their marks. Match each kana to its sound.
questions.explanation: Plain ふ is fu; with ゛ it's ぶ bu, with ゜ it's ぷ pu. The same goes for ほ ho, ぼ bo and ぽ po. Two ticks means b, a circle means p.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "mizu" (water)?
questions.explanation: The zu sound is normally written ず: みず. づ is used only in compounds and repeats such as つづく. みす has no ゛ (it would be "misu") and みつ is "mitsu".

questions.stem: Why is "nosebleed" spelled はなぢ and not はなじ?
choices: ぢ is always used after な
じ is never used in the middle of a word
The two spellings are equally correct
It is はな (nose) + ち (blood), and the ち becomes voiced
questions.explanation: When the second part of a compound starts with ち and becomes voiced, it's written ぢ: はな + ち → はなぢ. In other words "ji" is written じ, even in the middle (かじ, kaji, a house fire), and はなじ is a misspelling.

questions.stem: When and where do you write ゛ or ゜?
choices: Last, at the top right of the kana
In the middle of the kana
questions.explanation: The marks are always the last strokes, placed at the top right inside the kana's own square.

questions.stem: Type "gohan" (meal) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: ごはん (gohan) — cooked rice, a meal: ご, は, ん. A final n becomes ん when you press Enter (or type "gohann").

questions.stem: Type "denwa" (telephone) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: でんわ (denwa) — telephone: で, ん, わ. The n before w becomes ん automatically.

questions.stem: Type "tsuzuku" (to continue) in hiragana. Its second kana is づ, which you type as "du": ___
questions.explanation: つづく: type "tsuduku". The repeated つ becomes voiced, so it's written づ, not ず. Typing "tsuzuku" would give つずく, a misspelling.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard かぎ (kagi), key, with a voiced g. かき (kaki) without ゛ is persimmon; かぐ (kagu) is furniture.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard でんき (denki), electricity or light, starting with a voiced d. てんき (tenki) is weather; でんわ (denwa) is telephone; げんき (genki) is well, healthy.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: みず (mizu) — water. The zu sound is written ず here, as in nearly all words.

questions.stem: はな (flower) + ひ (fire) join to make the word for "fireworks". How is it spelled?
questions.explanation: はなび (hanabi): when the words join, the h of ひ becomes voiced (rendaku), giving び. It's the second part that changes, not the first, and ゛ (b), not ゜ (p).

questions.stem: In the dialogue, Yumi asks つくえの うえ？ and Ken answers あ、 ここに ある！ Where was the key?
questions.explanation: つくえの うえ is "on the desk" (the top of the desk), and ここに ある means "it's here". The bag (かばん) was the first guess, but Ken said ない (it's not there).

questions.stem: Which word means "pig"?
questions.explanation: ぶた (buta) is pig: ふ with ゛. ふた (futa) without the mark means lid, ふだ (fuda) is a tag or label, and ぷた is not a word.

questions.stem: Which word means "a walk"?
questions.explanation: さんぽ (sanpo): ほ with the circle ゜ is po. さんぼ has ゛ (bo), the wrong mark.

questions.stem: How many hiragana have ゛ or ゜?
questions.explanation: Twenty with ゛ (the が, ざ, だ and ば rows) and five with ゜ (the ぱ row): 25. 46 is the number of basic kana, 33 the number of combinations in lesson 7.

questions.stem: How is きゃ read?
questions.explanation: き + small ゃ is one beat, kya. With a full-size や it would be きや, "ki-ya" in two beats. kyo is きょ.

questions.stem: Which is "sho"?
questions.explanation: しょ is sho: し with a small ょ. しよ with a full-size よ is "shi-yo"; しゃ is sha and ちょ is cho.

questions.stem: Which word means "hospital"?
questions.explanation: びょういん (byōin), with a small ょ: four beats. びよういん (biyōin), with a full-size よ, is a beauty salon. ぴょ has the wrong mark, and びよいん is not a word.

questions.stem: What does the small っ in きって (kitte, stamp) do?
choices: It makes the vowel before it long
It is silent and takes no time
It adds a one-beat pause before the t
questions.explanation: Small っ is a beat of silence while the next consonant is held: き・っ・て. It's not read tsu, it doesn't lengthen a vowel, and it does take time: one full beat.

questions.stem: Which word means "postage stamp"?
questions.explanation: きって (kitte) has a small っ. きて (kite) means "come!" or "wear it"; きいて (kiite) means "listen!"; きつて, with a full-size つ, is not a word.

questions.stem: Which word means "grandmother"?
questions.explanation: おばあさん (obāsan) has a long a: ば・あ. Without it, おばさん (obasan) means aunt. The other two are misspellings.

questions.stem: How is a long o usually written in hiragana, as in "gakkō" (school)?
questions.explanation: Most long o's are written with う: がっこう. おお appears only in a small set of words such as おおきい; the dash ー belongs to katakana; を is never used for length.

questions.stem: How is せんせい (sensei, teacher) usually pronounced in everyday speech?
choices: sen-sē, with the e held for two beats
questions.explanation: えい is the usual spelling of a long e, and in normal speech it's a long e, like ええ, held for two beats (not the ee of "see"). Careful speech may keep e-i, but not the English "say" glide; "sen-se" drops a beat.

questions.stem: How many beats does がっこう (gakkō, school) have?
questions.explanation: が・っ・こ・う: four. The small っ is a beat of its own, and so is the う that lengthens the o.

questions.stem: How many beats does とうきょう (Tokyo) have?
questions.explanation: と・う・きょ・う: four. きょ is one beat (small ょ joins the き), and each う adds a beat for the long o. English speakers hear "To-kyo", two syllables.

questions.stem: How many beats does しゃしん (shashin, photo) have?
questions.explanation: しゃ・し・ん: three. しゃ is one beat; ん is a beat of its own.

questions.stem: Match each combination to its sound.
questions.explanation: Each combination is one beat. し, ち and じ drop the y in romaji (shu, cho, ja) because sh, ch and j already contain the glide. "kiya" would be full-size きや.

questions.stem: Type "kyō" (today) in hiragana. Type the long o as "ou": ___
questions.explanation: きょう: type "kyou". きょ is one syllable, and the long o is written with う.

questions.stem: Type "kitte" (stamp) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: きって: doubling the t ("kitte") gives the small っ.

questions.stem: Type "gakkō" (school) in hiragana. Type it as "gakkou": ___
questions.explanation: がっこう: "kk" gives っこ, and "ou" writes the long o as こう.

questions.stem: Type "ocha" (tea) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: おちゃ: "cha" types ち with a small ゃ. Two beats: お・ちゃ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard おばあさん (obāsan), grandmother, with a long a. おばさん (obasan) is aunt; おじさん (ojisan) is uncle and おじいさん (ojīsan) is grandfather.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard きって (kitte), stamp, with the silent beat before the t. きて (kite) has no pause; きいて (kiite) has a long i instead.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: しゃしん (shashin) — photo: type "shashinn" or "shashin" (the final n becomes ん on Enter).

questions.stem: Yumi says: ろくじに えきで あおう。 What is she suggesting?
choices: Going to the cinema at six
Meeting at the station at nine
Meeting at the station at six
questions.explanation: ろくじ (rokuji) is six o'clock, えき (eki) is station and あおう (aō) is "let's meet". She is going to the cinema, but they meet at the station first.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "shi"?
questions.explanation: シ is "shi": its two short strokes sit on the left, and the long stroke rises from the bottom left. ツ is "tsu" (short strokes along the top, long stroke falling), ソ is "so" and ン is "n".

questions.stem: What is katakana mainly used for?
choices: Only in books for young children
Borrowed words, foreign names, sound words and emphasis
questions.explanation: Katakana writes loanwords (アイス, カメラ), foreign names (スイス), sound words and words that need emphasis. Grammar endings and particles are written in hiragana, and children's books use mostly hiragana.

questions.stem: How is コ read?
questions.explanation: コ is "ko", a box open on the left, like こ with its sides joined. ユ (yu) has a bottom line that sticks out, ロ (ro) is a closed box, and ニ (ni) is just two lines.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "ka"?
questions.explanation: カ is "ka"; it looks like hiragana か without its extra stroke. ク is "ku", タ is "ta" and ケ is "ke": they share a slanted first stroke, but none of them is カ.

questions.stem: Type "aisu" (ice cream) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: Typing AISU in capitals gives アイス. In lowercase you would get あいす, which is hiragana: the word for ice cream is a loanword, so it is written in katakana.

questions.stem: Type "kokoa" (cocoa, hot chocolate) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: KOKOA gives ココア: コ, コ, ア, three beats. Check that you used capitals, or you'll get ここあ in hiragana.

questions.stem: Match each katakana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The first row is the five vowels in table order: ア a, イ i, ウ u, エ e, オ o. ウ has a dot on top, like う; "wa" is ワ, which looks like ウ without the dot.

questions.stem: Match each katakana to its sound.
questions.explanation: カ ka and キ ki look like か and き; ケ ke has a long stroke dropping from its horizontal. サ sa has two verticals through a horizontal, and セ se looks like せ. "ku" is ク and "so" is ソ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard アイス (aisu), ice cream: a-i-su. アイソ ends in "so", オイス starts with "o", and ウイス starts with "u".

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard スキー (sukī), skiing: the last vowel is held, so the word has the ー at the end. スキ has no long vowel, スーキ lengthens the wrong vowel, and シキー starts with "shi".

questions.stem: Listen and type the word in katakana. Use CAPITALS, and - for ー: ___
questions.explanation: The word is ケーキ (kēki), cake: ke, a long e, then ki. Type KE-KI. Writing the long vowel as ケエキ is wrong in katakana: loanwords use ー.

questions.stem: Which hiragana does katakana キ look most like?
questions.explanation: キ (ki) is き without its bottom curve: both have two horizontals crossed by a slanting stroke. さ and ち have one horizontal, and ま has a loop.

questions.stem: How many beats does ケーキ have?
questions.explanation: ケーキ is ke-e-ki: three beats, because ー counts as one beat of its own. Counting only the two kana gives 2, which misses the long vowel.

questions.stem: Which word means "Switzerland"?
questions.explanation: スイス (Suisu) is Switzerland. スキー is skiing, アイス is ice cream and システム is system.

questions.stem: What does the dash ー do in a katakana word?
choices: It makes the vowel before it one beat longer
It shows that the word is a name
questions.explanation: ー holds the vowel before it for one more beat: ソース is so-o-su. A pause is small ッ (lesson 11), and words and names are separated by spaces or the middle dot, not ー.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "kēki" (cake)?
questions.explanation: ケーキ is right: a loanword in katakana, with ー for the long vowel. ケエキ writes the long vowel with a vowel kana, ケキ drops it, and けーき is in hiragana.

questions.stem: In シ (shi), which way is the long stroke written?
choices: From the top right down to the bottom left
From left to right along the top
From the bottom left up to the right
questions.explanation: The long stroke of シ rises from the bottom left up to the right. Falling from the top right is the long stroke of ツ (tsu) and ソ (so), which is how they're told apart.

questions.stem: Why is スイス (Switzerland) written in katakana?
choices: It is a foreign place name
It is a native Japanese word written for emphasis
questions.explanation: Names of foreign countries, cities and people are written in katakana. Grammar words are hiragana, and スイス is neither a sound word nor a native word.

questions.stem: Which of these is katakana, not hiragana?
questions.explanation: セ (se) is katakana: straight strokes and a sharp corner. せ is its hiragana partner, and さ and き are hiragana too.

questions.stem: In this app, what do you type to get ココア?
questions.explanation: Capitals give katakana, so KOKOA gives ココア. Lowercase kokoa gives hiragana ここあ, ko-koa adds a ー, and a single capital letter at the start (Kokoa) is treated as ordinary capitalisation, so it stays hiragana.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "tsu"?
questions.explanation: ツ is "tsu": two short strokes along the top and a long stroke falling from the top right. シ (shi) has its short strokes on the left and a rising stroke; ソ is "so" and ン is "n".

questions.stem: In ツ (tsu), how is the long stroke written?
choices: It rises from the bottom left up to the right
It falls from the top right down to the left
It is a straight horizontal line
questions.explanation: ツ's long stroke falls from the top right down to the left. A rising stroke makes シ (shi) instead: "shi rises, tsu falls".

questions.stem: How is フ read?
questions.explanation: フ is "fu", the same soft sound as hiragana ふ. ワ (wa) adds a short stroke on the left, ク (ku) starts with a separate slant, and ラ (ra) has a line on top.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "nu"?
questions.explanation: ヌ is "nu": its second stroke crosses the sweep. In ス (su) the second stroke only starts on the sweep. メ is "me" and ナ is "na".

questions.stem: Which katakana is "na"?
questions.explanation: ナ is "na": a flat horizontal with a long stroke crossing it. メ (me) has no horizontal, チ (chi) starts with a slant at the top, and オ (o) has a third stroke.

questions.stem: Type "tenisu" (tennis) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: TENISU gives テニス. English "tennis" has a double n, but Japanese has no pause there, so there is no small ッ.

questions.stem: Type "naifu" (knife) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: NAIFU gives ナイフ: na-i-fu. FU (or HU) gives フ.

questions.stem: Type "nekutai" (necktie) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: NEKUTAI gives ネクタイ: ne-ku-ta-i, four beats. "Tie" becomes タイ, two beats.

questions.stem: Match each katakana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The タ row: タ ta, チ chi, ツ tsu, テ te, ト to. "shi" is シ and "so" is ソ, the lookalikes of ツ.

questions.stem: Match each katakana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The ハ row: ハ ha, ヒ hi, フ fu, ヘ he, ホ ho. In katakana words ハ is never "wa" and ヘ is never "e": those readings belong only to the hiragana particles は and へ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard テニス (tenisu), tennis. チニス starts with "chi", テヌス has "nu" in the middle, and テニシ ends in "shi" instead of "su".

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard ホテル (hoteru), hotel. ホタル (hotaru, firefly) is a real word that differs only in the middle beat: "ta" instead of "te". ハテル and ヘテル start with the wrong kana.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word in katakana. Use CAPITALS, and - for ー: ___
questions.explanation: The word is ノート (nōto), notebook: no, a long o, then to. Type NO-TO.

questions.stem: Which word is "tsuna" (tuna)?
questions.explanation: ツナ is tsu-na, tuna. シナ starts with "shi", ソナ with "so" and ンナ with "n": the three lookalikes of ツ.

questions.stem: Which word means "necktie"?
questions.explanation: ネクタイ (nekutai) is a necktie. ナイフ is a knife, テキスト a textbook and ハイテク means high-tech.

questions.stem: What does ノート mean in Japanese?
questions.explanation: ノート is a notebook. Loanwords often keep only one meaning of the English word; a short written note is メモ.

questions.stem: How is ハ read in ハイテク (high-tech)?
questions.explanation: Katakana ハ is always "ha": ha-i-te-ku. Only the hiragana particle は is read "wa".

questions.stem: Which katakana looks the same as hiragana へ?
questions.explanation: Katakana ヘ (he) is written the same way as hiragana へ. ハ is two separate strokes, ノ is a single slant and ホ has four strokes.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "shītsu" (bed sheet)?
questions.explanation: シーツ is shi, a long i, then tsu. ツーシ swaps the two kana, and シーシ and ツーツ repeat one of them.

questions.stem: How many strokes does ネ have?
questions.explanation: ネ has four strokes: a dot on top, a horizontal that turns down to the left, a vertical, and a short dot on the right. Many learners write the last two as one stroke and count three.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "n"?
questions.explanation: ン is "n": a short stroke lying almost flat at the upper left and a long stroke rising from the bottom left. ソ (so) has the same two strokes, but its long stroke falls from the top.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "u"?
questions.explanation: ウ is "u": ワ plus a dot on top. ワ (wa) has no dot, フ (fu) is a single stroke, and ラ (ra) has a separate line on top.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "yu"?
questions.explanation: ユ is "yu": its bottom line sticks out past the vertical. コ (ko) is a box open on the left, ヨ (yo) has a middle line, and ロ (ro) is a closed box.

questions.stem: How is メ read?
questions.explanation: メ is "me", like め without its loop. ナ (na) has a flat horizontal, ヌ (nu) starts with a stroke like フ, and モ (mo) has two horizontals.

questions.stem: How is ル read?
questions.explanation: ル is "ru": two legs, the right one kicking up. レ (re) is only that right leg, リ (ri) is two short verticals, and ロ (ro) is a box.

questions.stem: Type "meron" (melon) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: MERONN gives メロン. Typing NN for ン is safest; a single N at the very end also becomes ン when you press Enter.

questions.stem: Type "remon" (lemon) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: REMONN gives レモン. English "lemon" has an l, but Japanese uses the same ラ-row sound for l and r.

questions.stem: Type "rāmen" (ramen noodles) in katakana. Use CAPITALS, and - for ー: ___
questions.explanation: RA-MENN gives ラーメン: ra, a long a, me, n. Four beats. Leaving out the ー gives ラメン, which is not the word.

questions.stem: Match each katakana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The マ row: マ ma, ミ mi, ム mu, メ me, モ mo. "a" is ア, the lookalike of マ, and "na" is ナ, the lookalike of メ.

questions.stem: Match each katakana to its sound.
questions.explanation: The ラ row: ラ ra, リ ri, ル ru, レ re, ロ ro. ラ is not フ (fu): ラ has a separate line on top. Nor is it ワ (wa), which has a short vertical on the left.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard メロン (meron), melon. メロソ uses ソ (so) in place of ン, ナロン starts with "na", and メレン has "re" in the middle.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard ワイン (wain), wine. ウイン and フイン start with ウ and フ, the lookalikes of ワ, and ワイソ ends with ソ instead of ン.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: The word is トイレ (toire), toilet or restroom: to-i-re. Type TOIRE.

questions.stem: What is ヲ used for?
choices: The "o" in loanwords such as オイル
The particle を when a whole sentence is written in katakana
The "wo" sound in ウォーキング
It is the small form of ヨ
questions.explanation: ヲ is the katakana partner of を, a particle, so it only appears when a whole sentence is in katakana (old telegrams, robot speech in comics). Loanwords use オ for "o" and ウォ for "wo".

questions.stem: Which word means "Italy"?
questions.explanation: イタリア (Itaria) is Italy. アメリカ is the United States, ロシア is Russia and メキシコ is Mexico.

questions.stem: レモン (lemon) and ラジオ (radio) both start with the ラ row. Why?
choices: The ラ row is only for fruit names
Japanese uses one tap sound for both English l and r
The l in lemon is silent in Japanese
questions.explanation: Japanese has one sound, a light tap, that does the work of both English l and r, so both become the ラ row. Nothing is silent or misspelled.

questions.stem: Which katakana is フ with a short stroke added on the left?
questions.explanation: ワ (wa) is フ plus a short vertical on the left. Add a dot on top of ワ and you get ウ (u). ヲ has an extra line across the middle, and ラ has a line on top.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "sain" (signature, autograph)?
questions.explanation: サイン ends with ン (n), whose long stroke rises. サイソ uses ソ (so), whose stroke falls; サイシ and サイツ end with シ and ツ.

questions.stem: How many beats does サイン have?
questions.explanation: サイン is sa-i-n: three beats, because ン is a beat of its own. English "sign" has one syllable, but Japanese counts every kana.

questions.stem: Which word means "toilet, restroom"?
questions.explanation: トイレ (toire) is a toilet or restroom. タオル is a towel, ホテル a hotel and メール an email.

questions.stem: Which katakana is "ga"?
questions.explanation: ガ is カ (ka) with ゛, which voices k to g. カ has no mark, パ is "pa" and ザ is "za".

questions.stem: How is ピ read?
questions.explanation: ピ is ヒ (hi) with the small circle ゜, which makes "pi". ビ, with ゛, is "bi". "fi" is written フィ.

questions.stem: How do loanwords write the sound "ji"?
questions.explanation: Loanwords use ジ: ジーンズ, ラジオ. ヂ sounds the same but is very rare. シ is "shi" and チ is "chi", both unvoiced.

questions.stem: Type "kōhī" (coffee) in katakana. Use CAPITALS, and - for ー: ___
questions.explanation: KO-HI- gives コーヒー: four beats, ko-o-hi-i. Typing KOOHII gives コオヒイ, which is not how the word is written: loanwords use ー.

questions.stem: Type "chiketto" (ticket) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: CHIKETTO gives チケット: doubling the t makes the small ッ. Four beats: chi-ke-(pause)-to.

questions.stem: Type "nyūsu" (news) in katakana. Use CAPITALS, and - for ー: ___
questions.explanation: NYU-SU gives ニュース: ニュ is one beat, ー makes it long, then ス. Typing NIYU would give ニユ, with a full-size ユ: two beats instead of one.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard コーヒー (kōhī), coffee: both vowels are long. コヒー and コーヒ each drop one long vowel, and コーピー has "pi" instead of "hi".

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard ビール (bīru), beer, with a long i. ビル (biru) is a building, ピール starts with "pi", and ベール starts with "be".

questions.stem: Listen and type the word in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: The word is ベッド (beddo), bed: be, a pause, do. Type BEDDO; the double d makes the small ッ.

questions.stem: Match each katakana to its sound.
questions.explanation: ゛ voices k→g, s→z, t→d and h→b; ゜ turns h into p. "ka" and "ha" are カ and ハ without a mark.

questions.stem: Match each combination to its sound.
questions.explanation: A small ャュョ makes one beat with the kana before it: キャ kya, シュ shu, チョ cho, ニュ nyu, ジャ ja. "kiya" would be キヤ, with a full-size ヤ; "sho" is ショ.

questions.stem: How many beats (mora) does チケット have?
questions.explanation: チケット is chi-ke-(pause)-to: four beats, because small ッ counts as one. Answering 3 forgets the pause.

questions.stem: How is ー written in vertical text?
choices: Horizontally, the same as in horizontal text
As the vowel kana, such as オ or イ
questions.explanation: ー follows the direction of the text: in vertical text it becomes a vertical line. It never turns into ッ or a vowel kana.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "kyanpu" (camping)?
questions.explanation: キャンプ has a small ャ (kya is one beat) and ends in プ (pu). キヤンプ uses a full-size ヤ, キアンプ uses ア, and キャンブ has ブ (bu) instead of プ.

questions.stem: Which word has a small ッ?
questions.explanation: ベッド (beddo) has a small ッ before ド. ッ follows the Japanese sound, not English spelling: tennis has a double n in English, but テニス has no pause.

questions.stem: What does ジュース usually mean in Japan?
choices: Any sweet soft drink, including fruit juice
questions.explanation: In Japan ジュース covers sweet soft drinks in general, not just fruit juice. Loanwords often shift their meaning a little.

questions.stem: バス means "bus". What does パス mean?
questions.explanation: パス (pasu) is a pass (a ticket pass, or passing the ball). ゛ and ゜ make different words: バ is "ba", パ is "pa". (バス can also mean a bath, as in バスタオル, but パス never means bus or bath.)

questions.stem: What does コンビニ mean?
questions.explanation: コンビニ (konbini) is a convenience store: "convenience store" shortened to four beats. A computer is コンピューター or パソコン.

questions.stem: Where are ゛ and ゜ written?
choices: At the top right, as the last strokes
At the top left, as the first strokes
At the top right, as the first strokes
questions.explanation: The marks go at the top right and are written after the kana itself, just as in hiragana.

questions.stem: Which pair of katakana is very rare and almost never used in loanwords?
questions.explanation: ヂ and ヅ are very rare: loanwords write the same sounds as ジ and ズ (ジーンズ, ズボン). You'll see ヂ in チヂミ, a dish name from Korean.

questions.stem: How is "fa" written in katakana?
questions.explanation: ファ is フ plus a small ァ: one beat, "fa". フア has a full-size ア, so it is two beats (fu-a), and ハ is "ha".

questions.stem: Which is the usual spelling of "pātī" (party)?
questions.explanation: パーティー uses ティ (small ィ) for "ti", with ー after pa and ti. パーテイー has a full-size イ, パーチー uses the old "chi" sound, and パティー drops the first long vowel.

questions.stem: Which is the normal Japanese spelling of "team"?
questions.explanation: チーム (chīmu) is the usual spelling: team came into Japanese before ティ was common and kept the older spelling. ティーム exists but is rare.

questions.stem: Type "fōku" (fork) in katakana. Use CAPITALS, and - for ー: ___
questions.explanation: FO-KU gives フォーク: FO gives フォ (one beat), - gives ー, then ク. Typing HO-KU gives ホーク, which is "hawk".

questions.stem: Type "shefu" (chef) in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: SHEFU gives シェフ: SHE gives シェ (shi with a small ェ), then フ. The u after f is the extra vowel Japanese adds.

questions.stem: Write the name "John" (said "jon") in katakana. Use CAPITALS: ___
questions.explanation: Names are written by sound: John is said "jon", so it is ジョン. Type JONN. The silent h in English doesn't appear.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard パーティー (pātī), party. パーテイー spells "te-i" with a full-size イ, パティー has no long a, and パーチー has "chi" instead of "ti".

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard フォーク (fōku), fork. ホーク (hōku) is "hawk", with an h; ポーク (pōku) is "pork", with a p; フォク drops the long vowel.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word in katakana. Use CAPITALS, and - for ー: ___
questions.explanation: The word is ディナー (dinā), dinner. Type DHINA-: DHI gives ディ. DI on its own gives ヂ, the wrong kana.

questions.stem: Match each spelling to its sound.
questions.explanation: Each pair is one beat: ファ fa, ティ ti, ウェ we, シェ she, ツァ tsa. "fua" and "tei" would need full-size vowels: フア and テイ.

questions.stem: Match each English word to its katakana form.
questions.explanation: The extra vowel follows a pattern: u after most consonants (ミルク), o after t and d (テスト, ベッド), i after ch (マッチ). ミルコ and テストゥ put the wrong vowel on the end.

questions.stem: Why does "milk" become ミルク (miruku) in Japanese?
choices: Japanese adds a vowel after a consonant that stands alone
The English word used to be spelled with a u
ミルク is a native Japanese word
questions.explanation: Every Japanese beat ends in a vowel (or is ン or small ッ), so lone consonants get an extra vowel: l → ル, k → ク. The u is pronounced, softly, and ミルク is a loanword from English.

questions.stem: What can ライト mean?
questions.explanation: English l and r both become the ラ row, so light and right are both ライト; context tells you which. "Late" is レイト.

questions.stem: Which is the usual spelling of "computer"?
questions.explanation: コンピューター: the final "-er" becomes ー. Technical writing sometimes drops it (コンピュータ), but it never becomes ル or テル, and コンプター misses the "pyu".

questions.stem: What is a マンション in Japan?
questions.explanation: マンション is an apartment or condominium building, usually a sturdy concrete one. It is wasei-eigo: the English word with a new Japanese meaning, not a mansion.

questions.stem: How is the English name "Michael" usually written?
questions.explanation: マイケル follows the sound "MY-kel". ミチャエル and マイカエル follow the spelling, which is the classic mistake, and マイクル gets the second vowel wrong.

questions.stem: What sound does ヴ stand for?
choices: "v", though many speakers say it like "b"
questions.explanation: ヴ is ウ with ゛, written for a "v". Many speakers pronounce it like "b", and most words use the バ row instead (バイオリン). "w" is ウィ, ウェ, ウォ and "f" is ファ and the like.

questions.stem: Which word is wasei-eigo (Japan-made English)?
questions.explanation: リモコン is made in Japan from "remote control", cut down to four beats. テニス, ホテル and ピアノ are ordinary loanwords with the same meaning as in English.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "wōkingu" (walking)?
questions.explanation: ウォーキング uses ウォ (u with a small ォ) for "wo". ヲ is only for the particle, ワーキング would be "working", and ウオキング has a full-size オ and no long vowel.

questions.stem: In a name like ジョン・スミス (John Smith), what does the dot ・ do?
choices: It separates the given name from the family name
questions.explanation: The middle dot separates the parts of a foreign name. A long vowel is ー, and a pause is small ッ.

questions.stem: How is は read in "わたしは がくせいです。" (I'm a student.)?
questions.explanation: Here は is the topic particle after わたし, and as a particle it is always read "wa". The kana は is "ha" only inside an ordinary word, such as はな (hana, flower).

questions.stem: How is へ read in "がっこうへ いきます。" (I go to school.)?
questions.explanation: After a place, へ is the direction particle ("to, toward") and is read "e". Inside a word it keeps its sound "he", as in へや (heya, room).

questions.stem: How is the particle を pronounced in standard Japanese?
questions.explanation: In standard Tokyo speech を sounds exactly like お: "o". Some people say "wo" in songs or very careful speech, but "o" is the everyday pronunciation, so "wo, never o" is wrong. You do type it as wo.

questions.stem: In which of these is は read "ha"?
questions.explanation: In はな the は begins an ordinary word, so it's "ha": hana. In わたしは and ほんは it's the topic particle, and in こんにちは it's an old particle frozen into the greeting, so all three are read "wa".

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of "I drink water."?
questions.explanation: The object particle is written を even though it sounds like お, and it comes after the word it marks: みずを. みずお spells the sound instead of the particle, みずわ uses the wrong particle and a wrong spelling, and をみず puts the particle in front.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I go to school."?
choices: うちへ かえります。
がっこうを のみます。
がっこうへ いきます。
がっこうは がくせいです。
questions.explanation: がっこう (school) + へ (to) + いきます (go). うちへ かえります is "I'm going home"; がっこうを のみます would be "I drink the school", and がっこうは がくせいです "The school is a student".

questions.stem: Write "I'm a student." in kana (watashi wa gakusei desu). Type the particle by its kana: ___
accept: わたしは がくせいです
questions.explanation: わたしは がくせいです。 The topic particle sounds like "wa" but is written は, so type ha: watashi ha gakusei desu. Typing wa gives わ, which is a spelling mistake here.

questions.stem: Write "I drink water." in kana (mizu o nomimasu): ___
accept: わたしは みずを のみます
questions.explanation: みずを のみます。 The object particle is を, typed wo. Typing o would give お (みずお), which is how the sentence sounds but not how it's spelled.

questions.stem: Write "I'm going home." in kana with the particle へ (uchi e kaerimasu): ___
accept: うちへ かえります
わたしは うちへ かえります
questions.explanation: うちへ かえります。 The direction particle is へ, typed he; e alone would give え. (うちに かえります is also correct Japanese, but this question asks for へ.)

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard "hon o yomimasu", I read a book: ほんを よみます. ほんは would sound "hon wa", and のみます (drink) starts with "no", not "yo".

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: うちへ かえります

accept: うちへ かえります
questions.explanation: "Uchi e kaerimasu", I'm going home: うちへ かえります. The "e" after a place is the particle へ, so type he. Typing e gives うちえ, a misspelling.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: わたしは がくせいです

choices: わたしは がくせいです。
わたしは せんせいです。
わたしも がくせいです。
わたしは がくせいですか。
questions.explanation: "Watashi wa gakusei desu", I'm a student. せんせい (teacher) starts with "sen", わたしも would be "watashi mo" (me too), and the question would end with "ka".

questions.stem: Match each particle to how it is read.
questions.explanation: The particles は, へ and を keep an old spelling and are read wa, e and o. Every other particle, like the question marker か, is read just as it's written. ha and he are the readings of は and へ inside ordinary words, not as particles.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: みず water, ほん book, がっこう school (with small っ), うち home, ごはん meal or cooked rice. Teacher would be せんせい.

questions.stem: With this app's converter, what do you type to get the topic particle は?
questions.explanation: The converter types what you spell, so は is ha, even though the particle sounds like "wa". Typing wa gives わ. Japanese keyboards work the same way.

questions.stem: What does a particle do in Japanese?
choices: It comes after a word and shows that word's job in the sentence
It comes before a word, like English "to"
It shows that a word is borrowed from English
questions.explanation: A particle follows the word it belongs to: がっこうへ is "school + to". English puts words like "to" before the noun, which is why learners are tempted to write へがっこう. Japanese nouns don't change for plural at all.

questions.stem: Spot the misspelling.
choices: うちえ かえります。
はなは きれいです。
おちゃを のみます。
questions.explanation: The direction particle must be へ: うちへ かえります. The others are right: へや is "heya" (へ inside a word), はなは has は as "ha" and then as the particle "wa", and おちゃ begins with お because を is only ever a particle.

questions.stem: Where does the verb go in a Japanese sentence?
questions.explanation: The verb (or です) always comes last: わたしは みずを のみます。 English puts the verb before the object ("drink water"), but Japanese says "water drink".

questions.stem: What does か do at the end of "にほんへ いきますか。"?
choices: It makes the sentence a question
questions.explanation: か at the end turns a statement into a question: "Are you going to Japan?" It's read "ka", as written. "To" is へ, "too" is も, and the object marker is を.

questions.stem: Ken asks, "ゆきさんは がくせいですか。" Yuki answers, "いいえ、せんせいです。" What does Yuki's answer mean?
questions.explanation: いいえ is "no" and せんせいです is "(I) am a teacher". Yuki leaves out わたしは because the topic is already clear from the question. A yes would start with はい.

questions.stem: Which mark ends a Japanese sentence?
questions.explanation: 。 (kuten, or まる) is the full stop. 、 is the comma, ・ separates parts of a name, and 〜 shows a range such as 10:00〜20:00.

questions.stem: What are the brackets 「 」 used for?
choices: Separating a first name from a surname
questions.explanation: 「 」 (kagikakko) are the Japanese quotation marks: せんせいは 「おはようございます」と いいました。 Names are separated by ・, sentences end with 。 and ranges use 〜.

questions.stem: What is the usual way to write the name "John Smith" in katakana?
questions.explanation: The middle dot ・ (nakaguro) shows where the first name ends: ジョン・スミス. Without it the katakana runs together into one long word, and 、 and 。 are a comma and a full stop, not name separators.

questions.stem: Where do you start reading a page of vertical writing (tategaki)?
questions.explanation: Vertical text runs top to bottom in columns that go from right to left, so you start at the top right. Top left is where horizontal text (yokogaki) starts.

questions.stem: In vertical text, where does a small kana such as the ょ in きょう sit in its square?
questions.explanation: In vertical text small kana (ゃ ゅ ょ っ) and the marks 。 and 、 move to the top right of their squares. Bottom left is where they sit in horizontal text.

questions.stem: A café sign says "10:00〜20:00". What does 〜 mean here?
questions.explanation: Between two numbers, the wave dash 〜 means "from … to": open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. In a casual message it can also stretch a sound (ありがと〜), but on a sign it's a range.

questions.stem: You're writing a formal letter. Which is the best way to end the question "Are you a student?"
questions.explanation: In careful writing a question ends with か and a full stop: がくせいですか。 ？ is common in messages and manga but isn't needed after か in a letter. がくせいです？ drops the か, which only works in casual writing.

questions.stem: What are the double brackets 『 』 used for?
choices: A book title, or a quote inside a quote
questions.explanation: 『 』 (nijūkagikakko) go around titles, as in 『こころ』, and around a quote inside a 「 」 quote. Names don't need brackets, questions end with か。 and times need nothing.

questions.stem: Write "It's raining today." in kana (kyou wa ame desu): ___
accept: きょうは あめです
questions.explanation: きょうは あめです。 きょう (today) has the small ょ (type kyo) and a long vowel spelled う; the topic particle is は, typed ha; あめ is rain.

questions.stem: Type "koohii" (coffee) in katakana (use CAPITALS, and the hyphen key for each long vowel): ___
questions.explanation: コーヒー, typed KO-HI-. Loanwords use katakana and the long-vowel mark ー, which is part of the word, not a dash or a 〜.

questions.stem: Write "I write a letter." in kana (tegami o kakimasu): ___
accept: てがみを かきます
わたしは てがみを かきます
questions.explanation: てがみを かきます。 てがみ (letter) is the object, so it takes を, typed wo; かきます is the polite form of かく (to write).

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard "ashita", tomorrow: あした. あたし (a casual word for "I") has the same kana in a different order, あさ is morning, and きょう is today.

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: いっしょに いきましょう

accept: いっしょに いきましょう
questions.explanation: "Issho ni ikimashō", let's go together: いっしょに いきましょう. Hold the pause for the small っ (type ssho), and spell the long ending of いきましょう with う (type shou).

questions.stem: Match each mark to its name.
questions.explanation: 。 kuten ends a sentence, 、 tōten is a pause, 「 」 kagikakko quote speech, and ・ nakaguro separates parts of a foreign name. nijūkagikakko is the double form 『 』.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard "tegami", letter: てがみ. かがみ (mirror) starts with "ka", かみ (paper) has only two beats, and てまえ (this side) ends in "mae".

questions.stem: How do most Japanese books and newspapers print "He said, 'Thank you.'"?
choices: 「ありがとう」と いいました。
"ありがとう" と いいました。
ありがとう、と いいました.
（ありがとう）と いいました。
questions.explanation: Speech goes in 「 」, followed by と いいました, and the 。 of the quoted sentence is usually dropped before 」. English quotation marks, an English full stop and round brackets are not used for quotes. (Some school writing keeps the 。 inside: 「ありがとう。」)

questions.stem: A book in vertical text prints コーヒー. What happens to the ー marks?
questions.explanation: In vertical text ー turns to run along the column, so it's drawn as a short vertical line. Left horizontal, it would cut across the column. It's part of the word, so it is never left out.

questions.stem: The carmaker Isuzu writes its name いすゞ. What is the ゞ?
choices: An iteration mark: it repeats the kana before it, voiced
