questions.explanation: ゝ repeats the kana before it, and ゞ repeats it with ゛, so いすゞ reads いすず. It's mostly seen in older texts and a few names. A long vowel would be ー or a vowel kana.

questions.stem: A note begins "ゆきさんへ" and ends "けんより". Who wrote it?
questions.explanation: Name + へ at the top means "To …", and name + より at the end means "From …". So it's to Yuki, from Ken.

questions.stem: Which use of ？ is the most natural?
choices: ゆきさんは？ — in a chat message, "And you, Yuki?"
がくせいですか？ — in a school essay
わたしは がくせいです？ — stating a fact
？がくせいですか — at the start of a question
questions.explanation: ？ belongs in everyday writing, and it's the only way to show a question without か, as in ゆきさんは？ A school essay would end がくせいですか。, a plain statement takes 。, and Japanese never puts ？ at the start.

questions.stem: You meet your teacher at 8 in the morning. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Morning plus a teacher calls for the polite おはようございます. おはよう is the casual form for family and friends; こんばんは is for the evening and おやすみなさい for bedtime.

questions.stem: Why does こんにちは end in は, not わ?
choices: That は began as the topic particle, so it keeps the particle's spelling
は and わ can always be swapped
Because the word came from another language
questions.explanation: こんにちは started as the beginning of a longer sentence, roughly "as for today …", and the は is the topic particle, read "wa". は and わ are not interchangeable: こんにちわ is a misspelling.

questions.stem: Your friend is heading home after class. Which goodbye is most natural between friends?
questions.explanation: じゃあね (or またね) is the everyday goodbye between friends. さようなら is real but sounds rather final or formal for friends who'll meet again tomorrow. いらっしゃいませ is a shop's welcome, and はじめまして starts a first meeting.

questions.stem: What do you say just before you start eating?
questions.explanation: いただきます comes before the meal, ごちそうさまでした after it. ただいま is "I'm home" and いってきます is said when leaving home.

questions.stem: You come home from school. What do you say as you walk in?
questions.explanation: The person arriving says ただいま (I'm home); the person at home answers おかえりなさい (welcome home). いってきます and いってらっしゃい are the pair for leaving.

questions.stem: Your sister leaves for work and says "いってきます". What do you answer?
questions.explanation: いってらっしゃい ("go and come back", see you later) answers いってきます. Saying いって きます back would mean you're leaving too; ただいま and おかえりなさい are for coming home.

questions.stem: In a restaurant you want to call the waiter over. What do you say?
questions.explanation: すみません is how you get someone's attention: "excuse me". ごめんなさい is a personal apology, どういたしまして answers thanks, and いただきます is said before eating.

questions.stem: Which is the right way to ask for a coffee?
choices: コーヒー、ごめんなさい。
コーヒー、おねがいします。
questions.explanation: おねがいします is the "please" for asking for something. どうぞ is the "please" for offering, so コーヒー、どうぞ means "Here's your coffee" or "Have some coffee".

questions.stem: Which spelling of "good afternoon" is correct?
questions.explanation: こんにちは ends in the particle は, read "wa". こんにちわ spells the sound and is a common mistake; こにちは is missing the ん, which is a beat of its own.

questions.stem: Which is true of さようなら?
choices: It's the everyday goodbye between friends
It's real, but it sounds rather final, so it's used less than learners expect
It's only used on the phone
questions.explanation: さようなら suits a long parting, a formal event or children leaving their teacher at the end of the day. Friends say じゃあね or またね; good night is おやすみなさい.

questions.stem: Someone thanks you for holding the door. Which short reply fits?
questions.explanation: いいえ ("not at all") is a common way to brush off thanks, more common in practice than どういたしまして. いただきます is for meals, ただいま for coming home, and はじめまして for a first meeting.

questions.stem: When is "おげんきですか" most natural?
choices: Meeting someone you haven't seen for a while
To a shop assistant as you walk in
questions.explanation: おげんきですか (are you well?) is for catching up after time apart. It isn't a daily "how are you": with family in the morning you'd say おはよう.

questions.stem: Type "arigatou gozaimasu" (thank you, polite) in hiragana: ___
accept: ありがとうございます
questions.explanation: ありがとうございます. The long "ō" in arigatō is spelled with う, and the polite ending ございます follows. ありがとう alone is the casual form.

questions.stem: Type "konbanwa" (good evening) in hiragana. Careful with the last kana: ___
questions.explanation: こんばんは, ending in the particle は (type ha). Typing wa gives こんばんわ, a common misspelling.

questions.stem: Type "hajimemashite" (how do you do) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: はじめまして. Here は begins the word, so it's read "ha" as usual. It's said only at a first meeting.

questions.stem: Listen. Which phrase did you hear?
questions.explanation: "Gochisōsama deshita", said after a meal. いただきます is said before the meal; the other two are good night and "I'm off".

questions.stem: Listen. Which phrase did you hear?
questions.explanation: "Oyasuminasai", good night. おかえりなさい and ごめんなさい share the ending なさい but start differently, and おはようございます is good morning.

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear, in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: "Sumimasen": すみません. In fast speech it can sound like すいません, but the standard spelling is すみません. End with nn for ん.

questions.stem: Match each word or phrase to its meaning.
questions.explanation: ありがとう thanks (casual), すみません excuse me or sorry, ただいま I'm home, はい yes, いいえ no. Good night would be おやすみなさい.

questions.stem: Mr Smith is meeting his new neighbour. How should he finish introducing himself?
choices: スミスさんです。よろしく おねがいします。
スミスです。いただきます。
スミスさんです。さようなら。
スミスです。よろしく おねがいします。
questions.explanation: Give your name with です and finish with よろしく おねがいします. さん is a polite title for other people, never for yourself, and いただきます is only for meals.

glossary.definition: Chinese characters used only for their sound, ignoring their meaning, to write Japanese words, names and poems; for example, {也|や} and {麻|ま} together spell やま. Named after the 8th-century poetry collection, the Man'yōshū. Both hiragana and katakana grew out of them.
A fast, flowing style of brush writing in which a character's strokes run together into a few curves. Hiragana came from man'yōgana written in this style and simplified further.
The period of Japanese history from 794 to 1185, named after its capital Heian-kyō (today's Kyoto). Hiragana became a full writing system then, with classics such as The Tale of Genji written in it.
"Women's hand": an old name for hiragana writing, which in the Heian period was linked with women at court, while writing in Chinese characters was thought of as men's writing.
A sentence or poem that uses every letter of a writing system at least once. The iroha is a perfect pangram: it uses each of its 47 kana exactly once.

A poem, known since at least the 11th century, that uses each of the 47 kana of its time exactly once (ん is not part of it). For centuries it was the usual order for lists and dictionaries, and it still labels sub-items (イ, ロ, ハ) and musical notes.
The traditional kana spelling, based on how words were written in classical texts, used until 1946: けふ for きょう (today), こゑ for こえ (voice), with ゐ and ゑ.
The kana spelling standard issued in 1946 (revised in 1986), which spells words largely as they are pronounced today. It dropped ゐ and ゑ but kept は, へ and を for the particles.

"Variant kana": hiragana shapes from other source kanji that were set aside in 1900, when one shape per sound was fixed for schools. They survive in calligraphy, old documents and traditional shop signs, and were added to Unicode in 2017.
The step in Japanese typing where the input software turns the kana you typed into kanji (or katakana), usually with the space bar, and you accept the result with Enter.
One of the possible spellings the input software offers when you convert, such as {橋|はし}, {箸|はし} and {端|はし} for はし. Press Space again to move through the list.
Suggestions of whole words and kanji that appear above a phone keyboard (and in some computer input software) while you type, so you can choose a word after typing only its first kana.
Typing Japanese by entering romaji on an ordinary keyboard, which the input software turns into kana (k + a gives か). The most common way to type Japanese on a computer.
Typing Japanese with the kana printed on the keys of a Japanese keyboard, one key press per kana. Faster once learned, but used by fewer people than romaji input.
Characters that fill a whole square of the Japanese text grid: all normal kana and kanji, and the wide letters and digits (ＡＢＣ１２３) sometimes used in Japanese text.
Characters that take half a square: ordinary English letters and digits, and a narrow form of katakana (ｶﾀｶﾅ) found on receipts and in old computer systems. Use full-width kana in normal writing.
The usual Japanese phone keyboard: a grid like an old phone's number pad, with one key for each row of the gojūon table (あ, か, さ … わ), plus keys for ゛゜ and small kana and for punctuation.
Choosing a kana on the 12-key layout by tapping a key repeatedly: one tap of あ gives あ, two give い, three give う, and so on.
Choosing a kana on the 12-key layout by touching a key and sliding: a tap gives the a-sound, and left, up, right and down give the i, u, e and o sounds of that row.
The main Japanese book type: thin horizontal strokes, thicker vertical strokes and small triangular tips at stroke ends. Used for books, newspapers and long text; comparable to a serif typeface.
Japanese type with strokes of even thickness and plain ends, used for signs, headings, labels and screens; comparable to a sans-serif typeface.
Gothic type with rounded stroke ends, giving a soft, friendly look; common on children's materials, packaging and casual signs.
"Textbook style": a typeface that imitates careful handwriting stroke for stroke, used in Japanese school textbooks so that children read the same shapes they write.
Japanese manuscript paper printed with a grid of squares, one square for each character, including small kana, ー and punctuation. Used in schools for essays.
A stroke ending in which the pen stops firmly and lifts straight off, giving a blunt end.
A stroke ending in which the pen turns sharply and flicks off, often toward the next stroke, as at the end of the first stroke of い.
A stroke ending in which the pen keeps moving as it lifts, so the stroke thins to a point, as at the end of ノ.

The rounded Japanese script of 46 basic kana (plus voiced forms and combinations). It writes grammar endings, small grammar words, words without a common kanji, and anything meant for children or beginners: ねこ (neko, cat), ありがとう (arigatō, thank you).

The angular Japanese script that spells the same sounds as hiragana. It is used mainly for words borrowed from other languages, foreign names, sound effects and emphasis: コーヒー (kōhī, coffee). Module 2 teaches it.

Characters borrowed from Chinese, each with a meaning and one or more readings, such as {山|やま} (yama, mountain). Most Japanese nouns, verbs and adjectives are written with kanji plus hiragana endings. This course writes everything in kana; kanji start in the N5 course.
The two Japanese syllable scripts, hiragana and katakana, together. Each kana stands for a sound (one beat), not a meaning: か is "ka", カ is "ka" too.

Japanese written in the Latin alphabet: sushi, Tōkyō, arigatō. It is used on signs for visitors and for typing on a computer, but ordinary Japanese is not read in romaji. Common spellings follow the Hepburn system (shi, chi, tsu, fu), with ō or ou for long vowels.
Small kana printed above (or, in vertical text, beside) a kanji to show how it is read: {毎朝|まいあさ}. Children's books, learner texts and difficult or unusual kanji use it.

One beat of Japanese rhythm. Each ordinary kana is one mora, and so are ん, small っ and the second half of a long vowel; a combination such as きゃ is also one. Morae take about the same time each: にほん (ni-ho-n) has three, がっこう (ga-k-ko-u) has four.

The fixed order and direction in which the strokes of a kana (or kanji) are written. In general: top before bottom, left before right, horizontals left to right, verticals top to bottom. Following it keeps shapes balanced and makes handwriting easy to read.

"Fifty sounds": the table that orders the kana, with the vowels a, i, u, e, o across and the rows あ, か, さ, た, な, は, ま, や, ら, わ down. Japanese dictionaries and lists are sorted in this order. The modern table has 46 basic kana because some places are empty.

A sound made with the vocal cords vibrating, which you can feel as a buzz at the throat: z, g, d, b are voiced; s, k, t, p are voiceless. In kana, the dakuten ゛ turns a voiceless consonant into its voiced partner: か ka → が ga.
The mark ゛, two short strokes at the top right of a kana, written last. It makes the consonant voiced: k → g (が), s → z (ざ, じ ji), t → d (だ; ぢ ji, づ zu), h → b (ば).
The small circle ゜ at the top right of a は-row kana, written last. It gives the p sound: ぱ pa, ぴ pi, ぷ pu, ぺ pe, ぽ po.

The voicing of the first consonant of the second part of a compound word: ひと + ひと → ひとびと (hitobito, people), はな + ひ → はなび (hanabi, fireworks), はな + ち → はなぢ (hanaji, nosebleed). It is common but not predictable, so each word is learned as it comes.
A one-beat combination of an "i"-column kana and a small ゃ, ゅ or ょ: きゃ (kya), しゅ (shu), ちょ (cho). Hiragana has 33. Written full size, the same kana make two beats: きや is ki-ya, きゃ is kya.
The small っ, a one-beat pause in which the next consonant is held before it is released. Romaji doubles that consonant: きって (kitte, stamp) has three beats, きて (kite) two.

A vowel held for two beats. In hiragana it is written with a second vowel kana: ああ, いい, うう, usually えい for a long e and おう for a long o (おおきい and a few other words use おお). Length changes meaning: おばさん (obasan, aunt), おばあさん (obāsan, grandmother).

A word Japanese has borrowed from another language, mostly English but also Portuguese, Dutch, French, German and others. Gairaigo are usually written in katakana: アイス (ice cream), カメラ (camera), パン (bread, from Portuguese).

Words that imitate a sound (ニャー, miaow) or describe a movement, state or feeling (ドキドキ, a pounding heart; ピョンピョン, hopping). Japanese has thousands of them; comics and advertising often write them in katakana.

The dash ー that lengthens the vowel before it by one beat, used mainly in katakana: コーヒー (kōhī, coffee), ケーキ (kēki, cake). It is horizontal in horizontal text and vertical in vertical text. Type it with the - key.

Katakana spellings for sounds that the basic table lacks, made with a small ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ (or with ヴ): ファ (fa), ティ (ti), ウェ (we), シェ (she), ツァ (tsa). Each pair is one beat. Newer loanwords and foreign names use them: フォーク (fork), パーティー (party).
A vowel added to a borrowed word so that a consonant can stand as a Japanese beat. Usually u (milk → ミルク), o after t and d (test → テスト, bed → ベッド), and i after ch and j (match → マッチ, bridge → ブリッジ).

Words made in Japan from English parts, or English words given a new meaning, that English speakers would not recognise: リモコン (remote control), ジェットコースター (roller coaster), サラリーマン (office worker), マンション (an apartment building, not a mansion).

A short word, usually one or two kana, that comes right after another word and shows its job in the sentence: は marks the topic, を the object, へ the direction, か a question. Particles follow the word they belong to, whereas English prepositions come before theirs (がっこうへ, "to school").
What a sentence is about, marked in Japanese by the particle は after it: わたしは がくせいです (as for me, I am a student). Once the topic is clear it is usually left out of the following sentences.
The particle は, which marks the topic of a sentence. It is written は but read "wa". Inside ordinary words は is still read "ha" (はな, flower).
The thing an action is done to: in "I drink water", water is the object. Japanese marks it with the particle を, read "o" and typed wo: みずを のみます.

Writing with a space between each word or chunk (a word and its particles), as in picture books for small children written mostly in hiragana. Ordinary Japanese has no spaces; this course adds one after each particle to help beginners.
The Japanese full stop 。, a small hollow circle at the end of a sentence, including a question ending in か. Its everyday name is まる (circle). In vertical text it sits in the top right of its square.
The Japanese comma 、, a short slanted tick marking a pause inside a sentence: はい、がくせいです. Its everyday name is てん (dot). Japanese writers use it more freely than English writers use commas.

The brackets 「 」 used as Japanese quotation marks, for speech, thoughts, and names or terms being pointed out. A quote is usually followed by と いいました (said). The full stop of the quoted sentence is usually left out before the closing 」.
The double brackets 『 』, used for a quotation inside a quotation and for the titles of books, films and albums: 『こころ』.
The dot ・ in the middle of its square. It separates the parts of a foreign name written in katakana (ジョン・スミス) and short items in a list (コーヒー・こうちゃ).
The mark 〜, meaning "from … to" in a range (10:00〜20:00). In casual messages it also stretches a sound out (ありがと〜). Not to be confused with ー, which lengthens a vowel inside a word.
A mark that repeats the character before it. For kana it is ゝ (ゞ to repeat it voiced; ヽ and ヾ in katakana): いすゞ is read いすず. Today it is mostly seen in older texts and a few names.
Japanese written in horizontal lines from left to right, with each new line below the last, as in English. Used on websites and phones, in science and maths books, most textbooks and forms.

Japanese written in columns from top to bottom, with the columns running from right to left, so reading starts at the top right. Used in novels, newspapers and manga. In vertical text ー, 「」 and 〜 turn to run downward, and 。、 and small kana move to the top right of their squares.

references.title: Hiragana chart
references.body:
## The 46 basic hiragana (gojūon)

Read across for a row, down for a vowel column. Empty cells are sounds modern Japanese doesn't
have.

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| – | あ a | い i | う u | え e | お o |
| k | か ka | き ki | く ku | け ke | こ ko |
| s | さ sa | し shi | す su | せ se | そ so |
| t | た ta | ち chi | つ tsu | て te | と to |
| n | な na | に ni | ぬ nu | ね ne | の no |
| h | は ha | ひ hi | ふ fu | へ he | ほ ho |
| m | ま ma | み mi | む mu | め me | も mo |
| y | や ya | | ゆ yu | | よ yo |
| r | ら ra | り ri | る ru | れ re | ろ ro |
| w | わ wa | | | | を o (wo) |
| | ん n | | | | |

As particles, は is read wa, へ is read e and を is read o.

## Voiced kana: ゛ (dakuten) and ゜ (handakuten)

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| g | が ga | ぎ gi | ぐ gu | げ ge | ご go |
| z | ざ za | じ ji | ず zu | ぜ ze | ぞ zo |
| d | だ da | ぢ ji | づ zu | で de | ど do |
| b | ば ba | び bi | ぶ bu | べ be | ぼ bo |
| p | ぱ pa | ぴ pi | ぷ pu | ぺ pe | ぽ po |

ぢ and づ sound like じ and ず. Use them only when ち or つ is voiced in a compound (はなぢ,
てづくり) or repeated (ちぢむ, つづく); otherwise write じ and ず.

## Combinations (yōon)

An "i"-column kana plus a small ゃ, ゅ or ょ: one beat.

| | ゃ | ゅ | ょ |
|---|---|---|---|
| k | きゃ kya | きゅ kyu | きょ kyo |
| s | しゃ sha | しゅ shu | しょ sho |
| t | ちゃ cha | ちゅ chu | ちょ cho |
| n | にゃ nya | にゅ nyu | にょ nyo |
| h | ひゃ hya | ひゅ hyu | ひょ hyo |
| m | みゃ mya | みゅ myu | みょ myo |
| r | りゃ rya | りゅ ryu | りょ ryo |
| g | ぎゃ gya | ぎゅ gyu | ぎょ gyo |
| z/j | じゃ ja | じゅ ju | じょ jo |
| b | びゃ bya | びゅ byu | びょ byo |
| p | ぴゃ pya | ぴゅ pyu | ぴょ pyo |

## Small っ and long vowels

| Spelling | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| っ (small) | a one-beat pause before the next consonant; romaji doubles it | きって (kitte) — stamp |
| ああ | long a | おかあさん (okāsan) — mother |
| いい | long i | おじいさん (ojīsan) — grandfather |
| うう | long u | くうき (kūki) — air |
| えい, ええ | long e (えい is the usual spelling) | せんせい (sensei) — teacher; おねえさん (onēsan) — older sister |
| おう, おお | long o (おう is the usual spelling) | がっこう (gakkō) — school; おおきい (ōkii) — big |

## Stroke counts

Standard school forms, written by hand. Some printed fonts join strokes (き, さ, り) or split
them (そ), so count from handwriting, not from print.

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| – | あ 3 | い 2 | う 2 | え 2 | お 3 |
| k | か 3 | き 4 | く 1 | け 3 | こ 2 |
| s | さ 3 | し 1 | す 2 | せ 3 | そ 1 |
| t | た 4 | ち 2 | つ 1 | て 1 | と 2 |
| n | な 4 | に 3 | ぬ 2 | ね 2 | の 1 |
| h | は 3 | ひ 1 | ふ 4 | へ 1 | ほ 4 |
| m | ま 3 | み 2 | む 3 | め 2 | も 3 |
| y | や 3 | | ゆ 2 | | よ 2 |
| r | ら 2 | り 2 | る 1 | れ 2 | ろ 1 |
| w | わ 2 | | | | を 3 |
| | ん 1 | | | | |

゛ adds two strokes and ゜ one, always written last at the top right.

## Typing in this app

| To get | Type |
|---|---|
| し, ち, つ, ふ | shi or si, chi or ti, tsu or tu, fu or hu |
| じ, ぢ, づ | ji or zi, di, du |
| を | wo |
| ん | nn, or n before a consonant; n' before a vowel or y (kin'en → きんえん) |
| っ | double the next consonant (kitte, gakkou, matcha); alone: xtu or ltu |
| small ゃ ゅ ょ | as part of a syllable (kya, sho, ju); alone: xya, xyu, xyo |
| long vowels | as spelled in kana (okaasan, sensei, gakkou, ookii) |

references.title: Katakana chart
references.body:
## Basic katakana

Read across: each row is one consonant, each column one vowel. The hiragana partner is in
brackets.

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | ア a (あ) | イ i (い) | ウ u (う) | エ e (え) | オ o (お) |
| k | カ ka (か) | キ ki (き) | ク ku (く) | ケ ke (け) | コ ko (こ) |
| s | サ sa (さ) | シ shi (し) | ス su (す) | セ se (せ) | ソ so (そ) |
| t | タ ta (た) | チ chi (ち) | ツ tsu (つ) | テ te (て) | ト to (と) |
| n | ナ na (な) | ニ ni (に) | ヌ nu (ぬ) | ネ ne (ね) | ノ no (の) |
| h | ハ ha (は) | ヒ hi (ひ) | フ fu (ふ) | ヘ he (へ) | ホ ho (ほ) |
| m | マ ma (ま) | ミ mi (み) | ム mu (む) | メ me (め) | モ mo (も) |
| y | ヤ ya (や) | | ユ yu (ゆ) | | ヨ yo (よ) |
| r | ラ ra (ら) | リ ri (り) | ル ru (る) | レ re (れ) | ロ ro (ろ) |
| w | ワ wa (わ) | | | | ヲ o (を) |
| | ン n (ん) | | | | |

## Voiced katakana (゛ and ゜)

| | a | i | u | e | o |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| g | ガ ga | ギ gi | グ gu | ゲ ge | ゴ go |
| z | ザ za | ジ ji | ズ zu | ゼ ze | ゾ zo |
| d | ダ da | ヂ ji | ヅ zu | デ de | ド do |
| b | バ ba | ビ bi | ブ bu | ベ be | ボ bo |
| p | パ pa | ピ pi | プ pu | ペ pe | ポ po |
| v | | | ヴ vu | | |

ヂ and ヅ are very rare; loanwords write "ji" and "zu" as ジ and ズ.

## Combinations (small ャ ュ ョ)

| | ya | yu | yo |
|---|---|---|---|
| k | キャ kya | キュ kyu | キョ kyo |
| s | シャ sha | シュ shu | ショ sho |
| t | チャ cha | チュ chu | チョ cho |
| n | ニャ nya | ニュ nyu | ニョ nyo |
| h | ヒャ hya | ヒュ hyu | ヒョ hyo |
| m | ミャ mya | ミュ myu | ミョ myo |
| r | リャ rya | リュ ryu | リョ ryo |
| g | ギャ gya | ギュ gyu | ギョ gyo |
| j | ジャ ja | ジュ ju | ジョ jo |
| b | ビャ bya | ビュ byu | ビョ byo |
| p | ピャ pya | ピュ pyu | ピョ pyo |

## Loanword sounds (small ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ)

| Sound | Katakana | Example |
|---|---|---|
| fa fi fe fo | ファ フィ フェ フォ | ファン (fan), フォーク (fork) |
| ti di | ティ ディ | パーティー (party), ディナー (dinner) |
| tu du | トゥ ドゥ | タトゥー (tattoo), ヒンドゥー (Hindu) |
| dyu | デュ | デュエット (duet) |
| wi we wo | ウィ ウェ ウォ | ウィーン (Vienna), ウェブサイト (website), ウォーキング (walking) |
| va vi vu ve vo | ヴァ ヴィ ヴ ヴェ ヴォ | ヴァイオリン (violin; usually バイオリン) |
| she je che | シェ ジェ チェ | シェフ (chef), ジェットコースター (roller coaster), チェス (chess) |
| tsa tsi tse tso | ツァ ツィ ツェ ツォ | モーツァルト (Mozart) |

## Long vowels and small ッ

| Mark | What it does | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ー | holds the vowel before it for one more beat (vertical in vertical text) | コーヒー (coffee), ビール (beer) vs ビル (building) |
| ッ | a one-beat pause before the next consonant | ベッド (bed), チケット (ticket), カップ (cup) |

## Fitting English words to Japanese

| Pattern | Examples |
|---|---|
| a vowel after a lone consonant: usually u | milk → ミルク, golf → ゴルフ |
| o after t and d | test → テスト, bed → ベッド |
| i after ch and j | match → マッチ, orange → オレンジ |
| l and r both use the ラ row | light, right → ライト |
| final "er", "ar", "or" → ー | computer → コンピューター, doctor → ドクター |
| th → サ or ザ row | thank you → サンキュー, mother → マザー |
| v → バ row (sometimes ヴ) | video → ビデオ |
| -tion → ション | station → ステーション |

## Lookalikes

| Pair | How to tell them apart |
|---|---|
| シ shi / ツ tsu | シ: short strokes stacked on the left, long stroke rises; ツ: short strokes along the top, long stroke falls |
| ン n / ソ so | ン: long stroke rises from the bottom left; ソ: falls from the top right |
| ク ku / ケ ke / タ ta | ケ has a flat second stroke; タ has a stroke inside |
| フ fu / ワ wa / ウ u | ワ = フ plus a stroke on the left; ウ = ワ plus a dot on top |
| コ ko / ユ yu / ヨ yo | ユ's bottom line sticks out; ヨ has a middle line |
| ス su / ヌ nu | ヌ's second stroke crosses the sweep |
| ナ na / メ me | ナ has a horizontal; メ doesn't |
| マ ma / ア a | マ's inner stroke goes down to the right; ア's down to the left |
| チ chi / テ te | チ starts with a slant; テ with a flat line |

## Typing (CAPITALS give katakana)

| Type | Get | Type | Get |
|---|---|---|---|
| KOKOA | ココア | BEDDO | ベッド |
| KO-HI- | コーヒー | KYANPU | キャンプ |
| MERONN | メロン | PA-THI- | パーティー |
| FO-KU | フォーク | UXO-KINGU | ウォーキング |

references.title: Japanese punctuation and particles
references.body:
## Punctuation marks

Every mark fills one full square, like a kana. No extra space is typed after 。 or 、.

| Mark | Name | Everyday name | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 。 | kuten | まる | ends a sentence (also a question ending in か) | がくせいです。 |
| 、 | tōten | てん | a pause inside a sentence; between list items | はい、そうです。 |
| 「 」 | kagikakko | かぎかっこ | quotes speech or thought; points out a name or term | 「おはよう」と いいました。 |
| 『 』 | nijūkagikakko | にじゅうかぎかっこ | a quote inside a quote; titles of books and films | 『こころ』を よみました。 |
| ・ | nakaguro | なかぐろ | between parts of a foreign name; between short list items | ジョン・スミス |
| 〜 | wave dash | なみダッシュ | "from … to" in ranges; a stretched sound in casual messages | 10:00〜20:00 |
| ？ | question mark | はてなマーク | questions in everyday writing, especially without か | ゆきさんは？ |
| ！ | exclamation mark | びっくりマーク | excitement, in everyday writing | いいですね！ |
| ： | colon | コロン | after a label on a form or sign | なまえ：ジョン・スミス |
| …… | ellipsis | てんてん | trailing off; usually two three-dot marks in a row | ええと…… |
| ゝ ゞ | iteration mark | おどりじ | repeats the kana before it (voiced: ゞ); old texts and names | いすゞ (いすず) |

ー (the long-vowel mark) is part of a word, not punctuation: コーヒー.

## Rules worth remembering

- Formal writing (letters, essays, newspapers) ends questions with か。 and uses ？ and ！
  rarely. Messages, manga and ads use them freely.
- After ？ or ！ in the middle of a line, leave one full-width space before the next sentence.
- The 。 of a quoted sentence is usually left out before 」: 「ありがとう」と いいました。
- 「」 come first; 『』 go inside them.
- Some scientific and official documents written left to right use ， and ． in place of 、 and 。.

## Horizontal and vertical writing

| | Yokogaki (horizontal) | Tategaki (vertical) |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | left to right, lines downward | top to bottom, columns right to left |
| Start reading | top left | top right |
| Book opens | on the left | on the right |
| 。 and 、 | bottom left of the square | top right of the square |
| Small kana (ゃ ゅ ょ っ) | bottom left of the square | top right of the square |
| ー | horizontal line | vertical line |
| 「 」 | 「 」 | turned: ﹁ at the top, ﹂ at the bottom |
| 〜 | horizontal wave | vertical wave |
| Typical use | websites, phones, science books, forms | novels, newspapers, manga |

Kana and kanji stay upright in both.

## The three particles with special readings

| Particle | Read | Typed | Job | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| は | wa | ha | topic: "as for …" | わたしは がくせいです。 |
| へ | e | he | direction: "to, toward" | がっこうへ いきます。 |
| を | o | wo | object: the thing acted on | みずを のみます。 |

- Inside ordinary words は is "ha" and へ is "he" (はな, へや). を appears only as the particle.
- こんにちは and こんばんは end in the particle は, so they are written with は and read "wa".
- Every other particle is read as written: か (question), も (also), と (quoting; and), で (at),
  に (to, at), の (of, 's), ね (isn't it?), よ (you know).
- At the top of a note, name + へ is "To …"; at the end, name + より is "From …".

## Sentence shape

| Topic | Place or object | Verb or です |
|---|---|---|
| わたしは | がっこうへ | いきます。 |
| わたしは | みずを | のみます。 |
| わたしは | がくせい | です。 |

The verb (or です) comes last. Add か to ask a question: がくせいですか。 Real Japanese has no
spaces; this course leaves one after each particle.
